title: Four Palestinians killed as Israeli settlers raid occupied West Bank town
summary: One Israeli was also killed near town of Tal in Nablus, according to Israel's Magen David Adom rescue services.
full_text:
Four Palestinians killed as Israeli settlers raid occupied West Bank town
One Israeli was also killed near town of Tal in Nablus, according to Israel’s Magen David Adom rescue services.
Four Palestinians have been killed in an attack by Israeli forces and settlers southwest of Nablus in the occupied West Bank.
Four other Palestinians were injured in the attack on the town of Tal, “three of them critically”, the Palestinian Ministry of Health said in a statement on Friday.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items- list 1 of 3US court affirms release of pro-Palestine scholar as legal battle continues
- list 2 of 3Israel carries out blasts across south Lebanon despite ‘ceasefire’ deal
- list 3 of 3Trillion dollar US defence bill would deepen military ties with Israel
Israeli health officials separately reported that one Israeli settler was killed and others injured in the area.
The town of Tal, which is close to the illegal Israeli settlement of Havat Gilad, was attacked by Israeli settlers earlier on Friday, local and security sources said. The settlers opened live fire as Palestinians tried to protect their homes.
Essam Saifi, a local leader in the Palestinian Fatah party from Tal, told the Reuters news agency in a phone call that about 25 to 30 Israeli settlers initially attacked the eastern area of the town and tried to break into two houses there. The residents came out to confront them and the settlers opened fire.
Half an hour later, Saifi said, the Israelis returned and attacked the western part of the town, striking a child with a weapon. This caused chaos, and the Israeli military arrived and started shooting, along with the settlers, he added.
The Israeli army, however, said it had dispatched troops to the area near the Havat Gilad following what it called “an attack on Israelis hiking in the area”.
The military claimed a Palestinian had stolen a weapon from local security personnel and fired at the Israeli settlers.
According to Israel’s Magen David Adom (MDA) rescue services, one Israeli was killed in the area and two wounded people were evacuated by helicopter.
Reporting from Nablus, Al Jazeera’s Nida Ibrahim said Friday’s incident took place after Israeli settlers stormed Tal under the “pretext that they were hiking in the area”.
“Given what we’ve been seeing time and again in these attacks, it’s the settlers who are armed, who are provoking Palestinians and stealing their land. Sometimes we see these settlers pull up in caravans and start putting up temporary tents that later become illegal Israeli settlements,” Ibrahim said.
After the incident, Israeli forces imposed a security cordon around Nablus and Tal.
“In these situations, the Israeli army generally prevents the injured Palestinians from accessing medical help by setting up siege-like conditions around the city,” Ibrahim said. “And that’s what we’re seeing right now, as all checkpoints leading to Tal have been closed.”
‘A renewed image of the ongoing Nakba’
According to the Palestinian health ministry, the killings in Tal bring the toll to 86 Palestinians killed by Israelis across the West Bank since the beginning of the year, including 21 shot by settlers.
The Palestinian foreign ministry condemned the killing of Palestinians by settlers in the “strongest terms”.
“The Ministry affirms that this massacre represents a renewed image of the ongoing Nakba to which our Palestinian people are subjected, and reflects the integration of crimes and roles and the deliberate escalation of these coordinated crimes between the occupation authorities and their forces and settler gangs,” it said in a post on X on Friday.
Meanwhile in Israel, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu pledged to respond firmly after an Israeli was killed near Tal, and said he was convening an emergency meeting to discuss a response.
Far-right Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich also called on the army to act with an “iron fist” against the Palestinian town and its surroundings where the Israeli died.
“The people of the farms and the heroic settlement pioneers are the defensive wall of the State of Israel. We will continue to strengthen and honour them for their steadfast stand for our existence,” he said in a post on X.

title: Germany appoint Klopp as ex-Liverpool coach sought to lift World Cup blues
summary: Jurgen Klopp last coached in 2024 at Liverpool but was Red Bull's head of global football, leading Leipzig and New York.
full_text:
Germany appoint Klopp as ex-Liverpool coach sought to lift World Cup blues
Jurgen Klopp last coached in 2024 at Liverpool but was Red Bull’s head of global football, leading Leipzig and New York.
Germany has hired Jurgen Klopp to coach its national team, giving the ex-Liverpool manager a daunting task to turn around the fortunes of a squad which failed yet again at the World Cup.
Klopp, famed for his success during stints as coach at Borussia Dortmund and especially Liverpool, has been in talks with the German Football Association (DFB) about trying to lead Germany, long a football powerhouse, back to prominence.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items- list 1 of 4Sooryavanshi 18-ball fifty tops ‘tremendous’ India T20 win against Zimbabwe
- list 2 of 4A tournament of contradictions: What did we learn at World Cup 2026?
- list 3 of 4How a 64-team World Cup could transform football’s economics
- list 4 of 4Five key takeaways from FIFA World Cup 2026
“It’s a big honour to be sitting here,” Klopp said. “I had an idea how big the job of national team coach is, but when you’re being directly connected with it, you really feel the scale and the responsibility even more.”
Citing fatigue, Klopp stepped down from the Liverpool job in 2024. He was “recharged” in comments while in talks over the Germany job.
Klopp said on Friday he would be prepared to leave without any severance pay if it doesn’t work out, and threatened to resign if the media don’t “leave my family in peace”.
The 59-year-old is among the most decorated football coaches of his generation and has signed a contract with Germany that runs until 2030, the date of the next World Cup.
Since 2025, Klopp has been under contract with Austrian energy drink maker Red Bull as “Head of Global Soccer”, where he oversees the football clubs affiliated with the company such as RB Leipzig, Red Bull Salzburg and the New York Red Bulls.
German federation president Bernd Neuendorf said there wouldn’t be a typical release fee paid to Red Bull for Klopp. Instead, the federation will pay one million euros ($1.14m) to the Red Bull-linked Wings for Life charity foundation, which supports research into spinal cord injuries.
They have also agreed to hold three national team games in the eastern city of Leipzig, where Red Bull backs the city’s Bundesliga club team.
The DFB dismissed former head coach Julian Nagelsmann after Germany crashed out of this summer’s World Cup in disappointing fashion, losing to Paraguay on penalties in the round of 32.
That means the German men’s team has suffered three straight World Cup debacles since winning their fourth title in 2014.
Germany made first-round exits in both 2018 and 2022. They have won just one knockout match at the past five major tournaments, reaching the quarterfinal as hosts at Euro 2024.
Klopp had successful coaching tenures at German clubs Mainz, where he was a player for more than a decade, and then Dortmund.
He then became a legend at Liverpool, where he coached the English side to a league title in 2020, ending a 30-year drought. He also led the club to a Champions League triumph, their sixth European crown.
Klopp faces a tough introduction to his first national team job with four Nations League games in 11 days against the Netherlands, Greece and Serbia in late September and early October.

title: Philippines accuses China of using water cannon on vessels for second day
summary: The Philippine Coast Guard says 12 China Coast Guard vessels and three Chinese maritime militia vessels were involved.
full_text:
Philippines accuses China of using water cannon on vessels for second day
The Philippine Coast Guard says 12 China Coast Guard vessels and three Chinese maritime militia vessels were involved.
Tensions between China and the Philippines are continuing after Manila’s coastguard accused its Chinese counterpart of firing a water cannon at government vessels near a disputed shoal for the second day.
The Philippine Coast Guard said on Friday that a Chinese vessel at the Scarborough Shoal, in the Philippines’ exclusive economic zone, came within about seven metres (23 feet) of a Philippine fisheries boat, creating a “serious risk of collision”.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items- list 1 of 3AI, China, ‘dark factories’ and the future of the US auto industry
- list 2 of 3How shipping insurance rates are rising, as Hormuz, Bab al-Mandeb shut down
- list 3 of 3Trump imposes new double-digit tariffs on dozens of countries
“The PCG strongly condemns the dangerous and unprofessional actions of the China Coast Guard,” spokesperson Jay Tarriela said in a statement.
Tarriela added that the shoal was a traditional fishing ground of Filipinos, “whose rights cannot be lawfully impeded by any foreign power”.
The coastguard added that 12 China Coast Guard vessels and three Chinese maritime militia vessels were involved in the incident, and water cannon hit two Philippine ships, while two others had to make dangerous manoeuvres, risking collisions.
The vessels were delivering fuel subsidies to Filipino fishermen and conducting routine patrols at the Scarborough Shoal, also known to locals as Bajo de Masinloc, which lies within the Philippines’ exclusive economic zone.
Earlier on Friday, the China Coast Guard said it had imposed “control measures” on several Philippine vessels it claimed were operating illegally in waters around the shoal.
In a more detailed statement, it accused the Philippines of organising several government and coastguard vessels, along with a large number of fishing vessels, to “illegally gather” in the waters.
It said it had taken legal measures to warn, block and deploy water cannon after the official vessels from the Philippines ignored those measures from the coast guard and “insisted on intruding.”
A similar incident took place on Thursday.
On Friday, China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said the coastguard’s actions were “reasonable, lawful and beyond reproach.”
“The Philippine side should immediately stop the infringement, provocation and hype,” ministry spokesperson Lin Jian said at a regular briefing.
The two incidents at Scarborough Shoal, the South China Sea’s most contested area, came after a confrontation on Monday at the disputed Second Thomas Shoal, 650km (400 miles) away from where Manila said a Filipino sailor was injured after being hit with a baton by Chinese coastguard personnel.
Beijing had accused the Philippine Navy of ignoring warnings and of trying to ram a Chinese patrol boat. Both countries have summoned each other’s ambassadors in protest.
But China has long occupied the Scarborough Shoal, deploying an armada of coastguard ships throughout the South China Sea.
Beijing also claims sovereignty over nearly all of the waterway, including parts of the Exclusive Economic Zone of Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines and Vietnam.
The tensions also come as Southeast Asian foreign ministers finished regional meetings in Manila that were attended by Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi and United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who called Beijing’s actions in the sea “disturbing”, reaffirming support for the Philippines, with which the US has a defence treaty.

title: Trump’s latest ‘forced labour tariffs’: Who’s been hit, how badly?
summary: Countries accounting for almost all of the US's trade have been hit with tariffs between 10 and 12.5 percent.
full_text:
Trump’s latest ‘forced labour tariffs’: Who’s been hit, how badly?
Countries accounting for almost all of the US’s trade have been hit with tariffs between 10 and 12.5 percent.
US President Donald Trump has imposed new double-digit tariffs on dozens of trading partners of the United States.
This announcement came just as the clock ran out on Friday on stopgap levies he announced after a stinging defeat at the Supreme Court.
What was announced?
The US has slapped levies of 10 to 12.5 percent on imports from 60 countries accounting for 99 percent of US imports, accusing them of inadequately enforcing bans on goods produced by forced labour.
“The United States has had a forced labor import ban for nearly a century, and rigorously enforces it; it’s well past time for our trading partners to do the same,” US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said in a statement on Thursday.
“Today’s action will begin to correct what is both a human rights abuse and distortive trade practice to improve the welfare of workers everywhere.”
When will these new tariffs take effect?
The new tariffs took effect just as the temporary 10 percent worldwide tariffs expired at 12:01am on Friday in Washington, DC (04:01 GMT). Trump had turned to the temporary levies after the Supreme Court struck down his biggest and boldest tariffs in February.
Which countries were hit by these tariffs?
In the Federal Register notice, where the tariffs were announced, there were details of the countries hit by the tariffs.
These countries and economies are: Algeria; Angola; Argentina; Australia; the Bahamas; Bahrain; Bangladesh; Brazil; Cambodia; Chile; China, People’s Republic of; Colombia; Costa Rica; Dominican Republic; Egypt; El Salvador; Guatemala; Guyana; Honduras; Hong Kong, China; India; Iraq; Israel; Japan; Jordan; Kazakhstan; Kuwait; Libya; Malaysia; Morocco; New Zealand; Nicaragua; Nigeria; Norway; Oman; Peru; the Philippines; Qatar; Russia; Saudi Arabia; Singapore; South Africa; South Korea; Sri Lanka; Switzerland; Taiwan; Thailand; Trinidad and Tobago; Turkiye; United Arab Emirates; United Kingdom; Uruguay; Venezuela; Vietnam; Canada; Ecuador; the European Union; Indonesia; Mexico; and Pakistan.
What is the legal basis for these tariffs?
Trump is tapping more durable tariffs under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which permits the president to impose import taxes and other sanctions against countries found to engage in “unjustifiable”, “unreasonable”, or “discriminatory” trade practices.
Trump used Section 301 to impose major tariffs on China in his first term, and they survived court challenges.
Trump, who argues that high tariffs will revive US manufacturing, last year overturned decades of US policy that favoured lower tariffs and freer trade.
Invoking the 1977 International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), he imposed double-digit tariffs on imports from almost every country, saying that the US’s longstanding trade deficit amounted to a national emergency.
But the Supreme Court ruled that IEEPA did not authorise tariffs. The decision forced the Trump administration to pay refunds to importers that had paid the levies.
In response, Trump announced 10 percent worldwide tariffs under Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974. But he can only use Section 122 levies for 150 days, and the time ran out at the start of Friday.
John Diamond, director of the Center for Tax and Budget Policy at the Baker Institute, said the administration was looking for a new authority to replace the expiring tariffs and decided to use Section 301.
“It’s a little bit ridiculous to think that over 60 major trading partners, including countries in the EU, are really relying on that much forced labour. It’s kind of hard to believe,” Diamond told Al Jazeera. “But I don’t think the courts will want to overrule these tariffs as they did the IEEPA tariffs.”
Why have some been charged 10 percent, others 12.5 percent?
Countries that have laws against the import of products made using forced labour, including India, Pakistan and Argentina, have been hit with a 10 percent tariff.
Nations without such laws, including China and the United Kingdom, have been slapped with a 12.5 percent tariff.
What’s next?
Additional tariffs on the basis of Section 301 are likely coming: Greer’s office has launched a probe into whether 16 countries, accounting for 70 percent of US imports, have overproduced goods, pushing down prices and putting US companies at a disadvantage in global markets.
The administration has yet to complete that investigation.

title: Oil surges to $100 per barrel. And, Trump imposes a new round of tariffs
summary: Oil surged to $100 per barrel after Iran-backed Houthi rebels attacked two Saudi tankers in the Red Sea. And, President Trump overnight replaced expiring tariffs with a slew of new ones.
full_text:
Oil surges to $100 per barrel. And, Trump imposes a new round of tariffs
Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.
Today's top stories
The House yesterday approved a resolution to remove U.S. forces from the war in Iran as the conflict continues to escalate in the Middle East. The non-binding resolution reflects lawmakers' disapproval of a war they did not vote to authorize. It marked the second such rebuke passed by the House since the war began. Soon after the House vote, Senate Democrats attempted to advance their own war powers resolution, but it failed 47 to 49. In the past two weeks of renewed fighting, the U.S. has launched strikes on Iran, while Iran has targeted American bases in the Gulf and Jordan, impacting global energy markets.
- 🎧 Brent crude oil reached its highest level since May yesterday when it surged more than 6% to $100 a barrel, NPR's Hadeel Al-Shalchi tells Up First. The spike will impact everyday people, increasing costs for school supplies and fresh food. Shipping companies like UPS are tacking on fuel surcharges. Prices rose after Iran-backed Yemeni Houthis attacked two Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea. The Houthis said they got involved in the war to retaliate against Saudi Arabia for its siege on Yemen and assaults on the capital's international airport. Earlier this week, the rebel group also threatened to blockade the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The strait is another crucial chokepoint for oil and fuel transport, in addition to the Strait of Hormuz, which the U.S. and Iran have been fighting for control over. The ongoing conflict has also led some foreign missions to reduce their presence in Iran, according to Al-Shalchi.
The Trump administration announced overnight that it is imposing tariffs on 59 countries and the European Union. The new tariffs have two tiers — 10% and 12.5% — and went into effect at midnight, at the same time as when a 10% global tariff struck down by the Supreme Court earlier this year expired. The administration said it imposed these new tariffs because these countries are importing goods made with forced labor. The tariffs cover more than 99% of imports to the United States. Major categories like energy and many foods will remain exempt. Earlier this week, President Trump also signed proclamations to impose 50% tariffs on a selection of Canadian goods.
- 🎧 Polls show that Americans largely disapprove of tariffs and that their approval of Trump's handling of the economy has declined, NPR's Danielle Kurtzleben says. Despite public opinion, she says Trump views tariffs as a tool to pressure other countries into making concessions on things like trade deals. As the midterm elections approach, the administration continues to assert that its tariff policies will yield long-term economic benefits. Some economists caution that it is risky to ask voters to back a potentially unpopular approach, given the uncertainty of future outcomes.
A vigil last night in Madison, Wisconsin, drew hundreds of people mourning 38-year-old Corey Ruiz, a man shot and killed by police on Wednesday. Madison Police Chief John Patterson said that officers responded to a call about a man checking cars. When they arrived, Ruiz fled on his bike. When officers attempted to arrest him, he produced a knife and injured one officer, according to the police chief. Four officers were involved in the incident. The officer who was injured was the one who shot Ruiz. Authorities have not yet released his name. The four officers have been placed on administrative leave.
- 🎧 Emotions are running high in the city since the shooting, says Sarah Lehr of NPR network station Wisconsin Public Radio. The community is particularly raw to this incident, having experienced two other deadly shootings by police in the same neighborhood since 2012, Lehr adds. The Wisconsin Division of Criminal Investigation is looking into the shooting. The officers involved in the incident were not wearing body cameras, as the Madison police don't have them department-wide. Madison police do have dashboard cameras, and there are multiple bystander videos circulating of the incident, Lehr says.
Living better
Living Better is a special series about what it takes to stay healthy in America.
A growing number of consumers are interested in avocado oil's purported health benefits. But some people might not be getting what they think they're buying. A new study finds that consumers paying a premium for foods advertised as containing avocado oil are probably not receiving it, highlighting ongoing authenticity issues in the industry. Selina Wang, the lead author of the study, says the findings are particularly disheartening, as avocado oil products are often much more expensive than those made with olive or other vegetable oils. Here's what we know:
- 🥑 In a study, researchers conducted a chemical analysis of 54 products that listed only avocado oil. They found that 89% were adulterated with cheaper oils like soybean.
- 🥑 In comparison, researchers found that, out of 20 packaged foods made with olive oil tested, only one showed signs of adulteration.
- 🥑 Some see avocado oil as a healthier alternative to seed oils like canola and soybean. According to Sarah Berry, a nutrition professor at King's College London, there's limited direct evidence supporting its health benefits compared to data about eating avocados.
- 🥑 Avocado oil costs more largely because avocados are costly and produce a limited amount of oil.
Weekend picks
Check out what NPR is watching, reading and listening to this weekend:
🍿 Movies: Can't get to Broadway? Don't worry! Catch the film adaptation of Hadestown: The Musical, a retelling of the Greek tragedy of Orpheus and Eurydice. The show is in theaters for a limited time.
📺 TV: Netflix's new series The Hawk stars Will Ferrell as a past-his-prime golfer. In the show, he reunites with some former collaborators, including Molly Shannon, Luke Wilson and Chris Parnell.
📚 Books: Grace Farris' graphic memoir See One, Do One, Teach One gives readers an insider's look at medical school, including the stresses of student loans, friendships built under pressure and the impossible pursuit of work-life balance.
🎵 Music: NPR's New Music Friday is breaking down the best new albums out today, and Charli xcx, Tyla and Shania Twain are on that list. Check out the other albums that made the cut and listen to a playlist of new songs.
🕹️ Gaming: Discover the best games of 2026 so far as NPR staff members spotlight some of their favorites with this interactive list.
❓Quiz: This week's quiz features a variety of topics, from a deformed yet adorable animal to international politics. Fortunately, the Up First newsletter answered several questions throughout the week.
3 things to know before you go
- Theresa Aletheia and Danielle Lussier, two Catholic sisters in Kentucky, are seeking to establish a new official order in the Catholic Church dedicated to helping survivors of clergy abuse.
- Wang Hong was awarded the Fields Medal yesterday, making her the first Chinese woman to win the world's most prestigious mathematics prize.
- More than 1,000 people in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo have now died from the Ebola outbreak. Officials say that the virus is spreading at the fastest rate on record.
This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

title: Trump threatens Iran escalation as tit-for-tat airstrikes continue
summary: The U.S. continued airstrikes in Iran while Tehran launched retaliatory attacks on U.S. targets in the Gulf as the region braced itself after President Trump said he was close to deciding whether to launch "a massive attack".
full_text:
Trump threatens Iran escalation as tit-for-tat airstrikes continue
AMMAN, Jordan - The U.S. Friday continued airstrikes in Iran while Tehran launched retaliatory attacks on U.S. targets in the Gulf as the region braced itself after President Trump said he was close to deciding whether to launch "a massive attack".
"I am considering a massive attack. Bigger than ever before. I am close to making a decision," Trump told the Axios news outlet.
The U.S. military later said it conducted its 13th consecutive night of strikes against Iran in attacks aimed at degrading Iran's ability to threaten maritime traffic.
Iran's control of the Strait of Hormuz – a vital waterway between Iran and Oman – on Thursday pushed global oil prices to over $100 per barrel – their highest level since May. The price for benchmark crude oil eased to under $100 in trading Friday morning.
Iranian state media reported explosions overnight including along the strait of Hormuz in Qeshm and Bandar Abbas.
UN Secretary General António Guterres told the security council that the Middle East was being pushed to the "edge of the unimaginable".
"The situation is getting out of control," Guterres said. "The region is being pulled into an ever-widening circle of confrontation. One crisis feeds another. One escalation triggers the next."
The collapse of the ceasefire has brought Yemen's Houthi rebels, a key Iranian ally, further into the conflict. The Houthis this week attacked Saudi tankers in the Red Sea near Bab el-Mandeb. The Houthis control that waterway, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and is vital to global container traffic moving through the Suez Canal.
Trump threatened "major military punishment" against the Houthis if the attacks continue. Saudi Arabia backs an internationally recognized Yemeni government that controls the north of Yemen. The Houthis blame Saudi Arabia for an attack on the airport in the Yemeni capital last week.
In the Kurdistan Region of Iraq, security forces shot down explosive-laden drones near the capital Erbil's international airport. The airport director said it had closed temporarily but was operating again normally later Friday morning.
Iran did not issue claims of responsibility for the strikes in the Iraqi Kurdish region where the U.S. has a military presence. Armed Kurdish-Iranian opposition bases in the Kurdish region have been a frequent target of Iranian and Iranian-backed attacks.
Newly appointed Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi said after a visit Thursday to Iran he had promised not to allow attacks on Iran from Iraqi soil. Zaidi met President Trump this week in Washington, where he promised to intensify efforts to rein in Iran-backed Iraqi militias which have attacked U.S. forces.
In response to the increased tension, the U.K. announced it was temporarily withdrawing diplomatic staff from Iran. Some airlines began canceling flights to the region. Qatar Airways, a major regional carrier, announced it would suspend flights to Bahrain, Kuwait and Erbil until the end of July.

title: US allies hit with new tariffs object to Trump's forced labor claims
summary: Australia and the European Union were among U.S. trade partners who condemned the tariffs.
full_text:
US allies hit with new tariffs object to Trump's forced labor claims
Many of America's key allies on Friday criticized the U.S. administration's new tariffs against them, after President Trump renewed the tax on more than 60 countries just as the previous tariffs expired.
The U.S. Supreme Court had earlier this year ruled that many of the tariffs imposed under emergency powers were illegal.
The president cited lax enforcement of a ban on the use of forced labor to produce goods as his reason for renewing the tariffs, an allegation Australia and the European Union vehemently rejected.
Those targeted with the latest penalties face between 10 and 12.5 percent on almost all American imports.
Here's some reaction from around the world:
Australia and New Zealand
Australian Trade Minister Don Farrell said the 12.5 percent tariffs on his country's exports were "unjustified" and called it "an extremely disappointing decision."
"We believe we do take the issue of modern slavery seriously. We have some of the most progressive legislation anywhere in the world. We say that these tariffs are unjustified and we call on the United States Government to reverse them," Farrell said.
In New Zealand, Prime Minister Christopher Luxon called the tariffs "extremely disappointing."
"The U.S. investigation did not provide meaningful evidence to support claims in relation to forced labour. Tariffs are not the way - they drive up costs and uncertainty for businesses," he said.
European Union and the United Kingdom
The EU's foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas also questioned Trump's rational for the new tariffs., "
"If you compare our labour laws to the ones of the United States, I mean, we have paid vacations, we have very good labor conditions for our employees, so it's not really grounded," she told Reuters.
The British government said Trump's latest 10 percent tariffs will amount to "no negative change" for British exports. Former Prime Minister Keir Starmer was able to strike a better U.S. trade deal than many other countries, with lower tariff rates. And King Charles III got the U.S. tariff on Scotch whisky reduced to zero when he visited the White House in April.
But a government spokesperson said: "We take forced labour very seriously to ensure that in global supply chains U.K. businesses are not complicit."
Asia
Japan's Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said his country had been reassured by the Trump administration that they would not be slapped with more tariffs. He said: "It is regrettable that the measure imposes tariffs on the grounds of non-existence of measures banning imports of goods made by forced labor, even though Japan's industry and trade are in line with international rules."
The world's second-largest economy, China, was hit with 12.5 percent new tariffs and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs condemned the move.
"Tariff wars and trade wars do not serve any parties' interests," ministry spokesman Lin Jian told a regular press conference on Friday.

China and Asean eye closer energy cooperation as fighting flares up again in Middle East
The region is heavily reliant on oil imports and has been severely affected by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz
A joint statement, released after a meeting between the bloc’s foreign ministers and their Chinese counterpart in Manila, came amid an ongoing energy crisis.
According to the World Economic Forum Asia, 55 per cent of Southeast Asian crude oil imports originate from the Middle East, leaving up to 28 per cent of the region’s final energy consumption exposed to direct disruption.
Kao Kim Hourn, the secretary general of Asean, warned last month that the crisis in the Middle East had “laid bare the vulnerability of global energy and food supply chains to geopolitical shocks” and called for deeper cooperation with China.
Building on a previous statement from the 11-member bloc, the joint statement welcomed the ongoing US–Iran negotiations mediated by Pakistan and Qatar and called for a ceasefire and “a peaceful and lasting resolution” to the conflict.

full_text:
Why a Chinese political scientist wants the public to take a test on foreign affairs
Tsinghua University scholar Yan Xuetong is challenging people to avoid social media sensationalism and sit a 60-minute exam
In an era where short-form videos and viral commentary can dominate public discourse on geopolitics, one Chinese political scientist is on a mission to correct what he calls a “negative one” level of understanding.
The fourth edition of the annual exam – known as the International Relations Basic Knowledge Proficiency Test – was held on July 5 at the Liaoning International Hotel in the Chinese capital.
“With the rise of short videos on social media, misleading narratives about international relations have become increasingly severe,” Yan said.
Chinese authorities maintain strict scrutiny over online content. But in the field of international affairs, the controls are comparatively looser. This flexibility provides content creators with greater room to generate traffic by capitalising on international events and diplomatic issues.
“In some disciplines at Tsinghua University, teaching starts from zero – introducing students to what they don’t know,” Yan said.

title: VW profits plunge and deep job cuts loom amid tough Chinese competition
summary:
Carmaker, which is pushing through cost-cutting programme, expects sales to fall by up to 3% this year

Volkswagen has reported a steep fall in profits and cut its revenue forecast amid a sales slump in China, as the German carmaker pushes through a brutal cost-cutting programme that includes slashing up to 100,000 jobs.

The world’s second-largest maker of vehicles said it expects sales to fall by up to 3% this year, a dramatic reversal on a previous forecast for a 3% increase on last year’s €321.9bn (£275.3bn), because of a sales slump in the highly competitive Chinese market.

Continue reading...
full_text:
Volkswagen has reported a steep fall in profits and cut its revenue forecast amid a sales slump in China, as the German carmaker pushes through a brutal cost-cutting programme that includes axeing up to 100,000 jobs.
VW said it expects sales to fall by up to 3% this year, a reversal of a previous forecast for a 3% increase on last year’s €321.9bn (£275.3bn), because of a sales slump in the highly competitive Chinese market.
The sales slump will increase pressure on the world’s second-largest maker of vehicles to cut costs. Earlier this month VW’s supervisory board rejected the plans by the chief executive, Oliver Blume, to shut four factories in Germany, as the manufacturer confirmed it was raising the job cuts target to 100,000, double the number already agreed by unions.
Volkswagen’s operating profit fell by 9.5% to €3.5bn in the second quarter, below analysts’ estimates of a small increase to €3.9bn, as Blume battles with unions to push through a restructuring programme.
On Friday the company said the proposed additional job cuts would mostly be in administrative positions across its global business.
The plans also include reducing Volkswagen’s model line by up to half.
Volkswagen employs more than 650,000 people across all its brands, which include Audi, Bentley, Skoda, Seat, Porsche and Cupra, and has been hit hard by growing – and cheap – Chinese competition and the struggle to shift to electric cars.
In the first half of this year, Volkswagen delivered 6.3% fewer cars globally, about 4.1m, mostly because of its travails in China.
Volkswagen sales in China have fallen by more than 31% in the first half, against increases in Europe and North America.
“The extent to which western carmakers are being squeezed out of the Chinese car market by domestic operators is laid bare by Volkswagen’s latest update,” said Russ Mould, the investment director at AJ Bell.
Blume said on Friday that Chinese carmakers had sharply increased exports, which was adding pressure in Europe. The restructuring was essential to make the company “more innovative, faster, more attractive and robust”.
Volkswagen’s share price fell 1.5% after the release of its latest financial results and is down 66% over the past five years.
“After nearly four years at the wheel as chief executive, Oliver Blume is likely to come under increasing pressure,” Mould said. “His plan to steer Volkswagen back on to a growth path involves drastically cutting costs, including by slashing the company’s headcount. There are also plans to reduce the number of models and sell off non-core assets to make Volkswagen a more efficient machine. Pushing these through may be difficult given likely opposition from unions, and whether they are enough to win over the market is an open question.”
The tough market in China has also hit other carmakers, with BMW last month cutting its profit guidance for this year because of the disruption caused by the Iran war and the company’s struggles in the Chinese market.

title: Four Palestinians and one Israeli killed during West Bank settler attack
summary:
Several others seriously injured in attack that residents of Palestinian village say also involved Israeli military

Four Palestinians and one Israeli have been killed in a shooting in the northern West Bank, health officials have said, during what residents described as a settler attack also involving the Israeli military. Several more people were seriously injured.

The serious incident in the Palestinian village of Tell, near Nablus, is the deadliest attack in the West Bank this year and has the potential to lead to a series of reprisals between Israeli-backed settlers and Palestinian communities.

Continue reading...
full_text:
Four Palestinians and one Israeli have been killed in a shooting in the northern West Bank, health officials have said, during what residents described as a settler attack also involving the Israeli military. Several more people were seriously injured.
The serious incident in the Palestinian village of Tell, near Nablus, is the deadliest attack in the West Bank this year and has the potential to lead to a series of reprisals between Israeli-backed settlers and Palestinian communities.
A Palestinian resident of the village said Israeli settlers had come to the village early on Friday morning and that they were soon joined by the military. The Israeli military said it had come to the aid of Israeli hikers.
Walid Zidan, the head of Tel village council, told Agence France-Presse that about 20 Israeli settlers had entered the village at about 8.30am local time. “Villagers came out to defend their homes and property. Clashes and physical altercations broke out between the residents and the settlers,” Zidan said.
“Israeli soldiers were present and together with the settlers began opening fire … It was the settlers who stormed the village, with the intention of killing, vandalising and setting property on fire,” he said.
The Palestinian foreign ministry condemned what it described as a “massacre committed by settlers in partnership with the occupation forces in the village of Tell”.
The circumstances of the shooting were not immediately clear, but video of the attack posted online has shown several people who appear to be Palestinians on the ground in a field near the village who appear to have been shot.
The Israeli military said it had deployed soldiers after reports of an attack against Israeli civilians who were hiking near Havat Gilad, a West Bank settlement near Tell. According to the military, the attackers seized the weapon of a member of the security forces at the scene and opened fire.
The Palestinian health ministry in Ramallah said the four Palestinians were killed by Israeli forces. All four were from the same family and have the same last name, according to people from the village.
Israel’s Magen David Adom rescue services did not say who had killed the Israeli, a man in his 30s. Social media channels run by settler communities said he was from Havat Gilad.
Violence in the Israeli-occupied West Bank has flared in recent days.
The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, will meet his defence minister and chief of staff to discuss a response, his office said. A statement said Israel would “act forcefully against the terrorists”, although the incident has not been investigated.
Israeli settlers have called for a wave of attacks to “erase” the village. 
All Israeli settlements in the West Bank are illegal under international law.
Palestinian health officials said they were treating four injured Palestinians, three in critical condition. Israel’s rescue service said two injured Israelis were being airlifted out of the West Bank.
The Israeli military said it had imposed a “temporary cordon” around Nablus and Tell.

title: 5 Killed in West Bank Shooting, Officials Say, Among the Deadliest in Months
summary: The authorities said four Palestinians and an Israeli were killed in the incident. The details of events remain unclear, with officials offering differing accounts.
full_text:
Supported by
5 Killed in West Bank Shooting, Officials Say, Among the Deadliest in Months
The authorities said four Palestinians and an Israeli were killed in the incident. The details of events remain unclear, with officials offering differing accounts.
Four Palestinians and an Israeli were killed in a shooting in the Israeli-occupied West Bank on Friday morning, according to health officials, in one of the most deadly incidents in the territory over the past year.
The health ministry of the Palestinian Authority, which administers parts of the West Bank, said four people were killed and four others were wounded, including three in critical condition. Magen David Adom, the Israeli ambulance service, said one person in his 30s was killed and two others were wounded — one seriously and the other moderately.
The exact details of the shooting remain unclear, with conflicting versions of events from Israeli and Palestinian officials.
The Israeli military said that soldiers were sent to the Palestinian village of Tell, close to the city of Nablus, after receiving a report about an attack on Israeli hikers in the area.
The military said that “terrorists” had opened fire and injured several Israelis after stealing the weapon of a security officer. It was unclear from the military’s statement whether the officer was an Israeli soldier. Later on Friday, the military said it had killed the person who attacked the Israelis.
Walid Zeidan, the mayor of Tell, offered a differing account based, he said, on conversations with Palestinian eyewitnesses.
“A number of settlers attacked the village,” Mr. Zeidan said in a phone interview. “It started with verbal altercations between our residents and the settlers and evolved into a physical fight before they started shooting” at village residents.
Mr. Zeidan said he had no information to suggest that residents of his community had opened fire on Israelis that morning.
Adam Rasgon is a reporter for The Times in Jerusalem, covering Israeli and Palestinian affairs.

title: Russia and Ukraine Trade Blows With Missiles and Drones
summary: Ukrainian strikes set fire to warehouses and other sites in Russia, and Russian bombing rocked Ukraine’s capital, as the two countries escalated a deadly air campaign.
full_text:
Russia and Ukraine Trade Blows With Missiles and Drones
Ukrainian strikes set fire to warehouses and other sites in Russia, and Russian bombing rocked Ukraine’s capital, as the two countries escalated a deadly air campaign.
Explosions rocked Kyiv in the middle of the day on Friday as Moscow targeted the Ukrainian capital with a barrage of missiles. Hours earlier, Ukraine sent hundreds of drones swarming deep into Russian territory and struck sites including warehouses belonging to Russia’s largest online retailer, Wildberries.
The dueling bombardments were the latest salvos in an air campaign that has escalated as the war’s front line remains mostly static.
Residents in Kyiv were alerted to the incoming barrage shortly before noon, with the familiar sound of air raid alerts blaring and of warnings from Ukraine’s air force.
The missile attack in Kyiv came after Ukrainian drone and missile strikes were reported at Russian fuel facilities, a military production plant and commercial warehouses.
President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine posted video of fires in the aftermath of several strikes, including one in Russia’s Kirov region, east of Moscow. That strike appeared to have been conducted with newly developed Flamingo missiles, which are made by Fire Point, a Ukrainian company, according to video and comments by the head of the company.
Mr. Zelensky said the facility in Kirov was a “key military enterprise” that supplied components for Russian aircraft and missile systems. The Russian authorities said at least six people were killed and 20 wounded in the strike.
The Ukrainian attack on Wildberries was the sixth since Saturday, and it targeted a major logistics center in St. Petersburg. Video showed smoke billowing from one of the buildings.
The company’s chief executive, Tatyana Kim, said no employees were injured in the strike. Eight people were killed in attacks on Wildberries sites on Saturday and one person on Wednesday, the Russian authorities have said.
Marc Santora has been reporting from Ukraine since the beginning of the war with Russia. He was previously based in London as an international news editor focused on breaking news events and earlier the bureau chief for East and Central Europe, based in Warsaw. He has also reported extensively from Iraq and Africa.

title: With Hopes High for New H.I.V. Prevention Pill, Merck Takes Steps to Ensure Access
summary: Companies in Africa and India will make generic versions of the pill that could cost as little as $5 per person per year. But access to the drug and other new products in much of Latin America remains uncertain.
full_text:
Supported by
Global Health
With Hopes High for New H.I.V. Prevention Pill, Merck Takes Steps to Ensure Access
Companies in Africa and India will make generic versions of the pill that could cost as little as $5 per person per year. But access to the drug and other new products in much of Latin America remains uncertain.
The pharmaceutical company Merck said on Friday that it would license seven generic drugmakers to produce a low-cost version of a new monthly H.I.V. prevention pill that has generated significant optimism about the role it could play in ending the H.I.V. epidemic.
The decision is intended to make stockpiles of the drug immediately available in developing countries if clinical trial results next year live up to expectations for the pill.
The company’s announcement on Friday comes as a major international AIDS conference begins in Rio de Janeiro, against a backdrop of disappointment with limited progress on cutting H.I.V. infection rates.
The new drug, alimatravir, is a pill taken once a month for what is called pre-exposure prophylaxis, or PrEP. It is being tested in a late-stage trial involving young women in three sub-Saharan African countries, and in a separate trial in countries across Latin America, Asia, Europe and Africa that involves transgender people and men who have sex with men.
There were 1.2 million new H.I.V. infections in 2025, according to UNAIDS, a United Nations agency. More tools to prevent infection are available, but they are not reaching many of the world’s most vulnerable people. Slow but steady progress toward the goal of lowering H.I.V. transmission rates was derailed over the past 18 months by sharp reductions in funding from the United States and other major donor countries.
A recent analysis by the Clinton Health Access Initiative found a 42 percent decline in the number of people who were started on oral PrEP in 2025 in 10 sub-Saharan African and Asian countries with high rates of H.I.V. infection, compared to the year before.

title: Trump’s New Tariffs on Over 80 Countries, Explained
summary: The new levies come after the Supreme Court struck down most of the Administration’s previous tariffs.
full_text:
New U.S. tariffs on 60 economies take effect Friday, in the latest recourse by President Donald Trump’s Administration to impose alternative taxes on imported goods after the Supreme Court struck down most of his aggressive ones earlier this year.
The Office of the U.S. Trade Representative (USTR) announced the new tariffs on Thursday, citing these economies' alleged failure to impose and “effectively” enforce a ban on the import of goods “produced with forced labor.”
“The United States has had a forced labor import ban for nearly a century, and rigorously enforces it; it’s well past time for our trading partners to do the same,” said U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer in a statement. “Today’s action will begin to correct what is both a human rights abuse and distortive trade practice to improve the welfare of workers everywhere.”
Since the U.S.’s top court ruled in February that Trump lacked the authority to impose sweeping import taxes through emergency powers, he has turned to temporary measures.
The new round of levies takes effect just as a previous 10% global tariff expired Friday. Trump has argued that high tariffs will boost American manufacturing and thus bring jobs, despite studies showing that American importers and consumers take the economic hit for them.
Here’s what to know.
Which countries are covered?
The USTR on March 12 launched an investigation into countries and economies’ forced-labor import policies, which the office said included two rounds of public hearings, public comments, and engagement with trading partners. The results of these investigations were released in June.
The 60 countries and economies covered by these investigations were Algeria, Angola, Argentina, Australia, the Bahamas, Bahrain, Bangladesh, Brazil, Cambodia, Canada, Chile, China, Colombia, Costa Rica, Dominican Republic, Ecuador, Egypt, El Salvador, the European Union, Guatemala, Guyana, Honduras, Hong Kong SAR, India, Indonesia, Iraq, Israel, Japan, Jordan, Kazakhstan, Kuwait, Libya, Malaysia, Mexico, Morocco, New Zealand, Nicaragua, Nigeria, Norway, Oman, Pakistan, Peru, the Philippines, Qatar, Russia, Saudi Arabia, Singapore, South Africa, South Korea, Sri Lanka, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand, Trinidad and Tobago, Türkiye, United Arab Emirates, the U.K., Uruguay, Venezuela, and Vietnam. The E.U. includes 27 countries.
These partners cover about 99.4% of U.S. imports, according to a USTR factsheet. Some goods, however, will not be covered, such as informational materials, donations, and accompanied baggage, among others.
The tariff rates vary. A 10% tariff applies to goods from 17 economies that “have made commitments to adopt, and effectively enforce, forced labor import prohibitions,” among them Canada, India, Mexico, and the U.K.
For certain non-exempt products from the E.U., Japan, South Korea, Switzerland, and Taiwan, the U.S. will charge an extra tax so that the total tariff—including the normal most-favored nation (MFN) tariff—comes to either 10% or 12.5%.
The other countries face a 12.5% tariff rate.
Some of the affected economies, however, have already targeted goods in their supply chains that are linked to forced labor. Beginning December 2027, the European Union will ban products made with forced labor in its markets. Politico reports that other countries successfully lowered the tariff rate on their goods by enforcing a forced-labor ban after the proposed tariffs were announced last month.
Why is the U.S. imposing this?
An unnamed senior Trump Administration official previewing the new tariffs described the measure to reporters as “the most sweeping international labor rights action the United States has ever taken—that any country has ever taken.”
The official said that the Trump Administration views that countries without enforced bans on forced labor have an “unfair advantage” over the U.S., which has those prohibitions. “It encourages stronger labor rights enforcement abroad, it will restore fairness in the global market for American workers, and it incentivizes our trading partners to join the United States in eliminating forced labor from global supply chains,” the official added.
Section 307 of the U.S. Tariff Act of 1930 prohibits the import of foreign goods produced “wholly or in part” by forced labor, convict labor, or indentured child labor.
The International Labor Organization (ILO) Forced Labor Convention of 1930 defines “forced labor” as “all work or service which is exacted from any person under the menace of any penalty and for which the said person has not offered himself voluntarily.” Latest statistics from the ILO show that about 28 million people were in forced labor worldwide in 2021.
What’s the legal authority behind the latest tariffs?
The Trump Administration used Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 for the latest round of tariffs. Under the Act, the U.S. Trade Representative, subject to the President’s direction, can impose levies and other sanctions on countries found to engage in unreasonable or discriminatory trade practices.
During Trump’s first-term Administration, Section 301 played a crucial role in the U.S. trade war with China.
In Trump’s second-term Administration, more Section 301 tariffs are expected as the Office of the USTR continues its ongoing investigations, including one into whether 16 trading partners—including China, the E.U., and Mexico—are overproducing goods and diminishing U.S. advantages in global markets. Earlier this month, Washington imposed a 25% tariff on Brazil through Section 301.
The latest regime comes after Trump imposed tariffs under Section 122 of the same act on Feb. 24. That, however, was merely a stopgap put in place after the Supreme Court ruling, as Section 122 of the Act specifies that such import surcharges can only be prescribed over 150 days unless Congress extends it.
But the new tariffs are still likely to face a legal hurdle. Alan Wolff, a senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics, wrote in a Thursday note: “These new tariffs would represent another case of presidential overreach. If they were challenged in court, the Supreme Court would likely overturn them.” Wolff, who also argues are likely to be ineffective at addressing global forced labor, says the Constitution vests the authority to determine and implement tariff policy in Congress, not the President.
How have affected economies reacted?
Several countries have called out the latest tariff policy, and the related accusations of underperformance in preventing forced labor. Australia’s Trade Minister Don Farrell said in a statement that the levies were “unjustified” and “should be removed,” arguing that Australia’s policies against forced labor and modern slavery “are among the strongest in the world.”
Brazil, which faces a 12.5% tariff rate, accused the USTR in a statement of “[manipulating] an issue dear to human rights and the global struggle of workers for accusing 59 countries and the European Union of unfair practices.” Brazil’s government added that the new taxes can activate its “Reciprocity Law”—which could allow countermeasures—and that it will bring the dispute to the World Trade Organization.
Canada, which faces a 10% tariff rate, took on a more neutral tone and said the U.S. action “is not unexpected.” Minister for Canada-U.S. Trade Dominic LeBlanc said in a statement that Ottawa “shares the United States’ objective of ensuring goods produced with forced labour do not enter our supply chains” and is willing to continue “engaging constructively” with Washington on the issue.
Speaking to Radio New Zealand, New Zealand’s Trade and Investment Minister Todd McClay said he rejects insinuations of any support for forced labor in the Oceanic country. “We’re not involved in it,” McClay said. “It doesn’t happen through our trade. It doesn’t exist in New Zealand. But [the U.S. is] looking for any way to put a tariff rate back on.”

title: Trump Weighs ‘Massive Attack’ as Iran Rejects Cease-Fire Proposal
summary: President Donald Trump said Iran is “not ready” to make a deal and hasn’t “received enough pain yet.”
full_text:
It appears there will be no hasty retreat from weeks of escalating attacks between the U.S. and Iran, which have destabilized energy markets yet again.
On Thursday, President Donald Trump told Axios that he is weighing restarting major combat operations in Iran. Trump said he could carry out even larger strikes than the Operation Epic Fury strikes that killed dozens of Iranian leaders and started the war on Feb. 28.
“I am considering a massive attack. Bigger than ever before. I am close to making a decision. We are all set for it,” Trump said, adding that he knows there would be consequences to such an attack and that a final determination has not been made. The President said Israel “would join in two minutes” if asked but that “we don’t need anybody.”
Trump also said that Iran is “not ready” to make a deal and that its leaders “have some evil intentions.” Trump’s remarks came after Iran reportedly rejected a 15-point cease-fire proposal from the U.S. that was delivered by Iraq on Wednesday.
Trump appeared to suggest that the U.S. may escalate its attacks on Iran in order to force it to the negotiating table.
“They haven’t received enough pain yet,” Trump told Axios.
Tensions around the Strait of Hormuz
The sticking point appears to be the Strait of Hormuz, which Iran had militarized at the start of the war, halting commercial shipping and skyrocketing energy prices around the world. The June 17 U.S.-Iran memorandum of understanding did not definitively answer the question of the Strait; instead it said Oman and Iran would carry out discussions over management of the narrow waterway. Since the start of the war, Iran said it wants to manage passage through the Strait, including possibly charging fees. Trump has also at times suggested that the U.S. could take over control of the Strait and charge tolls.
Days after the MOU was signed, Iran resumed attacks on commercial ships in the Strait. The U.S. retaliated with strikes on Iran. The U.S. has escalated its attacks since, carrying out daily strikes on Iran for the past two weeks. Trump has also repeated his threats to attack Iran’s civil infrastructure, including power plants and bridges, and to “wipe out” Iran’s Revolutionary Guards, while Iran has vowed to avenge the death of its Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
Iran has claimed responsibility for attacks on Gulf states since the MOU, citing retaliation for the U.S. strikes. The Associated Press reported a series of explosions near a military base in northern Iraq on Friday after the U.S. military had concluded its 13th consecutive night of strikes on Iran.
Tensions have escalated in recent days after Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen began attacking Saudi ships in the Red Sea, threatening to disrupt another maritime chokepoint. If shipping through the Bab-el-Mandeb Strait in the Red Sea halts, the world could face more economic pain. Already, Brent crude topped $100 a barrel on Thursday for the first time since May, and could climb further if the conflict continues to escalate. Trump warned on Thursday that “the U.S. will hold Iran responsible” for any further Houthi attacks, and that “major military punishment will be inflicted upon Iran and, of course, the Houthis, themselves.”
Iranian officials reportedly said they were not interested in any new deal that left the issue of the Strait unresolved.
Butting heads
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi visited Tehran on Thursday and was expected to convey the U.S. position after he visited the White House last week. But U.S.-Iran negotiations seem off the table for now.
“The problem is not passing messages,” Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told state television on Thursday. “The problem is America’s outlook, which is illogical, greedy and controlling.”
Israel has also continued attacks on Lebanon despite multiple U.S.-brokered cease-fire agreements. More than 4,000 people in Lebanon have been killed by Israel since March 2, according to the Lebanese Health Ministry. Analysts previously told TIME that Israel’s attacks could stand in the way of any longstanding peace with Iran, as Iran has repeatedly said any cease-fire deal must include Lebanon.
Trump and Iranian officials have butted heads on other issues. Trump threatened on Thursday to use frozen Iranian funds to pay for any damage to ships. The assets, that are under U.S. sanctions control, were meant to be released to Iran as part of the MOU.
Araghchi said on Friday that “seizing another nation’s assets to pay for unrelated future claims is an incendiary precedent.”
“Ensuing chaos will not be pretty or peaceful,” he added.

title: Meet Me in the Notes App
summary: Notes have staying power, writes Rainesford Stauffer, as vulnerable chaos, a counterpoint to hyper-curated feeds.
full_text:
“What’s the oldest note in your phone?” my younger sister asked, in the same tone one might use to share gossip. She was explaining what she called “notes app digest,” rereading notes like a kind of personal magazine of one’s own insight and nonsense.
I immediately scrolled. For better or worse, my notes app is the piece of technology closest to looking like the inside of my brain: a bit chaotic, annoyingly detail-oriented, and perhaps perpetually nostalgic. While handwritten to-do lists hold my life together, my notes app contains the catch-all, the weird (one that simply says “possum”), and the important (a list of people’s birthdays) coexisting.
Somehow, the mess of my notes resists all forms of optimization, or even coherence. Venturing back into our notes app isn’t just about fishing out that one password we swore we’d remember, or realizing we drafted a resignation letter in the same note as a reminder to get toilet paper. They are weirdly human markers of time, who and where we’ve been. Amid the endless push to optimize, streamline, and summarize our thoughts, notes have staying power.
For years, people have observed the delightful, vulnerable chaos of the notes app as a counterpoint to hyper-curated feeds. Charley Locke, writing for The Atlantic in 2024, noted that the app is “essentially built-in scratch paper on a phone, and it reveals a person’s digital subconscious.” A 2025 piece by Elahe Izadi for The Washington Post asked strangers to reveal the contents of their notes apps, an act somewhere between a confession and a grand reveal.
There are many reasons why people still default to writing notes, according to Dr. Bart Wojdynski, professor of journalism at the University of Georgia and director of the Digital Media Attention and Cognition Lab. It’s easy to use, and the icon connotes the idea of jotting on a post-it. “Maybe there’s an extent to which the basicness of the notes app also makes it feel less like it’s being read by our online overlords and used to market you ads,” Wojdynski says. (He noted he hadn’t read the user agreement in a bit, but it might feel “less likely that it’s being scraped to feed some LLM somewhere”). “I think this is related to people trying to have digital copies of their memory,” Wojdynski adds.
Recently, when looking back through notes, Andy Carr, 37, a PhD candidate and part-time adjunct instructor in New York, found something in addition to those for grocery shopping or lesson planning for college courses he teaches. In summer 2020, Carr, his brother, and his sister-in-law were navigating end-of-life care for his mother. There was a jumble of memories, from notes of contacts that hospice care nurses passed along to one reading “Skippy pb jingle—send writer to prison,” a vent about a peanut butter commercial that ran incessantly on the TV at home as the family worked to make his mom comfortable and provide as much physical help as they could.
Revisiting those notes, Carr found affirmation. For years after his mother’s passing, he struggled with feeling that he froze up at the time. The notes showed specific examples of all he had been present for and engaged with around his mother’s death, all of the things he’d taken down as important information to ensure nothing slipped through the cracks. He never deletes messages or notes, he said, and usually, rarely goes back to them: “But little things like this make me really grateful that I can.”
Nadia De Ala, 37, a leadership and negotiation coach who moved to Mexico from the Bay Area two years ago, still has the first note she ever put in the app in 2016: a poem she remembers writing while dreading her commute to a previous job. “I really feel like it’s a time capsule, because it keeps a lot of memories, the essence of who I’ve been at every iteration and season of my life,” she says, adding that it’s even interesting to look back on foods she liked to grocery shop for.
Our phones, in other words, can augment our memories. Julia Soares, assistant professor of psychology at New Mexico State University, says that devices can become “partners for helping us remember things.”
“You’ll find some very heartfelt things that are digital,” she explains, adding that sometimes people don’t think of these “digital scraps or mementos” as being particularly valuable, but many people hold onto voicemails or even emails.
Recently, over coffee, one of my dearest friends took me on a tour of her meticulously organized notes. If my notes app functions as the junk drawer of my mind, hers was like opening the door to different beautiful rooms: a list of good things that are happening, checklists for household maintenance, and a folder of notes her sister assembled of their mom’s recipes, complete with videos: a living cookbook. In our conversation, my sister talked about her own notes app discoveries: goals she’d written down only to be met with surprise at how much she’d grown since then, or the minutiae of everyday life she documented for no obvious reason. Other people shared their own earliest notes: addresses of apartments they were touring, passages of favorite books they kept for inspiration, a compliment they’d received, nonsensical thoughts that somehow got funnier the longer they kept them.
A slingshot backward through a scroll, and I meet: Myself from 2017 who saved a recording of her childhood cat purring; 2019 me, writing interview questions for my first book; my 2022 self nervously drafting multiple iterations of the same message asking for her stuff back at the end of a relationship; me in 2024, who apparently was fleetingly into logging everything she baked.
Look at this mess, I think, as I thumb through 1,781 half-baked thoughts, drafts, memories, and past selves. What chaos. I could never delete her.

title: How NATO Is Quietly Reinventing Itself for Trump
summary: NATO has been quietly reshaping itself toward America’s preferred vision of European security.
full_text:
The portents were not good. Before departing for the recent NATO summit in Ankara, President Donald Trump took to Truth Social to berate the alliance. He posted figures suggesting the alliance was a financial burden on the United States. He complained about allies neither contributing their fair shares nor standing with America. And he deemed it ridiculous for the U.S. to continue along this “one-sided” path.
Things didn’t improve when Trump touched down. During his first press conference at the summit, he singled out the big European allies—France, Germany, Italy, and the United Kingdom—for their lack of support over Iran. He reprised the demand that the Danish territory of Greenland be ceded to American control, and bashed the allies for insufficient defense spending. Trump suggested the allies were lucky to have him, claiming he only showed up as a favor to his “friend,” Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.
Yet a day later, the mood had changed. Trump departed Ankara praising “the love” among the allies. He was seduced by a carefully orchestrated procession of prime ministers and presidents of member countries of the alliance, each in turn swallowing hard and praising his leadership. They were following a script already played to great effect by NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, who has helped NATO survive Trump by perfecting the art of flattering the American president.
“Teflon Mark” and the art of the deal
When Rutte was appointed by the allies, he was not the obvious choice. As Dutch prime minister, he had led a country with a poor record of defense spending. There was also a strong argument at the time that NATO ought to select its first female Secretary General, or its first from an Eastern European ally.
But Rutte’s skill as a consensus-builder elevated his standing. Rutte had led Dutch coalition governments for nearly 14 years, and his reputation for deal-making and political survival had earned him the nickname, “Teflon Mark.” Crucially, for these reasons, Rutte also enjoyed the support of the Biden White House.
Rutte began work at NATO in Oct. 2024. Trump entered the White House for the second time three months later. Armed with an already well-honed gift for flattery, Rutte spared little time in cozying up to the incoming American president. At every opportunity since, he has praised Trump’s leadership. European and Canadian defense spending increases have, in Rutte’s telling, became the “Trump trillion.” He has an unerring ability to deflect difficult questions at press conferences—recently on Iran—so as to spare America any embarrassment.
When a Danish journalist accused him in Ankara of lacking self-respect for failing to counter Trump’s claims to Greenland, Rutte replied by comparing Trump’s impact on NATO to that of President Dwight D. Eisenhower, NATO’s first Supreme Allied Commander Europe and early advocate of fair transatlantic burden sharing. Trump rewarded Rutte by praising him as an “extraordinary person” and a “smart leader.”
Rutte’s unstinting support of Trump does carry a cost. Calling Trump “Daddy” at NATO’s 2025 Hague summit was cringeworthy for many diplomats. And sometimes Rutte’s spin on events rankles national sensitivities: his talking up of flights flown from bases in Italy to support Operation Epic Fury, the American war against Iran, recently drew a public rebuke from the Italian defense ministry. In January, Rutte intervened to set up a framework for discussing the Greenland question, prompting the Danish defense minister to point out that Rutte could not negotiate on Denmark’s behalf.
These reservations aside, Rutte remains, for now, an asset for the alliance: someone who can smooth over Trump’s impetuosity. NATO leaders understand his relationship with Trump is one of convenience, not political affinity. Rutte has worked tirelessly to support NATO’s broader agenda: standing up to Russia, supporting Ukraine, and, in his words, promoting “a stronger Europe in a stronger NATO.”
And Rutte is not averse to praising other NATO leaders. He commended German Chancellor Friedrich Merz for his “political courage” in ramping up German defense spending, and days before the NATO summit complemented then-British Prime Minister Keir Starmer for his “leadership” on Ukraine.
NATO’s savior?
Is it, then, too much to claim that without Rutte, NATO would be doomed? Similar questions were asked about Rutte’s predecessor, the Norwegian Jens Stoltenberg. As Secretary General during Trump’s first term, Stoltenberg too had an uncanny ability to read Trump’s mood and shield the allies from criticism.
Serious academic work has argued that Stoltenberg was, in part, responsible for NATO’s survival. Stoltenberg had to manage an American president who felt NATO was playing the U.S. as a sucker. In his memoirs, Stoltenberg recalls fearing, at the 2018 NATO summit, that the alliance “was about to stop functioning” if Trump made good on his threats to withdraw the U.S. security guarantee.
A deal brokered by Stoltenberg and Rutte—then at the summit as Dutch prime minister—kept Trump on board. Flattery, again, was the device. At the summit, Stoltenberg credited Trump’s strong leadership on defense spending for NATO’s revival.
What these examples suggest is that Secretary General of the NATO is no shrinking violet. Of the 14 office holders to date, five have been foreign ministers and two have served as defense ministers. The last three—Rutte, Stoltenberg, and his predecessor, the Dane Anders Fogh Rasmussen—came to the job as sitting prime ministers.
That standing allows the Secretary General to hold his own with NATO’s national leaders and with the alliance’s military commanders—the Supreme Allied Commander Europe and the Chair of the NATO Military Committee. The Secretary General can draw on considerable bureaucratic advantage: he heads up the International Staff at NATO headquarters, oversees the alliance’s polished public communications operation, and serves as the chief organizer of NATO summits.
But the Secretary General cannot countermand the nations. And here, ultimately, the U.S. carries the greatest influence. Despite his reservations, Stoltenberg could not prevent the U.S. from terminating NATO’s mission in Afghanistan in 2021. Today’s U.S. troop drawdowns in Europe, even if they directly affect NATO’s conventional defenses, are decided in the White House and the Pentagon. It is Rutte’s job to cast them in a positive light.
A shape shifting NATO
America has been critical of burden-shirking among the allies since NATO was formed. Trump has turned that sentiment into a weapon. Deference and sweet-talk have been Europe’s disarming response. It doesn’t always work: cozying up to the president—as Italian premier Giorgia Meloni recently found out—does not preclude a Trump tongue-lashing. Yet flattery did work in Ankara. Rutte deserves credit as the flatterer-in-chief.
Still, sycophancy only gets you so far. Practical measures aligned with American preferences are also needed. Away from the political theater, in recent months, the alliance has been quietly reshaping itself toward America’s preferred vision of European security: a “NATO 3.0.” Its chief architect, U.S. Under Secretary of War for Policy, Elbridge Colby, has spoken of the allies assuming “primary responsibility” for the conventional defense of Europe.
To that end, Europeans and Canadians are spending colossal sums on their militaries, and funneling more arms and aid to Ukraine, now that the U.S. is reluctant to do so. The transatlantic alliance may, as a result, be entering terra incognita.
The U.S. remains embedded in NATO’s command structure and is the ultimate guarantor of allied security through extended nuclear deterrence, but an unprecedented process of the Europeanization of NATO is under way. title: TikTok’s protection of minors should not be opt-in, warns EU
summary: TikTok has attracted the ire of the European Union over its protection of children who use the video sharing platform. The European Commission announced preliminary findings today under the Digital Services Act (DSA) that offer specific issues to address. The Commission suggests that TikTok should adjust the default settings of minors' "public" accounts so the […]
full_text:
TikTok has attracted the ire of the European Union over its protection of children who use the video sharing platform. The European Commission announced preliminary findings today under the Digital Services Act (DSA) that offer specific issues to address.
TikTok’s protection of minors should not be opt-in, warns EU
‘A high level of protection should not be an opt-in; it should be the default.’
‘A high level of protection should not be an opt-in; it should be the default.’
The Commission suggests that TikTok should adjust the default settings of minors’ “public” accounts so the content they post is only visible to TikTok users the teen has chosen to share it with, and that such content shouldn’t be recommended to other users in the For You feed. Even accounts set to private can be easily discovered through the ‘following’ lists of other users, and their profile photos can be seen by anyone. If TikTok fails to address the concerns, it could face a DSA non-compliance decision that imposes fines of up to six percent of the company’s global annual revenue.
“Minors deserve a safe experience from the moment they go online. The Digital Services Act requires platforms to build protections for minors into the design of their services, and holds them to account when they fail to do so,” EU tech chief Henna Virkkunen said in the announcement. “A high level of protection should not be an opt-in; it should be the default. This is our responsibility for current and future generations of European children.”
The preliminary findings follow UK communications regulator Ofcom launching a similar child safety investigation into TikTok last week, with updates expected in October. The EU says its separate probe to evaluate the addictive “rabbit hole effect” of TikTok’s recommender systems is still ongoing.
