title: Canadian government urged to block data-sharing deal between Thomson Reuters and US ICE
summary:
ICE will pay Canadian media giant US$125m to use its investigative database to identify ‘immigration fraud’

A Canadian federal opposition party leader is calling on the Mark Carney government to block the latest data-sharing deal between US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and the Canadian media giant Thomson Reuters.

Avi Lewis, the federal leader of the New Democratic party (NDP), demanded on Tuesday that Ottawa address the contract and further restrict Canadian corporations from doing business with ICE, after Canada’s National Observer reported on the deal.

Continue reading...
full_text:
A Canadian federal opposition party leader is calling on the Mark Carney government to block the latest data-sharing deal between US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and the Canadian media giant Thomson Reuters.
Avi Lewis, the federal leader of the New Democratic party (NDP), demanded on Tuesday that Ottawa address the contract and further restrict Canadian corporations from doing business with ICE, after Canada’s National Observer reported on the deal.
“My blood ran cold when I read about this development,” he added in a statement to the Guardian. “Complicity between Canadian corporations and ICE should absolutely be illegal.”
Under the US$125m deal, ICE will pay the technology and content conglomerate to access its Clear database – which includes property records, social media and geolocation information – in order to identify “voter fraud” and “immigration fraud”, according to reports.
In a procurement document obtained by 404 Media, Thomson Reuters says it is the only firm that allows ICE to have access to the “continuous monitoring” of millions of people.
Thomson Reuters’ contracts with ICE date back to 2015, when it first began providing US officials with access to Clear in order to track people for deportation. Critics have long alleged that the databases were being used to facilitate human rights abuses.
The latest contract, however, is the first to state that Clear software will be used to support the Trump administration’s objectives of addressing supposed “voter fraud”.
In a recent primetime television address, the president repeated false claims about the supposed fallibility of the 2020 US presidential election results, alleging voter fraud, noncitizen voting and a host of other misleading or incorrect statements. Election officials from across the political spectrum lambasted the speech and reasserted the reliability of US elections.
Thomson Reuters is owned by the Woodbridge Company, a holding company for the Thomson family, frequently described as the richest family in Canada. The media company also owns the news agency Reuters and the Globe and Mail newspaper.
A spokesperson for Thomson Reuters said it does not comment on customer contracts, and referred to a page on the company’s website about Clear.
The post says there are “misunderstandings” about the tool, and that it is licensed “exclusively to select businesses, law enforcement and government agencies to help expedite investigative processes in legitimate legal investigations”.
The company emphasises that “our investigative solutions are not surveillance tools.”
Lewis said the federal government should deny export permits to companies selling equipment to ICE, and pull public subsidies or contracts from any companies that have dealings with the agency. In January, the NDP made similar calls following the shooting deaths of two US citizens by ICE in Minneapolis.
“If the Carney government is serious about Canadian economic independence, it should move to block this contract,” Lewis said.
The prime minister’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the Thomson Reuters contract.
Joel Bakan, a law professor at the University of British Columbia and author of several books on the unethical behaviour of corporations, said the legal framework does exist in Canada to bar companies from working with ICE.
“Companies are not allowed to engage with various rogue regimes, authoritarian regimes, and certainly enemy regimes,” he said. “It’s definitely within the jurisdiction of the government, including the federal government of Canada, to impose various kinds of limitations.”
He pointed to Canada’s Special Economic Measures Act, the country’s primary sanctions law, which can authorise the government to restrict trade in relations to human rights violations. “As a matter of realpolitik, I can’t imagine the federal government invoking this against the US, but it is at least arguable that ICE has been involved in such violations,” he said.

summary:
Economists’ warning comes as escalating Middle East crisis pushes global crude oil back above $US100 a barrel

  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Australian households face the prospect of a Reserve Bank interest rate hike and petrol prices above $2 a litre over the coming weeks, economists warn, as the escalating Middle East crisis pushes global crude back above $US100 a barrel.

full_text:
Australian households face the prospect of a Reserve Bank interest rate hike and petrol prices above $2 a litre over the coming weeks, economists warn, as the escalating Middle East crisis pushes global crude back above $US100 a barrel.
Financial markets now see an even chance the RBA board will deliver a fourth cash rate increase at the next meeting on 11 August.
Warwick McKibbin, the director of the ANU’s Centre for Applied Macroeconomic Analysis, said crude oil prices were likely to stay elevated for “at least a year” as the US-Iran war entered a new and more dangerous phase.
The Houthis’ blockade of Saudi Arabian oil through the Red Sea and the Ukrainians’ increasingly successful destruction of Russian energy infrastructure had heaped further pressure on global oil supply, McKibbin said.
“Getting access to supplies looks different now than it did a few months ago. All the reserves have been run down, particularly in the US. It’s quite a serious situation for the world to be in.”
The phasing down of the government’s fuel tax relief to 16 cents per litre and this month’s 37% jump in the international Brent crude benchmark has pushed the cost of unleaded to $1.80 a litre, up from a recent low of about $1.50 at the beginning of the month, according to Motormouth.
Johnathan McMenamin, a senior economist at Barrenjoey, said higher global prices and the end of the remaining fuel excise discount after 2 August meant unleaded would march back above $2 a litre over coming weeks.
“That is an uncomfortable level for households, but it isn’t something we are too unfamiliar with,” McMenamin said.
Diesel prices are up by about 50 cents in July to about $2.20 a litre in the major East Coast cities.
Climbing fuel prices will be another blow to the Reserve Bank’s efforts to bring inflation down while managing the damage to the economy from high energy costs.
McMenamin believes the central bank will pull the trigger next month – a view he had even before the latest developments in the Middle East.
“People will start to see fuel prices go up again, and the concern will be that inflation expectations will once again lift among households and businesses,” he said.
“It does matter for how long the oil price is $US100 a barrel – if it’s here for only a couple of days and quickly reverses, then that will provide some relief.
“But, clearly, we’ve all lost confidence in where it [the oil price] will be in six months.”
With the economy already slowing sharply, not all economists are convinced that the RBA needs to hike again.
Sally Auld, NAB’s chief economist, said she had never assumed the sharp drop in oil prices during the ceasefire was sustainable, even without a major escalation in the conflict.
“But we did think it was going to be just one big spike around March and April, before it settled down. Now it looks like it will be more of a grind, or maybe rolling mini-spikes,” Auld said.
Inflation remains too high but is tracking a little below where the RBA had forecast, Auld said, while unemployment was running a little higher. That combination would be enough to keep the RBA on hold while they waited for a slowing economy to take the steam out of price pressures, she said.
Auld warned that not all Australians will be able to cope with higher borrowing costs and climbing fuel costs.
“If you get an intensification of cost of living pressures plus another rate hike, for a certain segment of households that would be a pretty challenging situation and you would start to worry the economic adjustment won’t be so benign.”

title: Pauline Hanson’s domestic violence comments were no stumble
summary:
The One Nation leader has allied herself with men’s rights activists for years, consistently suggesting women routinely make false allegations of violence

  • Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

For a decade, Pauline Hanson has been beating the same drum.

Her comments this week – suggesting domestic violence was a “two-way street” and questioning why women did not simply leave abusive relationships – have caused significant concern and been labelled “dangerous” by experts and other commentators.

Continue reading...
full_text:
For a decade, Pauline Hanson has been beating the same drum.
Her comments this week – suggesting domestic violence was a “two-way street” and questioning why women did not simply leave abusive relationships – have caused significant concern and been labelled “dangerous” by experts and other commentators.
But they are not, as they’ve been portrayed, another “gaffe” by the stumbling One Nation leader as she attempts to stabilise her party’s polls that show it might become a new electoral force in Australia.
The comments make plain something that has been a driving force for the populist leader since her return to parliament in 2016.
One Nation’s political ascendancy in recent months has been built on replicating anti-immigrant and hard right pivots in the United States and the UK. Hanson’s own second coming was built on an allyship with groups of anti-feminist men and heavily influenced by domestic violence allegations against her son, Adam Hanson, which she says were false.
In 2019, Hanson used parliamentary privilege to call her former daughter-in-law “nasty” and accuse her of making false claims about her son. She has consistently – inside and outside parliament – made claims, rejected by experts and evidence, that suggest women routinely make false allegations of violence for advantage in the family law system.
Speaking in 2017, on domestic violence orders, Hanson said: “Women, mostly women, are going around throwing them around left, right and centre.”
In 2021 on Sky News, Hanson said: “There are men who have been accused of these things that didn’t, it didn’t happen.
“It shows you how lies and perjury are leading to the failure of Australia’s family law system and contributing to the death of 21 men by suicide and the murder of one woman each week.”
The “21 men” figure has been repeatedly cited by Hanson, her colleague Malcolm Roberts, and others in One Nation as a campaigning point. The figure comes from a men’s rights organisation, the Australian Brotherhood of Fathers (ABF), and has been debunked by factcheckers.
The ABF have been among Hanson’s biggest cheerleaders since her re-election. Roberts has been particularly close to the group, visiting several times, and recording a special video message for a gathering.
One of the first things Roberts did after a federal parliament hearing in 2019 – when he claimed without evidence there were “many instances” of women making up domestic violence allegations – was to phone the ABF’s founder, Leith Erikson.
The ABF has claimed in Facebook posts to have received donations from One Nation, and the political party has held community barbecues in support of the men’s group.
The trope that women fabricate violence claims against men is a common grievance of men’s rights groups, but experts say there is no evidence to support this.
Growing political influence
After the 2019 election, Hanson’s return to the senate became more than a political curiosity. The Morrison government, four seats short of a senate majority, suddenly needed her support to pass legislation.
The government’s sop to Hanson was to accede to her request for a family law inquiry, and to make her the deputy chair (she introduced herself at hearings as the “co-chair”). 
 It is particularly instructive, for all those playing along at home and wondering what One Nation might do with newfound political influence, to understand that the last time Hanson was in a position to ask for something, she chose an inquiry that became a formal platform for misogynists and groups pushing unsupported claims that the system is loaded against men.
Hanson livestreamed the hearings to her Facebook page. Commenters called expert witnesses and MPs things like “man-hater” and “dirty snake”.
The hearings in March 2020 took place less than a month after the murders of Hannah Clarke and her children.
When an expert witness, the Griffith University law professor Zoe Rathus, mentioned the case, Hanson responded:
“I totally agree that what happened to Hannah and her children was horrendous and should never happen. But it’s on both sides. I have read your report, and it’s all about women. Do you agree that there are men who are aggrieved, men who face domestic violence, men who are taking their own lives?
“Do you admit that there are men facing domestic violence?”
 Rathus responded: “I would prefer if you didn’t ask me whether I ‘admit’ things. I’m not really here to admit things. I’m here to present my research.
“The statistics are very clear that domestic violence is something that is very gendered and that violence in the home happens more often by men towards women.”
Hanson carried on undeterred.
Her comments this week, in the shadow of four more alleged domestic violence homicides, have understandably triggered more backlash because of One Nation’s political ascendancy.
As a fringe politician needing only to win a senate quota every six years, Hanson’s views only needed to appeal to a small, angry cohort.
The common wisdom is that as One Nation heads for the mainstream – its founder will need to temper her more extreme ideas to keep her coalition of disengaged and aggrieved voters together.
But that’s not Pauline Hanson.
Ben Smee is Guardian Australia’s Queensland state correspondent

title: How dangerous are wildfires and how can we stop them from getting worse?
summary:
The conditions for ferocious fires are expected to worsen as the planet heats up, putting more people at risk

Fierce wildfires after back-to-back heatwaves have forced tens of thousands of people across southern Europe to flee their homes, while powerful infernos across Canada and the US choke big cities with thick smoke.

Continue reading...
full_text:
Fierce wildfires after back-to-back heatwaves have forced tens of thousands of people across southern Europe to flee their homes , while powerful infernos across Canada and the US choke big cities with thick smoke.
How deadly are wildfires? Wildfires directly kill hundreds of people each year. Though they may seem apocalyptic, the death toll is far lower than from floods , which kill thousands, and from heatwaves , which kill hundreds of thousands.
But when you factor in smoke, the human cost rises rapidly. The latest study  estimates that the air pollution spewed by wildfires kills a staggering 1.5 million people each year. The toxic fumes can reach so far that tendrils of smoke from Australian bushfires have menaced South America, while smoke from Canadian fires – which regularly suffocate cities across the US – have fouled the air in Europe. Last year, a study  attributed 22,000 early deaths in Europe to Canadian wildfire smoke in 2023, out of a total of 82,000 deaths.
What causes wildfires? Many things can spark a wildfire: natural causes such as lightning, faulty infrastructure such as downed power lines, or people behaving badly. Devastating blazes in recent years have been started by smokers tossing cigarette butts, tourists failing to put out campfires, and even arsonists intentionally setting nature alight.
But whether those sparks turn into small fires or raging blazes depends on the weather. Fires need hot, dry fuel to burn, and they spread further with strong winds.
How does climate breakdown affect wildfires? Fossil fuel pollution has heated the planet by about 1.3C, raising the risk of prolonged heat that turns forests and grasslands into tinderboxes. In some regions, such as the Mediterranean, global heating is also fuelling  droughts that dry out lush greenery.
Scientists have found that such shifts have made the wildfires that have happened this year in places including California, South Korea and Australia more likely – in some cases doubling the chance of extreme weather conditions that help fires spread.
A blaze engulfs trees in Llano, California, on 10 July.  Photograph: Ethan Swope/APAre wildfires getting worse? Even as the planet has heated up, the area torched by fires has fallen. This is because people have taken nature that used to burn freely and turned it into farms or cities – in recent decades mainly in Africa – that stop the spread of flames. The latest models  find land use changes and other human drivers have shrunk the burned area by 19.1% since 1900, while climate changes increased it by 15.8% – resulting in a small decline of 3.3% overall.
Will wildfires become more common? The conditions for ferocious fires are expected to worsen as the planet bakes. Two separate indices of fire weather project a steady rise in the number of days with high fire danger as temperatures inch higher, a recent study  found.
By the end of the century, the total burned area is projected to rise by 40% even in an optimistic scenario for cutting carbon pollution, according to a separate study . In a worst-case scenario, it is set to double.
Wildfire smoke engulfs Toronto as unhealthy air reaches New York - video How can we adapt to wildfires? The danger that wildfires pose to people and property can drop sharply by managing land better. This can include creating fire breaks to stem the spread of an inferno, stopping new settlement in places prone to fires, and even sending herds of goats into abandoned farmland to graze away overgrown vegetation.
In some places firefighters are trying the technique of intentionally burning land to avoid a buildup of fuel that could lead to catastrophic fires – a long-running Indigenous practice in Australia and North America that European fire experts are starting to adopt.
Would better forest management solve the problem? Not on its own. Land abandonment and fire suppression is a big contributor to the buildup of fuel that allows blazes in parts of the US and the Mediterranean to explode into mega-fires, but in Canada, most of the burning takes place in boreal forests that were never managed by humans. These fires are being intensified by rising global average temperatures that worsen the risk of severe fire weather.
How can I stay safe during a wildfire? If you live somewhere at risk of wildfires, put a plan together before disaster strikes. This could include identifying safe routes and nearby shelters, and packing an emergency bag. Some fire services recommend creating a safe zone around your home that is free from leaves and flammable materials.
Experts say you should vacate immediately if authorities tell you to – or if your home is at risk but warnings have not come. To avoid the smoke, keep windows closed and use respirator masks.

title: Poland’s main rightwing opposition splits after loyalty pledge ultimatum
summary:
Former prime minister Mateusz Morawiecki and allies say they were forced out over factional disagreements

Poland’s main opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party has split, after former prime minister Mateusz Morawiecki and his allies said they were forced out over factional disagreements on policy direction ahead of next year’s parliamentary election.

Speaking at a press conference, the party’s longtime leader, Jarosław Kaczyński, said dozens of members of parliament effectively left the party after refusing to sign a loyalty oath.

Continue reading...
full_text:
Poland’s main opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party has split, after former prime minister Mateusz Morawiecki and his allies said they were forced out over factional disagreements on policy direction ahead of next year’s parliamentary election.
Speaking at a press conference, the party’s longtime leader, Jarosław Kaczyński, said dozens of members of parliament effectively left the party after refusing to sign a loyalty oath.
All those who refused to sign the pledge were deemed by Kaczyński to have effectively resigned from the party. The rebel MPs insisted they did not intend to leave, but conceded they may be formally expelled at a party leadership meeting on Tuesday.
“Everyone knew what they were signing, and at the same time everyone knew what the consequences of not signing would be … it’s all done,” Kaczyński said, adding that the decision will be formally processed on Tuesday.
Law and Justice is one of Poland’s two most successful political parties since 1989, having ruled the country for 10 years in 2005-2007 and 2015-2023, with its candidates winning four out of eight presidential elections.
Despite losing to a coalition of pro-European parties led by former European Council president Donald Tusk and going into opposition at the last election in 2023, PiS remained the largest party in the Polish parliament – a status it could lose as a result of the split.
The resignations come after months of increasingly bitter disagreements in Poland’s main opposition party as it lost its grip on the Polish right.
Over the past two years, it struggled to respond to the emerging libertarian-right Confederation and the far-right ethno-nationalist Confederation of the Polish Crown, splitting the conservative vote into three.
In April, Morawiecki, who served as Poland’s prime minister between 2017 and 2023, set up a growth-oriented policy group in a bid to broaden the party’s electoral appeal on the centre-right. It is planning to host its inaugural public event later this month.
But the move was harshly criticised by Kaczyński and his allies, who questioned the former prime minister’s loyalty amid rumours of his growing disenchantment with the party’s drift towards the nationalist right and interests of the older electorate.
After tense talks behind closed doors, Kaczyński told all MPs to sign a loyalty pledge committing them not to work with any other political groups or face expulsion, with the deadline set for midnight on Thursday.
Speaking to reporters on Friday, Morawiecki said his group “until the very last moment fought for the unity of the party” as it wanted PiS to follow “a strategy of two lungs” to mobilise younger centre-right voters and entrepreneurs to boost its electoral prospects in 2027.
Morawiecki blamed a circle of “plotters” around Kaczyński for leading the party into the crisis and issuing the loyalty ultimatum. He confirmed the splinter group includes 40 MPs, three members of the European parliament and one senator.
“The situation emerging on the Polish right is that … there is no single dominant force, it comprises many different factions,” he said.
“For me and for us, these disputes within the right are like squabbles within a family, but in fact we will be directing the brunt of our attack at this very bad government by Donald Tusk.”
He declined to speculate on whether the group will form a new party, and instead urged PiS leaders to “take a step back”.
Morawiecki, a former senior banker and one-time economic adviser to Tusk, remains one of the most recognisable leaders on the right.
But he is also the face of the highly divisive eight years of Law and Justice’s last term in power, seen by critics through the prism of democratic backsliding, conflicts with the European Union and alleged irregularities and abuses of power.
He is also the leader of the European Conservatives and Reformists party in the European parliament, a grouping of like-minded parties in Europe, including Giorgia Meloni’s Brothers of Italy.
His departure is likely to further splinter the vote on the right. Hypothetical polls including a new party had it polling at about 6%.
The next parliamentary election is scheduled for October 2027.

title: Middle East crisis latest: US carries out strikes across Iran as Tehran targets American bases in region
summary:
Latest attacks come after Trump vowed ‘major military punishment’ for Tehran and its Houthi allies

Benjamin Netanyahu will meet Donald Trump at the White House on Tuesday, the Israeli prime minister’s office said.

“As part of the visit, the prime minister will meet with President Trump at the White House on Tuesday and attend the funeral service for Senator Lindsey Graham, a friend of Israel,” Netanyahu’s office said, adding that he will depart for Washington on Monday.

Continue reading...
full_text:
An Omani delegation has arrived in Iran to discuss a framework “to establish appropriate mechanisms for managing ship traffic in the strait of Hormuz,” Iranian state news agency IRNA reports.
Tehran has maintained that it’s open to managing the strait in coordination with Oman, though the US and Gulf states have rejected the idea.
BenjaminNetanyahu will meet Donald Trump at the White House on Tuesday, the Israeli prime minister’s office said.
“As part of the visit, the prime minister will meet with President Trump at the White House on Tuesday and attend the funeral service for Senator Lindsey Graham, a friend of Israel,” Netanyahu’s office said, adding that he will depart for Washington on Monday.
Netanyahu’s visit comes at a time when tensions have mounted between the two leaders over the handling of the war with Iran and as Trump threatens to escalate US military action.
Since Trump’s return to the White House last year, the two have already met six times, but this will be the first such meeting in five months. At the last one in February, Netanyahu made the case for the joint offensive against Iran that Trump launched with him weeks later.
Iran pushes back on report that it rejected US ceasefire proposal sent via Iraq
Iran has pushed back on a New York Times (paywall) report from Thursday that Tehran had rejected a US ceasefire deal presented by the Iraqi prime minister, calling the report “completely diversionary and misleading,” according to state media IRNA.
The NYT reported that the proposal was the only one on the table, and Tehran was not interested in a temporary deal which left the question of control of the strait of Hormuz unresolved, citing Iranian officials.
The IRNA report claimed the proposal was for a “temporary 10-day ceasefire”. Full details of the proposal have not been published.
“Iran has always regarded diplomacy as having intrinsic value,” an unnamed Iranian official said, according to IRNA. “The problem of the escalation of conflict in the region stems exclusively from the United States’ breach of its promises and violation of the commitments contained in the June 18 memorandum of understanding.”
Baghdad has also denied the NYT report. Ali al-Zaidi’s trip to Iran followed his recent visit to the White House where he met with Donald Trump.
The Iraqi prime minister’s media office said the “claims” in the report were “completely baseless and had no connection to reality”, according to a statement published by the Iraqi News Agency (INA).
The office urged media outlets “to verify information, rely on official sources and refrain from circulating unsubstantiated reports or claims attributed to anonymous sources”.
Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Corps warned civilians in the Middle East on Friday to stay away from US forces, state media reported.
In an interview carried out by state TV, the IRGC said:
We warn the general public in countries where American soldiers are stationed to immediately stay out of a radius of 500 metres from the places where American soldiers are hiding, in order to be safe.
Jordan’s military said it intercepted seven missiles and six drones launched by Iran on Friday.
The military said the interceptions, performed by air defence systems and air force planes, “resulted in no casualties or material damage,” according to AFP.
Earlier on Friday, the Iranian army said it had launched drone attacks targeting US military personnel and military targets in Bahrain and Jordan after the US carried out its 13th consecutive night of strikes against Iran.
US carries out strikes across Iran as Tehran targets American bases in region
US missiles struck targets across Iran on Friday after Donald Trump vowed “major military punishment” for Tehran and its Houthi allies in Yemen for extending the Middle East war to a second major shipping chokepoint, the mouth of the Red Sea.
The US Central Command said it targeted Iranian military command centres, communication networks, drone storage facilities, coastal surveillance sites and maritime capabilities.
Iranian state broadcaster IRIB reported that explosions were reported in Khondab, Khorramabad, Konarak and Jask.
Meanwhile, as Reuters reports, Iranian armed forces responded by firing a wave of retaliatory attacks on at US bases in neighbouring Arab countries and warning people there that they may strike non-military buildings used by US personnel.
The Iranian army said it used drones to target facilities in Bahrain and Jordan, with attacks also reported in Kuwait and Iraq.
It said Trump’s threats only strengthened its resolve.

summary: Many Argentines condemned their players’ racist chants and aggressive behavior, but rejected what felt like a sweeping stigmatization of their entire nation.

title: How OpenAI Lost Control of an AI Model—and What Needs to Change
summary: TIME spoke with experts and insiders about what must change to prevent the next AI escape.
full_text:
OpenAI was evaluating its artificial intelligence models’ ability to exploit vulnerable software when instead the models hacked the infrastructure surrounding the test, broke containment, and attacked a real company, OpenAI revealed on July 21. Observers say this is the first real-world instance of AI doing something researchers have long worried about: a loss-of-control scenario. If the industry fails to learn from it, it is unlikely to be the last.
Hugging Face, a company that hosts AI models and datasets, was the target of the autonomous attack, and reported the incident to local police before it knew OpenAI’s models were responsible. The breach was serious, but the immediate consequences were limited. Had similar behavior occurred inside a hospital, power grid, or other critical system, it could have been much worse.
Many have called the incident a “warning shot.” TIME spoke with experts and insiders about what it would take to heed that warning before a similar failure produces consequences that are harder to contain.
What happened?
On July 16, Hugging Face said it had been hit by an unusually automated cyberattack. Over the course of a weekend, AI agents carried out thousands of actions across many temporary virtual computers, moving through the company’s internal systems and shifting the infrastructure coordinating the attack between online services to keep it running. Five days later, OpenAI disclosed that its own models were responsible.
The models were trying to cheat on a cybersecurity test. OpenAI had placed them inside what it called a “highly isolated environment,” with only limited access to an internal service used to download approved software. They found a previously unknown flaw in that service, used it to break into other OpenAI systems and eventually reached the open internet. From there, they inferred that Hugging Face might hold material related to the test, broke into its systems and obtained information that helped them score higher.
“If a model of this capability level cannot be contained, what should we expect for future, much more powerful models? This is an important wake-up call both for risks from loss of control of powerful AI systems as well as organizational security for frontier labs,” says Marius Hobbhahn, CEO and founder of Apollo Research, which tests AI models for deception and scheming.
Requiring disclosures before incidents become catastrophic
How long were the agents running? Did they work in unison? What was the prompt? These details remain unknown, at least to the public. Several experts TIME spoke with stressed that the lack of details make the severity of the incident hard to judge.
OpenAI did not respond to TIME’s request for comment, but has said it has partnered with Hugging Face to conduct a thorough investigation and will share more details once complete. But perhaps more worryingly, OpenAI is not legally compelled to disclose the incident in the first place.
California’s SB 53 and New York’s RAISE Act are recently passed state-level laws that require large AI companies to disclose critical safety incidents, but only if an incident risks causing more than 50 deaths or serious injuries, or more than $1 billion in property damage. “They have made the bar so high for anything to qualify, only the most grievous incidents will actually be reported,” says Mackenzie Arnold, director of U.S. policy at LawAI, an independent think tank focused on the legal challenges posed by artificial intelligence.
“The version of the RAISE Act that the NY Legislature passed would have required disclosure of this ‘incident.’ After lobbying from OpenAI, Bloomberg, and a16z, the final version the Governor signed allows companies to hide events like this,” Alex Bores, New York state representative and the bill’s sponsor posted to X. “I'm glad OpenAI chose to disclose this crime. The law shouldn't give them a choice,” he wrote.
Stronger containment
If AI can slip out of its box, you need a stronger box.
“Externally, this feels like a big warning shot, but internally, related incidents have been happening for a while,” says an OpenAI staffer, who spoke under the condition of anonymity. The day before OpenAI disclosed the incident, the company revealed that it had shut down another internal deployment after it realized it had slipped out of its sandbox—a digitally, rather than physically, separated environment. “Models have broken out of sandboxes before, and we always try to patch them,” the staffer says. “But the problem is … it's impossible to patch every single thing that a creative AI can do.”
The problem is not unique to OpenAI. Anthropic disclosed in April that it realized an internal deployment of Mythos had gained unauthorized access after one of its researchers received an email from the model while having lunch in a park.
As models surpass human ability to craft escape routes, the challenge of containment becomes daunting. “I think we do need to do that, but I think we also need to be prepared for a world where even best practices aren't really good enough,” says Peter Wildeford, head of policy at the AI Policy Network, a nonprofit that advocates for policies to help America prepare for a world where AI matches human cognition.
But while in theory, a superhuman AI system might outmaneuver even the most secure containers, there are also actions AI companies could take right now to improve security. Currently, there are no laws governing the security of internal deployments.
“Sandboxes are actually notoriously insecure,” says Heidy Khlaaf, chief AI scientist at AI Now Institute, and a former safety systems engineer contractor at OpenAI. The fact that the models were permitted to connect to a service for downloading packages meant the environment was not truly sealed off, she adds.
In a previous role, Khlaaf audited security at dozens of technology companies. Before that, she worked auditing high-risk systems, like those used inside nuclear power plants—which often “air gap” systems, physically cutting them from internet access. “What we consider safe in a nuclear plant is so different from what big tech considers safe.”
Catching mischievous agents in real time
The Hugging Face incident reveals the importance of real-time monitoring.
Though details of the precise timeline are scant, Hugging Face has said the agents worked over a “weekend,” suggesting that they were able to break containment and get up to no good for an extended period before OpenAI noticed and intervened. Actions carried out internally by agents on OpenAI’s Codex platform are carefully monitored, the OpenAI staffer says, but models undergoing evaluation are deployed on a separate system that is not monitored by default.
Zack Korman, CEO of Oslo-based agent-oversight startup Embroidery, says real-time agent monitoring—even outside top AI companies—is commonplace, and to not carefully oversee a cybersecurity evaluation is “irresponsible.” You should be confident models cannot break free, “but also have monitoring just in case you're wrong,” he says.
OpenAI has said “this incident points to the need to further strengthen our model’s alignment, cyber protections during evaluation time, and monitoring during internal testing.”
Steering development towards safer AI systems
To prevent models from taking actions, OpenAI typically installs guardrails on its models after training to reduce the chance they’ll engage in harmful actions. In this instance, those cyber guardrails were disabled to properly measure its performance.
But the ultimate aim of the field of “AI alignment” is to ensure that such guardrails become less necessary as AI models naturally behave as intended. This is seen as particularly important to those who believe AI may become smart enough to route around guardrails.

title: Christopher Nolan on Helen, Athena, and His New Ending for The Odyssey
summary: The director discusses Zendaya and Lupita Nyong'o's characters
full_text:
This spring, I was among the first journalists to speak with Christopher Nolan about his highly anticipated adaptation of The Odyssey. Now, the movie is out and has become Nolan’s biggest worldwide opening ever.
In our initial interview, Nolan was reluctant to discuss the ending of The Odyssey. He’s known as the master of the last-act twist, and likes leaving the audience with more questions than answers. He told me he never wants to impose his interpretation on others. (Are Cobbs’ kids in Inception real or imagined? You decide.) But when I hopped on the phone again shortly before the film’s release to have a spoiler-filled chat about the film’s final act—readers beware!—he offered some insight as to why he made certain changes when adapting the epic poem.
We discussed the surprising parallels between The Odyssey and Oppenheimer, why Nolan decided to give Odysseus and Penelope the happy ending they don’t get in Homer’s epic poem, and how to interpret Zendaya’s mysterious character: Is she actually a goddess or merely a manifestation of Odysseus’ guilt? We also dug into Zeus’ Law and the deeper meaning behind Helen’s scarred face.
TIME: Odysseus is a man who suffers from PTSD, and, in your interpretation, who believes he’s responsible for the end of a civilization because he violated the ethical code by which the ancient Greeks lived their lives.
Nolan: My form of storytelling is, you take a hero, as we did with Oppenheimer, and Oppenheimer has all these flaws, all of these complexities. You find an actor who can take the audience on a journey with that character and make mistakes with that character and not judge that character. And then you step back from that character and go, “Well, how did we get here?”
[For this movie,] you do that through Odysseus’ men. That’s one of the things in the poem that’s breezed over—the way in which the crew ends up getting killed one by one, despite his leadership. In the process of adaptation, you go, “That’s actually pretty interesting. Maybe we need to make that more center stage.” What’s the relationship between him and his crew? How do they feel about how he’s leading them and the things that befall them?
He’s a guy who makes a lot of mistakes. His ultimate mistake is the horse. So there’s a sort of tragic flaw right from the beginning in our telling.
My interpretation of Zendaya’s character is that she is not Athena as Odysseus initially present her—gods don’t exist in this world—but a manifestation of his guilt. During the sack of Troy, we see her as a priestess in the Temple of Athena, and the Greeks behead her. For Odysseus, she encapsulates the chaos that the horse has wrought on the world. But my editor did not interpret it that way. I am hoping you will settle our disagreement.
I couldn’t possibly answer that because I learned very early on with Memento that it’s unfair to define the experience for the audience by answering questions like that.
Here’s what I will say: For me, what was important was that we view the gods the way that people at the time might have viewed them. So they’re seeing evidence of the gods in nature. They’re seeking and finding gods and the influence of gods in the people around them. Odysseus says to Telemachus, “Don’t look for gods in men. You’ll just be disappointed.” And some of what Odysseus says about divinity, to me, is somebody who’s protesting a bit too much, someone trying to live in denial of their own instincts and their own practices.
I was struck by the parallels between Oppenheimer and Odysseus, two brilliant men who create a tool of devastating destruction and then struggle with the guilt of what they have done. When I spoke to Matt Damon, I asked, “What did you think when you first read the script?” And he said, “It felt like Oppenheimer.” I assume that was a conscious choice.
Yes. If I’ve done a film right, it leaves me with questions. It leaves me with things I want to keep exploring and thinking about. And Oppenheimer fed very much into my reading of the story of Odysseus.
John Leguizamo [who plays Odysseus’ friend Eumaeus] says it at the very beginning: “That’s very clever, but your cleverness will get you in trouble.” As it does again and again and again. This is where it ties into Oppenheimer: Just because you can doesn’t mean you should. The parallels were pretty apparent to me as I figured out how to adapt it.
The movie hinges on this idea that by creating the Trojan Horse, Odysseus destroys “Zeus’ law.” That’s the movie’s term for the ancient Greek concept of xenia—the respectful relationship between host and guest—which can be tricky to explain to a modern audience. Why was it important to include?
When you find these things are difficult to deal with, sometimes the solution is just to dive in and make it everything. I didn’t use the term xenia because you don’t want to throw too many terms at people. But it’s essentially the golden rule. It all comes back to weather, to geography. When you leave the house, you are depending on the kindness of strangers, and you have to trust that when you arrive somewhere after weeks or months of traveling, that you will be fed, you will be given water. Three thousand years ago, that was everything. You were always at the mercy of strangers. And so this idea that a stranger could be a god in disguise, it’s very powerful as the underpinning of a belief system.
At different points in the film, if man is given the opportunity, he becomes a beast. A soldier will behead a priestess. You imply that Menelaus purposefully scarred Helen’s face either because he believes she’s responsible for the Trojan War or to prevent anyone from taking her again.
That line, “The face that launched 1,000 ships, or maybe just 500” just occurred to me to write. Sometimes what you do as a writer is purely instinctive. I felt the poem didn’t necessarily address what it is for Helen to be brought back by Menelaus and how that would ever work. How would that relationship be? How could it possibly be anything other than the most acidic, awful marriage?
You don’t buy that he saw her face and said, “She’s so beautiful I can’t kill her after all,” as he does in the myth?
There’s a lot of sh-t that’s happened in that relationship, and we have a very brief moment of time with them in this story. I was looking for a shorthand way to communicate the aftermath of the war and how it’s been traumatic for the entire world.
You also see this idea of man as beast in the scene with Circe. She says that Odysseus’ men would have raped and killed her—that they’re pigs. Then you get to the end and see the sack of Troy and the horror of what they did. She’s right.
Circe articulates it well in the film. I love the way Samantha [Morton] has played the part. Talking about choices of adaptation, the end of the poem is so grim and so misogynistic, I had to exclude some of that material. But I didn’t want to completely take it off the table in terms of what it is saying about men and the way they wage war.
And yet you give Odysseus and Penelope a happy ending that they do not get in the poem.
Well, it is the fall of civilization, so there is a fairly bleak sensibility. The end is talking about cycles, and you can view cycles pessimistically: History is doomed to repeat itself. But there is also something optimistic about those cycles. As Penelope says, “Civilization will rise again.” There is rebirth and regrowth.
For me, it was important in looking at the ending to try and strike the right balance between pessimism and optimism—pessimism about what might have precipitated the Bronze Age catastrophe and the optimism that positive things will reassert themselves.

title: Here Are the Candidates Vying for Sen. Lindsey Graham’s Seat
summary: The race is looking crowded ahead of a key deadline for the special primary election to replace the late Senator on the November ballot.
full_text:
The deadline for candidates to file their intent to run in the special Republican primary election to fill the late Sen. Lindsey Graham’s seat is next week, and the race is already looking quite crowded.
Graham, who represented South Carolina in the Senate for more than two decades, had been seeking his fifth term in the upper chamber before he died of an aortic dissection last week. Days after his death, South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster appointed Graham’s sister, Darline Graham Nordone, to finish out the remainder of his term, which ends in January.
Voters, meanwhile, will have the opportunity to pick a new Republican nominee to vie for a full term in his seat in the special Republican primary election on Aug. 11.
Candidates have until July 28 to file their intent to run. Here are the candidates who have announced their plans to enter the race so far.
Darline Graham Nordone
Nordone told Fox News’ Sean Hannity in an interview released on Monday that she plans to run for a full term in her brother’s Senate seat.
“I’m in,” she said during the interview.
A few days earlier, President Donald Trump urged Nordone to run for a full term.
“Darline, who comes from an absolutely incredible family, has been a WINNER all of her life and, should she accept, has my Complete and Total Endorsement in the Special Election for U.S. Senate in South Carolina,” Trump said in a Truth Social post last week.
Nordone, a mother of two, was a fervent supporter of her brother’s political career, but she herself had never before held public office. She spent years working in disabilities services.
Read More: Who is Darline Graham Nordone? Lindsey Graham’s Sister Appointed to Serve Out His Senate Term
Russell Fry
South Carolina Rep. Russell Fry also announced on Monday that he intends to run for the seat.
“Too many South Carolina families are struggling to make ends meet,” he said in a post on X. “We need a conservative fighter in the Senate who delivers real results. I will be your conservative MAGA candidate in the special primary Senate election this summer.”
Fry is also running for reelection for the House seat he currently holds. If he were to win both the Senate and House races, he would only be allowed to take on one of those roles.
Mark Sanford
Mark Sanford, a former South Carolina congressman and governor, said on Thursday that he will be entering the race to fill Graham’s seat.
“Our country is at a financial tipping point, and I can’t sit on the sidelines while Washington adds a trillion dollars to the debt every 100 days,” he said in a social media post. “I’ve spent my entire time in politics fighting this fight, and I’m running for U.S. Senate to keep the American dream alive for our sons, my grandson, and those you love.”
Sanford was at the center of a public scandal while serving as governor in 2009, when he admitted to having an extramarital affair. The admission came amid widespread doubts about his whereabouts one week that June, when his staff initially said that the governor was taking some time off to write and later that he was hiking the Appalachian Trail. Instead, he had traveled to Argentina in secret to visit his lover.
Still, Sanford brushed off calls to resign and went on to finish his term as governor. Sanford, who held a seat in the House before he became governor, was later reelected to the lower chamber and went on to serve three more terms there.
He also previously mounted an unsuccessful 2020 presidential campaign.
Mark Lynch
On July 13, businessman Mark Lynch confirmed that he will run for Graham’s seat in the Senate.
“A lot of you have asked. Yes, it’s official,” he said in a social media post. “I’m committed to finish what God has called us to since February of 2025. To bring the U.S. Senate seat of South Carolina back to TRUE Conservative leadership for the Republican party.”
Lynch previously challenged Graham in the Republican primary race for the seat in the upper chamber. He ultimately lost the race to Graham in the June 9 primary election, but he earned the second highest share of the vote, with just under 29%.
Ralph Norman
South Carolina Rep. Ralph Norman announced on July 18 that he plans to enter the special Republican primary race.
“It’s official! I’m running to represent the people of South Carolina in the U.S. Senate because we need a fighter who will stand with President Trump and carry on Lindsey Graham’s legacy!” he said in a post on X.
On Thursday, Norman posted a video of himself and South Carolina Rep. Nancy Mace, in which she endorsed him in the race. Some people had previously speculated that Mace herself might launch a bid for Graham’s seat, but she announced earlier this week that she would not be running.
“This is a once-in-a-generation opportunity to send a tried and true conservative to the United States Senate,” Mace said in the video Norman shared. “Ralph Norman doesn’t bend, he doesn’t break, and he doesn’t back down.”
Duke Buckner
Duke Buckner is also joining the race for Graham’s seat, according to local news outlet WIS News 10. Buckner has unsuccessfully run multiple campaigns to represent South Carolina in the House and Senate over the years.
“I am running because too many Americans are working harder and falling further behind,” Buckner told WIS News 10. “People should be able to afford a home, raise a family, and build a better life. We need to make it easier to build, expand opportunities in the skilled trades, and lower the cost of living.”
Mark McBride
Mark McBride—a former mayor of Myrtle Beach, South Carolina—said in a social media post on Wednesday that he had filed his intent to run in the Senate race the previous day.
In his post, McBride said that “a solid underlying platform” to his campaign was his disagreement with Trump launching the war in Iran.
“A vote on Tuesday, August 11th for Mark McBride is NOT a vote to continue to have our troops as sitting ducks in uninhabitable, destroyed former U.S. Bases in the Middle East,” he said. “A vote for Mark McBride is for a new direction for the Republican Party.”
Samuel Shepherd
Samuel Shepherd, who is a biochemical and medical engineer, also joined the crowded race this week, according to South Carolina Public Radio.
Clark Neilson
Clark Neilson, a land surveyor who appears to live in Charlotte, filed his intent to run in the special election as well, according to South Carolina Public Radio. He told the local news outlet that he had been thinking about running for office for a while.

title: The bond market hasn’t been this calm since the dot-com bust and the financial crisis. History warns of a rude awakening.
summary: Junk-bond spreads are near the lows reached before the financial crisis of 2007-09. Here’s how to hedge before the market wakes up.

title: Tesla’s car door defect could lead to tougher rules for everyone
summary: Tesla's electronic door handles that have been linked to several deaths could lead to tougher safety rules for the entire auto industry. In a notice published today, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration said that complaints about Tesla's mechanical door release don't warrant a defect investigation. Instead, the issue is better addressed through a broader […]
full_text:
Tesla’s electronic door handles that have been linked to several deaths could lead to tougher safety rules for the entire auto industry.
Tesla’s car door defect could lead to tougher rules for everyone
Over a dozen people have died after becoming trapped in their Tesla vehicles following a crash. Tesla’s electronic door handles could now spur new rules for the whole industry.
Over a dozen people have died after becoming trapped in their Tesla vehicles following a crash. Tesla’s electronic door handles could now spur new rules for the whole industry.
In a notice published today, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration said that complaints about Tesla’s mechanical door release don’t warrant a defect investigation. Instead, the issue is better addressed through a broader rulemaking that would “mandate a robust and obvious door egress system in all motor vehicles,” the safety regulator said. If finalized, all new vehicles would be subject to the new requirements.
Tesla’s door handles, which operate electronically and sit flush against the vehicle for improved aerodynamics, have been linked to several incidents in which people have been trapped inside their vehicles. In several incidents, Tesla passengers who survived the initial crash later sustained serious injuries or died after being trapped inside a burning vehicle.
China’s government banned electronic door handles for safety reasons earlier this year. And NHTSA has been investigating instances in which Tesla’s handles become inoperable as a result of low-voltage battery problems.
The notice was published after Kevin Clouse, a Silicon Valley engineer, filed a petition requesting a defect investigation to address allegations that “the emergency egress controls for the mechanical door release are not readily accessible and clearly identifiable.” Clouse filed the petition after experiencing the door failure during a crash:
The Petitioner stated that following a head-on collision, the MY 2022 Tesla Model 3 suffered a total loss of electrical power and caught fire. Due to the loss of power, the electric door handles became inoperative. The Petitioner stated he was unable to locate the mechanical door handle, forcing him to climb into the back seat and exit the vehicle through a rear passenger window.
NHTSA denied the petition, but said a broader rulemaking was warranted.
That said, don’t expect any immediate changes to the rules for electronic door handles. The rulemaking process can take anywhere from two to five years on average, meaning any new requirement wouldn’t likely emerge until 2030 or later. The auto industry also has been known to push back strongly against new rules that impose additional costs, such as they did with a new proposal to require more robust automatic emergency braking. Congress has also weighed in, introducing legislation that would require manual door releases in new cars and means for first responders to gain access to vehicles when power is lost.
Last year, Tesla said it would redesign its electronic door handles, though it didn’t say on what timeline. In an interview with Bloomberg, Tesla design chief Franz von Holzhausen said that the company is looking to make the handles more intuitive for occupants in “a panic situation.”
That’s cold comfort for the families of the victims who already lost their lives. Andrew McDevitt, who represents families in two of the fatal cases involving Tesla vehicles, called on NHTSA to move swiftly through the rulemaking process to develop and implement new federal safety standards to protect future vehicle occupants.
“Since the release of the Model S, Tesla has repeatedly received reports from consumers that its doors trap occupants in every situation from supermarket parking lots to serious crashes,” McDevitt said in a statement. “It is hard to understand how Tesla continues to justify releasing such dangerously designed vehicles. These families deserve justice, and we will keep pursuing their cases in court.”

full_text:
Most Chromebooks ship with only 8GB of RAM, which is enough for some people, but certainly not enough for me. Multitaskers who want more memory in their next Chromebook should check out Best Buy, which is discounting Acer’s Chromebook Plus Spin 514 for the remainder of the day. Originally $749 for the configuration with 12GB of RAM, a MediaTek Kompanio Ultra 910 processor, and 256GB of UFS storage, it’s down to $559 right now. It’s a good price for what we consider to be one of the best Chromebooks you can currently buy.
One of the best 2-in-1 Chromebooks is almost $200 off for today only
Also, you can get a great deal on Anker’s four-port 140W wall charger, 20 percent off Nintendo gift cards, and more.
Also, you can get a great deal on Anker’s four-port 140W wall charger, 20 percent off Nintendo gift cards, and more.
My colleague Antonio G. Di Benedetto had a lot of nice things to say about this model in his October 2025 review. He praised the capabilities of its Arm-based processor, which is uncommon for a Chromebook review, as well as its day-plus battery life. The Spin 514 is great to use as a laptop, with a tactile keyboard and satisfying mechanical trackpad, but its 14-inch 1920 x 1200 120Hz IPS touchscreen can bend backwards to be used as a tablet. No stylus is included, but you can use any USI 2.0 stylus you’d like.
If you want to know about other good discounted options, Lenovo’s Chromebook Plus 14 that Antonio likes a bit more is $649 (originally $999) at Best Buy. While it has the same processor and storage amount, it’s the model to buy instead if you want a little more RAM (16GB), an OLED screen, superior speakers, and fingerprint biometric support.
Other great, Verge-approved deals
- Anker’s 140W wall charger with three USB-C ports and a USB-A port is selling at an especially low price at eBay via Best Buy’s seller page. The charger costs $55.99 (originally $79.99). Meanwhile, it’s $79.99 for Prime members at Amazon, but includes a USB-C cable whereas the Best Buy option doesn’t. One of the most notable traits of this charger — its downward facing ports that reduce its sag in the outlet — has become common since it launched early last year. The silver charger can deliver up to 140W through two of its USB-C ports when a single device is plugged in. It automatically splits the power depending on how many gadgets you have plugged in.
- If you’re a Sam’s Club member, or perhaps may soon become one, you can get $100 in digital Nintendo gift cards for $79.98. You can purchase up to five, which is enough to buy a bunch of games and accessories through Nintendo, or even a console. It’ll cost you $400 to get $500 worth of credit, meaning you can save on a Switch 2 console if you want to stack the savings to their maximum. The Switch 2 will increase in price starting in September, rising from $449.99 to $499.99, so if you’re on the fence, buying one sooner than later is a wise choice.
- Many of Logitech’s recent PC accessories can connect wirelessly via 2.4GHz to its Bolt receiver. Whether you lost your old one, or perhaps you want to upgrade to the newer USB-C version of the Bolt receiver that’s included with the MX Master 4 mouse, Amazon and Walmart have USB-C Bolt receivers available at just over half off. Originally $14.99, they’re $7.24, making it less expensive to grab a spare to connect your devices to. If you want to pair your device to a new Bolt receiver, you’ll need to do that through Logitech’s Options Plus app on desktop PC.

full_text:
Boox’s new Tile lineup will take on Xteink’s popular e-readers that are small enough to stick on the back of an iPhone with MagSafe. As spotted by Good E-Reader, the first one is the Picco, which will feature a 3.97-inch front-lit, black-and-white e-paper display and expandable storage with an SD card slot. Boox confirmed to The Verge that the Picco is in the works, noting that it’s part of a new Tile lineup and will have an “accessible price point,” but without any other details about its plans, like specs, the specific price, or a release date.
Boox is taking on Xteink with its own tiny e-reader
The Boox Picco will feature a 3.97-inch front-lit display and expandable storage.
The Boox Picco will feature a 3.97-inch front-lit display and expandable storage.
The front-lit display could put it on par with Xteink’s new $99 X4 Pro e-reader, which The Verge’s Andrew Liszewski calls “the best tiny e-reader you can buy.” However, part of the appeal of Xteink’s little e-readers is their ability to magnetically stick to the back of a phone, and it’s not clear yet if the Boox Picco will have a similar feature.
It appears to have buttons in a promotional image, but it’s also not clear yet if it will rely solely on buttons, like the original Xteink X4, or also include a touchscreen. According to Good E-Reader, the Picco will likely have a minimal, tiled UI limited to basic apps like Neoreader, a music player, and a podcast player, putting it in a very different category than the Android-powered Boox Palma.

title: The tech-broification of American science has officially begun
summary: The Trump administration unveiled the first "Genesis Mission" grants on Thursday, directing $5 billion toward hundreds of AI-driven science projects in an effort the White House has described as "comparable in urgency and ambition to the Manhattan Project." At roughly the same time, Trump's science adviser Michael Kratsios was on Capitol Hill selling lawmakers on […]
full_text:
The Trump administration unveiled the first “Genesis Mission” grants on Thursday, directing $5 billion toward hundreds of AI-driven science projects in an effort the White House has described as “comparable in urgency and ambition to the Manhattan Project.” At roughly the same time, Trump’s science adviser Michael Kratsios was on Capitol Hill selling lawmakers on an equally grandiose promise: “A New Golden Age” of American science, one that would prioritize artificial intelligence, robotics, and nuclear energy and downplay life sciences.
The tech-broification of American science has officially begun
Trump’s ‘Golden Age’ of American science starts with dismantling it, while funneling billions into AI.
The tech-broification of American science has officially begun
Trump’s ‘Golden Age’ of American science starts with dismantling it, while funneling billions into AI.
Taken together, the two announcements offer the clearest picture yet of how Donald Trump wants to remake American science. They mark the latest front in a wider war on the research establishment — one that has worked to suppress “woke” or DEI projects, threatened funding for universities, researchers, and projects on ideological grounds, curtailed the flow of international students and researchers, and handed unprecedented control over federal funding to political appointees. The result has been the gradual, systemic dismantling of the long-established norms and institutions that, for all their flaws, helped turn the United States into the world’s scientific superpower.
Researchers say the vision is ill-conceived, contradictory, and less a blueprint for scientific renewal than a politicized power grab that fundamentally misunderstands how science works. It treats public research more like a Silicon Valley startup than a public good, privileging measurable returns and speed over the slow, uncertain, and unpredictable work that has produced some of history’s most consequential discoveries. Far from reviving US science, they warn, the agenda could prove disastrous for American research.
“We may well end up in the situation where AI will have a few major insights buried under mountains of slop, and the number of people with the experience and knowledge to tell the two apart may rapidly dwindle.”
The Genesis Mission grants span fields ranging from drug discovery and biomedical science to energy, advanced materials, and robotics. The 278 projects, reportedly selected from over 5,000 applications, all share a common premise: leveraging AI to accelerate scientific discovery. The Energy Department, which led this round of funding, said the project will unite national laboratories, industry, and academia to pursue “breakthroughs in energy dominance, discovery science, and national security.” Technology companies including Google, Microsoft, and OpenAI are also contributing millions of dollars in compute, AI credits, and other support to the initiative.
Kratsios explicitly linked the program to the administration’s broader science agenda, calling Genesis Mission “the culmination of the reforms suggested in” its “Golden Age” manifesto. Styled as a modern successor to Vannevar Bush’s 1945 policy report “Science, the Endless Frontier,” which shaped much of the postwar system of federal research funding, the lengthy document proposes shifting support away from institutions and toward individual scientists, while giving private companies a larger role in directing and conducting research, and political appointees more power to block grants they disagree with. AI features heavily, both as a tool for scientists and as an engine for discovery itself, and Kratsios encouraged government funds to increasingly go to AI use and individual researchers, rather than universities, traditional hubs of scholarship and research.
More broadly, the manifesto favors a goal-oriented and results-driven approach that resembles a Silicon Valley startup more than traditional scientific enterprise. Venture capital and startup culture are built around identifying promising people, projects, and ideas, setting clear goals with measurable targets, and moving quickly, iterating constantly, and cutting work that seems unlikely to deliver results. Science operates differently. Basic research can take years or decades before its importance or practical implications become apparent and it requires a system capable of supporting work of uncertain, even seemingly dubious, value. Its outcomes cannot always be predicted, and some of the most important discoveries emerge serendipitously from research pursuing entirely different questions.
A science funding system needs to account for those differences, said Claes de Vreese, a professor of AI and society at the University of Amsterdam in the Netherlands. “You cannot use venture capital to force breakthroughs while virtually already selling the patent.”
That model also stands in stark contrast to Bush’s championing of open-ended basic research pursued without an eye for immediate dividends, on the grounds that such work would ultimately yield applied breakthroughs. The scientific system built around that principle is what helped turn the United States into the world’s research superpower. Even so, it is not the first time the Trump administration has invoked Bush’s legacy to sell policies that would dismantle the system he helped create.
“You cannot use venture capital to force breakthroughs while virtually already selling the patent.”
Some of its proposals have obvious appeal, including reducing the administrative burdens on scientists, speeding up grantmaking, and making the system more flexible. Jason Shepherd, a professor of neurobiology at the University of Utah, told The Verge that “there are certainly some aspirations in this agenda that most US scientists would agree with: we need more stability, faster peer review, and more incentives to do high risk science.”
But Shepherd said the document looks like it “was written by political appointees without any real consultation with scientists” and warned that its assumptions science functions like a business were misplaced. “Academic science is different to VC funded startups or tech companies.”
It’s an important distinction to make considering Kratsios’ background. Unlike most White House science advisers, Kratsios is not a scientist in any sense of the word, and has no scientific credentials. He has a background in tech policy and finance, spending part of his working life at a fund run by Silicon Valley investor Peter Thiel.
Researchers say the report is permeated by this Silicon Valley mindset, as well as a profound lack of scientific understanding. “The report has no vision for how science works,” said Harvard professor Jeffrey Flier, former dean of the university’s medical school, adding that it “seems blissfully unaware” of the academic environment scientific research needs in order to flourish. “This is completely insane as an approach to reforming US science funding and operations,” he said, branding the report’s proposals a “major threat” and an effort to politicize and control science.

full_text:
This is Optimizer, a weekly newsletter sent from Verge senior reviewer Victoria Song that dissects and discusses the latest gizmos and potions that swear they’re going to change your life. Optimizer will be taking a two-week break and will be moving to Wednesdays starting August 12th. Opt in for Optimizer here.
What I track in a day
Living an optimized, self-quantified life can get a little out of hand.
What I track in a day
Living an optimized, self-quantified life can get a little out of hand.
My For You page thinks I love “What I eat in a day” videos. Most of the time, I watch them in a bid to suss out the latest wellness fads. But they can be an illuminating look into what people perceive to be healthy (or less-than-healthy) eating habits — even if a portion of them are likely faked for clout. In the same vein, I’ve gotten many requests from Verge readers over the years for a glimpse into what I track in a day as the resident senior wearables reviewer.
I get why there’s interest! Social media has reinforced the idea that if you do the same things as the “experts,” you too can achieve success. That’s why many people want to know what their favorite influencers eat in a day. But I’m a wearables reviewer, and that can require me to self-quantify in ways that I wouldn’t recommend for normal people. I’m tracking health to evaluate products and claims. That means things like how accurate GPS is or how workout intensity impacts battery life. I’m evaluating whether the metabolic insights derived by a $600 scale from my foot sweat will at all correlate with a CGM. Or, given a device’s feature set, I’m trying to figure out what the most common-sense ways are to incorporate a particular device into your daily life. Most people are fitness tracking to improve their health.
What I track in a day also changes depending on the time of year. Winter through early spring, for instance, is usually a lighter load because the product launch season is over. Summer through late fall, I’m like a ship covered in wearable barnacles. And as health companies start branching out into bodily fluids, my tracking regimen has never been more involved. Right now is an interesting moment to look into my nutso tracking schedule because the doctor cleared me to restart training, product launch season is just beginning, and for the past few weeks, I’ve started building a digital twin for my metabolism using Twin Health, a system that incorporates continuous glucose monitors, blood tests, and an array of other health sensors. So without further ado…
The roster
I try to test in product blocks. Right now, I’m focusing on metabolic tech. Ideally, you want to have control devices. If I’m testing a new smart ring, for instance, I should test it against the Oura Ring since that’s what most people will want to compare it to. Where possible, I want to also long-term test the Oura Ring against other sleep trackers across multiple form factors like, say, a smart bed and a smartwatch. And so on and so forth.
With that in mind, the current roster is made up of screenless fitness trackers, smart scales, and sleep trackers because these are often the components in metabolic tracking. For instance, the Dexcom G7 (a continuous glucose monitor for diabetics), the Twin Health scale, the Apple Watch Ultra 3, and a Medline blood pressure cuff are a series of sensors that feed into a system that will create my metabolic digital twin. Because Garmin released the Cirqa, a screenless tracker, it makes sense for me to compare it to the Oura Ring and Fitbit Air — which are also Whoop competitors. And because Withings just released its $600 BodyScan 2, it makes sense for me to compare it to its other scales and the Twin Health scale I’m already using.
So this testing block consists of:
- Apple Watch Ultra 3 (left wrist; I use this for a general baseline)
- Dexcom G7 (alternating left and right underarms)
- Twin Health scale
- Google Fitbit Air (right wrist)
- Garmin Cirqa (also right wrist)
- Oura Ring 5 (right index finger)
- Withings BodyScan 2
- Withings Body Smart
- Withings BodyFit
- Eight Sleep Pod 4 Ultra (another control device for sleep metrics)
- Polar H10 chest strap (workout use only)
Morning
The art of wearable testing is steeped in comparison. The first thing I do when I wake up — besides hit the snooze button — is sync all my wearables and take note of how much battery is left. Whenever a new gadget is added to the testing roster, I make sure to also compare the first 24 hours of battery use to the initial charge time. For example, this week I got my hands on a Garmin Cirqa. As of this writing, it hasn’t been on my wrist for a full 24 hours yet, but tomorrow morning, I’ll be noting how much battery is left after sleep and set an alarm for the 24-hour mark.
Once syncing is done, I’ll go into each wearable’s individual app and note how long it said I slept. So today, that’s the Apple Watch’s Health app, the Oura app, the Google Health app for the Fitbit Air, and the Eight Sleep app as a control. This is when I generally look to see which trackers are good at marking nightly disturbances, if I remember any. (For instance, a needy cat smothering my face with his rotund belly at 2:30AM because my spouse is downstairs making themself a snack and bedtime rules have been violated.) If there are readiness scores to compare, I’ll look at those too. This is also when I’ll skim any AI-generated daily insights. These days, all the metrics say pretty much the same thing. If there’s a significant deviation or if the AI says something particularly harebrained, I’ll note it for a closer investigation. (Like a smart bed telling my spouse to drink alcohol to cure snoring.)
Before getting out of bed, I’ll then open the Dexcom G7 app and note my fasting glucose level and any overnight patterns.
At this point, it’s imperative to pee but not drink water, after which I’ll remove all my wearables and pajamas for smart scale testing. First, I’ll hop on the Twin Health scale and sync the data to build my little digital metabolic twin. (This will take three months of testing minimum, so look for a story on this later this fall.) Then I’ll hop on the Withings Body Smart, the Withings BodyFit, and the Withings BodyScan 2. Unless you’re also a health tech reviewer, there’s absolutely no need to weigh yourself this much! Once a week, I’ll then take my blood pressure using a cuff that also syncs with the Twin Health app. I’ll take that reading and then also input it into the Apple Health, Oura, and Withings apps. When these readings are done, I’ll put back on all my wearables.
Before sitting down to work, I’ll take my master baseline wearable — the Apple Watch Ultra 3 — and write down the previous day’s step count and my morning weight comparisons into an analog notebook so I can reference these measurements later come review time.
The last part of the morning review is breakfast. Building my digital twin requires that I log my meals so I can view how certain foods impact my glucose levels. After eating, I set a timer for two hours to check the results on the Dexcom G7. Now that’s done, I can start my damn day. Usually, this takes about an hour in total.
Daytime and workout tracking
After the morning review, I typically ignore my wearables and go about my day unless I’m testing for specific things or get an alert. These days, that translates to meals, workouts, low blood glucose notifications, or anomalous heart rate alerts. (The latter almost never happens.)
Meals follow the same routines, and after a year’s worth of continuous glucose monitoring testing, I am much more chill about how granular I get with food logging. I allow myself occasional Cheetos and cake. Workouts require more work.
