title: Texts reveal 14-year-old allegedly murdered by singer D4vd had pregnancy and abortion
summary: Prosecutors allege D4vd started abusing the girl when she was 13 and she had threatened to expose him.
full_text:
Texts reveal 14-year-old allegedly murdered by singer D4vd had pregnancy and abortion
- Published
WARNING: Readers may find details in this article distressing.
Texts between singer D4vd and Celeste Rivas Hernandez, the 14-year-old he is accused of murdering, reveal she had been pregnant and had had an abortion before her death.
The messages were shown during a hearing for a judge to determine if the singer, whose legal name is David Anthony Burke, should go on trial for the teen's death last year.
"What [if] the first abortion didn't work?" Celeste texted Burke in June 2024, according to prosecutors. She was 13 years old at the time and he was 19.
Prosecutors say Burke killed her after she threatened to reveal he had been abusing a minor and destroy his career. He has pleaded not guilty to charges of murdering and sexually abusing the girl.
In an exchange from January 2024, Burke apologised to the teen for "putting her through this", according to messages shown in the Los Angeles court on Friday.
She responded, "neither of us are capable of watching and taking care of the baby. it's for the best no?"
Burke asked, "also my mother always told me to ask this question if I was ever in this situation … it is mine right?"
Celeste replied "of course its yours David", according to testimony from a detective.
The court heard that in another text to the teen, sent in June 2024, Burke wrote: "Let's let this abortion be the last one til we have the real one…"
Prosecutors presented iCloud data recovered from the defendant's iPhone, showing texts between him and Celeste dating back to 8 August 2022, when she was 11 years old and he was 17.
The device belonging to Burke also had photos of the teenager during the alleged sexual abuse, prosecutors and Los Angeles Police Detective Corey Farell said on Friday.
The victim's mother, Mercedes Rivas Hernandez, became visibly emotional and left the court with her husband as details of some of the pictures were described during the proceedings.
Burke's phone also showed conversations the two had had about moving in together, which they had dubbed "Operation Awesome".
The pair "broke up" in November 2024, but stayed in contact, according to a memo filed by prosecutors earlier this year.
Prosecutors allege they argued on the night before her death, allegedly over Burke's relationships with other women.
Dr Grant Ho of the Los Angeles County Department of Medical Examiner, who conducted the post-mortem examination on Celeste, also testified on Friday.
Ho told the court it was "extremely difficult to tell" exactly when the girl died, owing to the state of decomposition when her remains were found.
Lawyers for the defence seized on that uncertainty, questioning whether it was possible that the teenager could have somehow harmed herself.
Farrell, the police detective, testified that DNA taken from blood found in Burke's Hollywood Hills home and garage was a match for Celeste.
D4vd, who rose to fame on TikTok with the viral hits Romantic Homicide and Here With Me, was on tour when police found Celeste's body in the front boot of his Tesla in September 2025 - the day after she would have turned 15.
His worldwide tour was cancelled and he largely retreated from public life and social media.
Police announced his arrest in April this year.
Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman has filed seven criminal charges against him, including murder, continuous sexual abuse of a child and the mutilation of remains.
They said the teen was reported missing by her family and was last seen at Burke's home on 3 April 2025 - five months before her remains were discovered in the Tesla.
Prosecutors have said he met Celeste online when she was 11, and allege he started sexually abusing her when she was 13 and he was 18.
Friday marked the fourth day of testimony in the pre-trial hearing.
Earlier revelations by prosecutors included that Hernandez had been brought by Burke to London and Texas to meet members of his family there.
Testimony is expected to resume on Monday.

title: Heatwave conditions to return for many as UK temperatures to peak at 35C
summary: Following weeks of mainly dry weather, we can welcome some rain this weekend, but it is not going to be that much.
full_text:
Heatwave conditions to return for many as UK temperatures to peak at 35C
- Published
Heat is set to intensify and become more widespread across England and parts of Wales next week with temperatures surging as high as 35C (95F).
Following much-needed rain in the north and north-west of the UK this weekend, temperatures will rise back to heatwave threshold levels in many locations.
For some, the new week may mark the start of the fourth heatwave of the year.
However a few locations are still experiencing their third with temperatures at Usk, Monmouthshire and Exeter, Devon reaching heatwave thresholds for the 20th consecutive day on Friday.
When is a heatwave declared and how many has the UK had?
Heatwaves are declared when temperatures reach or exceed a threshold temperature for three consecutive days.
This varies from 25C across the north and west of the UK to 28C in parts of eastern England.
These thresholds were widely met in late May, June and again in July - meaning we have had three heatwaves so far.
For most of England and Wales the third heatwave of the year ended last weekend when cooler air arrived, dropping maximum temperatures widely to 20-24C.
However, two locations - Usk and Exeter - have continued to just reach their heatwave criteria since then and have now reached 20 consecutive days - the longest run so far this year.
As temperatures drop further over the weekend, and parts of the UK see a little rain, even these local heatwaves are likely to come to an end.
However, it may only be a temporary break.
Next week, high pressure is set to build close to the south of the UK meaning rain-bearing weather fronts will stall.
Any wet weather will become confined to northern and western areas - especially north-west Scotland - and in southern parts of the UK temperatures look set to climb once again.
This could well mean a fourth heatwave is on the cards - although according to the Met Office isolated high temperatures might not be enough.
They say that: "If only one or two stations reach heatwave criteria, that would not be defined as a heatwave."

Will there be another heatwave?
For much of next week temperatures in England and Wales will peak around 25-32C.
The hottest weather will initially focus itself on central and eastern England by Tuesday before spreading northwards and westwards.
Scotland and Northern Ireland will remain cooler with temperatures generally in the high teens or low to mid-twenties.
Some computer models suggest an even more intense surge of heat could arrive next weekend.
East Wales and most of England could easily see temperatures between 30-35C, increasing the chance that a fourth heatwave could be declared.
It will also become warmer in Scotland and Northern Ireland with temperatures reaching the mid to high twenties.
You can check the latest forecast for your area on the BBC Weather website and app.
Boiling Point: The Week of Extreme Heat
The last week of June 2026 saw record-breaking temperatures across parts of the UK and Europe. While some enjoyed the sunshine, the heat caused trains, schools and emergency services to buckle.

title: ADHD has rewired the workplace. This is what it means for bosses and workers
summary: As ADHD diagnoses have risen, have workplaces caught up with the needs of the workforce?
full_text:
Taking one of the UK's biggest grocery chains to an employment tribunal was something that Ryan Toghill says almost took over his life.
"It was all I could think about for 18 months and more," he says.
The deputy store manager at Lidl, who'd told his bosses he'd been diagnosed with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), was called to a disciplinary meeting after breaking company rules by using equipment he hadn't been trained to use. After that meeting, Ryan was dismissed for gross misconduct.
He successfully appealed the decision and was offered a lower-paid role. He rejected it and took his case to a tribunal. Eventually, he was awarded more than £45,000 when the judge found his former employer hadn't fully taken his ADHD diagnosis into account during the disciplinary process.
The judgement found reasonable adjustments during the process hadn't been offered to him, such as additional breaks.
He'd been described by a manager as showing "a lack of remorse," something the tribunal found was clearly linked with his communication differences associated with having ADHD.
"I don't show a lot of emotions," Ryan explains. "I could be incredibly happy, angry, upset, or remorseful, and my facial expressions and tone of voice would essentially remain the same."
The tribunal upheld part of his claims for unfair dismissal, wrongful dismissal and a failure to make reasonable adjustments. Lidl says it's "committed to ensuring that everyone receives the reasonable adjustments, clear communication and support they need to thrive."
Campaigners, lawyers and HR teams say cases like this highlight a shift that businesses should be paying attention to.
Thousands of people have been diagnosed as neurodivergent in the last few years, an umbrella term that covers autism, ADHD and other conditions such as dyslexia and Tourette's syndrome.
Since the pandemic in particular, diagnosis rates for ADHD and autism have been rising, and they're featuring more regularly in disputes in employment tribunals.
While many people who are neurodivergent don't consider themselves disabled, the Equality Act 2010 may give them protection by recognising their condition as a disability, regardless of whether they have a formal diagnosis. They're entitled to reasonable adjustments if they can show that their condition has a substantial and long-term adverse effect on their ability to do normal day-to-day activities. These are widely defined and aren't limited to work tasks.
Cases going to tribunal can be around employers not making those adjustments, but they can also be about how people are treated at work.
For example, a 2025 tribunal found a software engineer who had ADHD had faced discrimination because a manager sighed and made other expressions of "non-verbal frustration" towards him.
"What we're seeing in tribunals is rarely the result of deliberate discrimination," says Lutfur Ali, a diversity and inclusion adviser at the Chartered Institute of Personnel and Development, the professional body for HR.
"Cases commonly stem from reasonable adjustments being overlooked, performance processes that were never designed with different thinking styles in mind, and managers lacking confidence because they haven't been given the training or the time to have the right conversations."
So, while awareness of neurodivergence has never been higher, why are more cases like this ending up in the legal system? And are businesses struggling to keep up with the needs of the workforce?
Overdiagnosis or underdiagnosis?
Irwin Mitchell is one of the biggest law firms in the UK, and its lawyers say their caseloads increasingly include grievances linked to neurodivergence at work.
Using the Ministry of Justice's online judgments database, the company identified 517 employment tribunal cases mentioning neurodivergent conditions in 2025, up from 265 in 2020. The most commonly cited conditions were autism and ADHD.
The live database is limited and gives only a partial picture. The Ministry of Justice says the figures should not be considered official statistics.
Diagnosis rates of ADHD and autism have soared, and waiting lists for assessments on the NHS in England are at record levels, with lists even closing in some areas due to the huge demand. Irwin Mitchell says those long waits have an impact on workplaces too. "Anecdotally, we're seeing a lot of people that are either threatening to bring claims or actually bringing claims, that don't have formal diagnoses," says Jo Moseley, a legal director at the firm.
Research from University College London suggests nearly a 20-fold increase in the number of UK adults diagnosed with ADHD between 2000 and 2018. Diagnosis rates for autism were eight times higher in 2018 than in 1998.
Despite these rises in diagnosis and referrals, some studies suggest both ADHD and autism are actually underdiagnosed.
In June, the Lancet Regional Health Europe journal published research suggesting that while around 1.2% of adults in England had an ADHD diagnosis, international prevalence data estimates it affects 3-5% of people. The authors of the study said this indicates it could still be under-diagnosed, particularly in older age groups.
Similarly, research by King's College London last year suggested that around 90% of autistic people over 40 remain undiagnosed.
Diagnosis levels aside, there has been a huge increase in awareness of the challenges neurodivergent people can face - whether it's in communication preferences, personal organisation, or sensory needs. In workplaces, many describe "masking," a term which means trying to hide their traits in order to fit in - something which can put a huge strain on the person's wellbeing.
"Society is playing catch-up," says Ben Branson, an entrepreneur who runs a charity called The Hidden 20%, which campaigns for better understanding of neurodivergence. He was diagnosed with autism in 2022.
"The recognition of adult neurodivergence has exploded," he says. "But we have always been here, we are just not hiding anymore, and there are millions of people finally understanding why they kept moving jobs, why they didn't fit, why they kept burning out and why they felt so exhausted, who are no longer willing to struggle in silence."
This year's City and Guilds Foundation's Neurodiversity Index found that while employers think they're "doing better" when it comes to inclusion, neurodivergent employees say they are seeing only small improvements.
The study found employers' confidence levels in their own "neurodivergent readiness" averaged between 70-75%. However, the proportion of employees who reported feeling psychologically safe telling their employer about their diagnosis, and who believed their organisation understood the impact of their condition, was between 32-38%.
Invisible disabilities
This disconnect between managers and staff is something employment lawyer Jodie Hill is familiar with. Her firm, Thrive Law, specialises in workplace wellbeing and works with both employees and businesses. She set it up in 2018 after getting her own ADHD diagnosis at the age of 35.
"In the last three months, I've seen more than I've ever seen before in terms of enquiries," she says.
So, what are some employers doing that leads to successful action being taken against them? Hill says one thing that comes up a lot is bosses asking for proof of a formal diagnosis, when this isn't the legal test. Another issue can be an employer looking to dismiss someone over performance before considering a possible disability. Both of which could leave them exposed to claims of discrimination.
In the training sessions she carries out for businesses, she says she hears from the employer's perspective that it can feel like "every other conversation is about people wanting support".
Fears over cost, and concern that doing something for one member of staff means they have to do it for all of them, can lead to what Hill describes as an "initial dismissiveness" from some employer

title: Claudia Winkleman's chat show ended after one series - can anyone replace Graham Norton?
summary: Many considered Claudia Winkleman as Norton's successor, but her chat show ended after just one series.
full_text:
Claudia Winkleman's chat show ended after one series - can anyone replace Graham Norton?
- Published
When Lisa Kudrow appeared on The Claudia Winkleman Show earlier this year, she was visibly delighted to meet Linda from The Traitors.
The Friends actress, probably the most famous guest the programme had during its seven-week run, said it was "thrilling" to meet one of the reality show's breakout stars, who she revealed had even inspired one of her own recent performances.
As host of The Traitors, Winkleman was ideally placed to introduce the pair, resulting the kind of wonderfully bizarre meeting of minds normally seen on The Graham Norton Show.
But Winkleman's own chat show did not last long enough for any more unusual guest combinations on its teal sofa. The presenter quit last week after just one series, saying she was simply "too nervous to enjoy it".
It had made sense for the BBC to commission The Claudia Winkleman Show, given the presenter's popularity on programmes such as Strictly.
There's a different level of pressure, however, hosting a show with your own name above the door.
"Everyone thought she could pull it off because she's smart and funny, but a chat show with multiple guests is very difficult to handle," the Telegraph's arts and entertainment editor, Anita Singh, tells BBC News.
"You have to marshall the conversation, give each guest equal time, help them to plug whatever they're plugging, then cue in whatever anecdote they've agreed beforehand with the researchers. Graham Norton makes that look deceptively easy."
She adds: "I think if Claudia had done a couple more series she would have become better at it. But she's at her best when she's being spontaneous, and the format allows very little space for that."
Winkleman's decision to quit surprised many. The viewing figures were lower than Norton's, but still respectable. The reviews from critics were mixed, rather than universally bad.
The BBC confirmed it was Winkleman's decision to stop, and implied that they would've happily commissioned a second series - and possibly already had.
"My understanding is they had made a deal beyond one season," says Deadline's Jake Kanter, who has reported on the talk show throughout. "How formal that was, I don't know. But there was an intention for it to continue."
He adds: "I wholeheartedly believe her that this perhaps didn't work out because of her own concerns and anxiety around the hosting."
Former BBC One controller Peter Fincham, who hosts the TV podcast Insiders, likens it to the Davina McCall chat show he commissioned in 2006, which also ended after one series.
"You have to remember, particularly chat shows where the presenter's name is in the title, it's very exposing for them," he tells BBC News.
"Had Claudia Winkleman wanted to carry on with her chat show, it could have been a slow burn," he reflects.
"But what she's done is rare, actually, for somebody to say, 'hmm, didn't really enjoy that, don't think I'll do it again'.
"That says something very positive about her that you don't often see among presenters."
Succession planning
Many considered Winkleman, 54, to be chat show emperor Graham Norton's presumptive successor - not least because he seemed to be ushering her through himself.
So Television, which Norton co-owns, also produced Winkleman's show, and it could have been a neat way for the company to retain work when Norton does eventually quit.
Admittedly, Norton's show is not vanishing any time soon - he signed a new three-year deal with the BBC in 2025. He has also taken on several new projects, including a podcast, more novels, and a short-lived ITV game show, The Neighbourhood.
But Norton, 63, has also spoken openly in recent years about working less. He reduced the number of chat show episodes he presents in 2022, and also stepped down from his Virgin Radio show two years later.
The short life of The Claudia Winkleman Show could make the Norton succession plan a key issue for the BBC's incoming entertainment chief, Ed Havard.
"This does leave the BBC with a problem if and when Graham decides to retire, because if Claudia can't do it, I don't know who can," says Singh.
"Graham doesn't want to do 52 weeks a year," Fincham notes, "so I'm sure the BBC would have been delighted to have another long-running chat show that you can balance with his, and they may have another try."
Dozens of presenters would love the gig and many would be perfectly capable - Jack Whitehall did a solid job when he stood in for Norton previously, or Alan Carr could probably be tempted to return to his Chatty Man days.
But the TV landscape is also littered with examples of cancelled chat shows. As well as Winkleman and McCall, Lily Allen and Charlotte Church also hosted series which didn't last long.
A cynic might say that the short life of Winkleman's series will have shown both her and the BBC that launching a new chat show is harder than it looks.
But Kanter has a more nuanced interpretation, reflecting: "My instinct is that this was always a bit of an experiment.
"Clearly it was something that Claudia wanted to do, and when you have a presenter at the peak of her powers, I think it's just good talent management to try and work together with that presenter on their dream project."
He adds: "I'm sure all sides will walk away with their heads held high, and it was worth giving it a crack, I think."
Do we still need chat shows?
Personalities aside, there's the more existential question of whether the BBC even needs a new talk series, when there are now hundreds of other platforms where celebrities can go to promote their product.
Stars can just as easily appear on YouTube strands such as Snack Wars or Hot Ones as a TV chat show, or spend as much time at press junkets being interviewed by TikTokers as legacy media outlets.
Talent agents know that seeing Hollywood stars talking to a lovable and sweary East London pensioner, external known as Grime Gran, or playing a game of Would You Rather, external with LadBible, is just as likely to generate publicity as traditional interviews.
Singh highlights that clips from programmes such as Norton's often go viral too, but adds: "I don't think the public is craving another TV chat show.
"Think back to the most memorable encounters from the heyday of chat shows," she says. "They were one-on-one: Parkinson with Muhammad Ali; Wogan with George Best or David Icke.
"Those long-form interviews have moved to podcasts now, where celebrities find it easy to be open and essentially treat them as an extended therapy session.
"And the most entertaining celebrity interviews around are on Amelia Dimoldenberg's Chicken Shop Date. Compared to content like that, a chat show in a TV studio seems quite old-fashioned."
Norton's show clearly still delivers huge value for the BBC, and Kanter says the the "chat show format remains strong" and is a "really important part of the BBC One schedule".
"It sprinkles a bit of stardust, it's appointment to view, I think people enjoy that it's a Friday night and they can tune in for some entertainment, it performs well online, it's an engine for clips and viral moments, and that's something that's to be valued in this attention economy," he notes.
And, speaking from experience, Fincham concludes he is "not a big fan of succession plans" anyway.
"I ran BBC One between 2005 and 2007," he recalls, "and at that time, a regular conversation was 'What's the succession plan for David Attenborough?'
"That was 20 years ago, and I can't help noticing he's still presenting programmes today. So beware of the assumption that a succession plan is needed.
"And Graham Norton, if he chooses to continue, has got plenty more in the tank."

title: Five ways to make the most of the summer holidays with kids
summary: The best tips and tricks to have a fun - yet affordable - summer break with the family.
full_text:
Five ways to make the most of the summer holidays with kids
- Published
The six-week summer holidays have officially begun and, for many parents, finding exciting but affordable activities for children can be tough.
For most families in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, the break has only just started. In Scotland, children have enjoyed some time off already, but will return to school earlier than those elsewhere in the UK.
Here are five tips to help children get the most out of the next few weeks of summer.
1. Not every holiday has to be abroad
A family's first instinct when summer is approaching may be to look at booking a trip abroad, but rising costs and travel expenses mean a holiday isn't feasible for everyone.
Mags Rivett, director at Family Holiday Charity, which supports families with UK trips, says there are many benefits to arranging time away with children that don't require expensive travel.
She says the social aspect of a holiday can help children develop their communication skills.
"Lots of kids have never really had the opportunity to meet people outside of their own community," Rivett says. "But if you go somewhere that's got social facilities, it's a really important opportunity."
She says getting recommendations from friends and family is a good place to start.
Rivett gives the example of Skegness, a coastal holiday destination in Lincolnshire, accessible by train or coach, which her charity has supported families to visit.
A family-of-four's accommodation in a holiday park there this August starts at around £750 for a week, while an off-peak return train from Manchester would cost around £280 for four.
By contrast, a last-minute trip to Majorca for a family-of-four at that time starts from around £2,000. Better deals can usually be found booking further in advance.
2. Prioritise the moments, not the cost
Samantha Thomas, creator of Budget Mum UK, says she focuses on the time she can give her children, rather than the money she could spend on a day out.
Thomas suggests focusing on your budget first to understand what you can comfortably spend, and then build your activities around that, to help remove any "stress or guilt" during the holidays.
"Children don't need a six-week programme of expensive activities," Thomas says. "Some of the memories that they'll treasure most will come from simple things, like baking together or a picnic in the park, or building a den in the living room."
Ingredients to bake fairy cakes with buttercream icing usually cost between £10 and £15 - depending on what you already have in the cupboard.
For a picnic - or picky bits - prices can vary. But it can easily be done on a budget of around £5.
Tasneem Abdur-Rashid, an author and single mum of two, echoes Thomas' opinion and wants to relieve the pressure she puts on herself to do something different with her children every day.
She says it's important to take time out, put work away, and spend one-on-one time with your children. This could be going to play in the park, or going swimming.
Trips to local pools or lidos can cost around £6 for adults, and £3.50 for children.
Abdur-Rashid says every night during the holidays she will play board games with her children, which blends quality time and fun. These can be picked up at local charity shops for very reasonable prices.
"You don't even have to leave the house for that," she says, "and they love it."
3. Use what's available in your area
Nilly Dahlia, a content creator and mum of three, says she prints out a six-week calendar with a range of activities for her kids during the holidays.
As part of their "summer bucket list", they are planning to check out all the parks in the local area and she is prioritising low-cost activities throughout the summer.
"I feel like there's this intense pressure to have Instagram-worthy holidays now," she says.
"What's wrong with just staying in the UK, staying out till sunset, riding your bike, just going to the river, like I did? I really want the kids to experience a nostalgic summer."
Dahlia stresses there are many things on offer during the holidays that won't break the bank, such as free kids' meals in cafes and discounts on local travel.
And there are often offers at bowling venues and cinemas, she says, while her family enjoys a movie night at home every Friday.
"They each have a bowl of popcorn and treats and we move the sofas into two rows so it's like a cinema."
James Gray, communications and advocacy manager at Libraries Connected, says the summer holidays are also where libraries "come alive".
He says libraries across the UK will hold the Summer Reading Challenge, encouraging kids to read more in a fun format, and many will be hosting events such as arts and crafts, performances and creative workshops, all for free.
4. Balance rest with some learning
Dahlia says she picks up books for her children to get them ready for the next school year.
Her youngest will receive some chapter books to help them transition into Year 3, while her eldest is moving to secondary school, and Dahlia has prepped suitable books to bridge that gap from primary.
She preps "summer baskets" which include puzzle books, reading books and snacks to curb any boredom.
"It's so important because by reading, they're still engaging their brain so they can go back to school in September, already having vocabulary in them."
As a busy parent, Abdur-Rashid says she doesn't always have the time to do everything she'd like with her children, but structures their days to make sure they are always doing an activity.
She allocates an hour a day for gaming which her boys enjoy, and then fills the rest of the time with playing, reading or writing.
She also wants to foster a passion for reading in her kids, and allows them to not finish books they don't enjoy so reading doesn't become a "punishment".
Gavin Morgan, an education psychologist at University College London, says it's important to let children be "bored" during the holidays.
"It's really important that they have opportunities to switch off from school and from that structure in order to experience and explore new things and get bored, because for some kids, that can really spark that creativity."
For those entering exam years, Morgan says parents should have a conversation with their child about what they need to do and what suits them best.
"The worst thing for parents to do is put their child under any kind of pressure, because they'll end up being switched off from learning," he says.
He says parents should encourage their children to take a break from their education, so they return to school in September "feeling really confident and refreshed".
5. Get ahead for the next holidays
Thomas says she starts planning her summer budget well in advance. She does this by contributing a little bit of money every month into a "sinking fund" - a pot of money set aside for a specific purpose.
This summer her budget is £500, and she sits down with her children to discuss how much they have budgeted and to brainstorm activities they can do together.
"You've got that open dialogue, so they understand there's only a finite amount of money, and we've got a plan on how to do that best," she says.
Thomas also uses cashback websites to get money back on things she has bought, which she says is "brilliant for hotels or travel".
If you are planning a holiday, whether abroad or in the UK, Thomas stresses to plan and book in advance to get better deals. She also recommends looking at attractions within your local area before travelling further afield.

title: 'The dogs were getting upset': How LA band Muna survived their worst ever gig
summary: The group discuss disastrous gigs, putting political action into music and the meaning of "queer pop".
full_text:
'The dogs were getting upset': How LA band Muna survived their worst ever gig
- Published
Every band has to earn its stripes. Some have it harder than others.
At AC/DC's first gig, the club owner cut the power because they were too noisy. Sam Smith started at barn dances, singing on top of a haystack. At Robert Smith's first concert, he got so drunk that he sang David Bowie's Suffragette City while the rest of the band played Jimi Hendrix's Foxy Lady.
But LA pop trio Muna can top them all.
At the start of their career, the band got a call from their record label. We know you've just flown overnight from London, they said, but you have to get to Las Vegas.
Why? Because they'd been booked to play Pet-A-Palooza, a dog adoption festival sponsored by the local radio station. If they turned up, the station would support their new single.
"We were all sick, so it was doomed from the start," recalls guitarist Josette Maskin.
"It was an acoustic set, but we didn't have a sound guy, and the guitar started feeding back."
The noise, according to singer Katie Gavin, was like an unholy screech.
"The dogs were getting upset," says Maskin, wincing at the memory. "They just howled the whole time.
"We were mortified, but looking back, it is so funny. And I've gotten to share those experiences with some of my best friends, and that's what life is really about."
Nowadays, that canine catastrophe is a dot in Muna's rear-view mirror.
Over the past decade, they've become one of the most compelling live bands around – a little bit punk, a little bit electronic, a little bit 80s, eminently watchable and endlessly impressive.
Fans include Harry Styles and Taylor Swift, who handpicked the trio (completed by guitarist/producer Naomi McPherson) to support them on tour.
They were won over by sing-along anthems like I Know A Place, a great big exuberant hug for the LGBTQ community; and the more introspective Stayaway, where Gavin locks herself in her bedroom to avoid anything - friends, music, drink - that could tempt her back into the arms of an ex.
In 2020, all their momentum nearly came to a crashing halt when RCA Records dropped the band, citing pandemic-era cost-cutting.
"That's obviously one where we had to put our heads together and be like, 'OK, we want to continue doing this. Let's just make an album and we'll figure it out'," says McPherson.
'We need movement'
That album, simply titled Muna, was eventually released by indie star Phoebe Bridgers, who swooped in to sign the band to her Saddest Factory label in 2021.
"Phoebe's manager had made it very clear that if we were ever single, she'd be interested in working with us," Gavin told the BBC at the time.
Bridgers also provided guest vocals on Silk Chiffon, a freewheeling sapphic love song that became Muna's breakthrough single.
It pegged the band, in its members' own words, as "the queer joy mini-skirt rollerblade, external" crew - but their music has always dug deeper than that.
I Know A Place, for example, was written as a response to the 2016 Pulse nightclub shooting, acknowledging the fragility of the communal LGBTQ spaces it celebrated.
Their fourth album, Dancing On The Wall, is their most powerful yet.
The music is darker. The lyrics hit harder. Ostensibly anchored to the dancefloor, it's a record that uses dance music to shake the listener out of complacency.
"I think it was a response to a feeling of helplessness in this moment in time that can lead to paralysis," says Gavin.
"Movement is what we need right now, and we also need to feel powerful and to connect to our sources of energy. The tempo of this album helps with that."
The standout, lyrically speaking, is Big Stick. A critique of American imperialism, it's written from the perspective of Big Brother, who "can make you want anything that I want you to" – from war in Gaza to the militarisation of US police forces.
"And If you've got a problem with it, you could end up in jail," Gavin seethes as militaristic synths patrol the beat.
"I think sometimes people want to go to concerts to feel a brief reprieve from the horrors of the world around them, but right now the horrors are so pervasive that what I found myself wanting was a container to express my anger together with other people," says the singer.
"It's an emotional release that I think we are often denied because we have to read tragedies in the news every day and then keep our heads down and work."
Given the polarised state of political discourse in the US, did they have any misgivings about releasing the song?
"Maybe this is actually stupid, but I don't think it was a big decision for us," says Maskin.
"We have always been a political band, and we've always been super open with what we believe in, so it really wasn't a question."
Elsewhere, the album transports the listener to sweaty, laser-lit nightclubs, where unyielding rhythms fuel feelings of "horniness and heartache".
The title track is full of thwarted desire, as Gavin tries and fails to get the attention of a girl who constantly leaves her dangling. Wannabeher, meanwhile, is a sticky, sleazy track about being so completely besotted with someone that you start to blur the boundaries between where your personality ends and theirs begins.
"I think that's a canon gay experience, where you don't know whether you want to be with someone or you actually want to be them," laughs Maskin.
Eastside Girls, meanwhile, is a tender depiction of Muna's neighbourhood, lovingly lampooning the staples of LA hipster culture – astrology, polyamory, roommate dramas and "negronis with the nice gin".
"It's a city that's run by sunshine," says McPherson, who moved to LA from her native San Diego.
"It's bohemian but it's also populated by some of the richest people in the world. It's a strange dichotomy."
The song's chorus is a masterclass in melody and, in Maskin's words, "smacks you in the face". It takes its place among Muna's most irresistible hooks (see also, Number One Fan, Stayaway, What I Want) – which all stem from Gavin's love of classic pop.
"She's been writing songs since she was eight years old, so it's a well-honed skill," says McPherson.
"I think it's a benefit of my obsessive personality, honestly," says Gavin.
"I am constantly searching for the next big chorus, and will probably always be. Also, once I have a seed in my head for a song that feels promising, it really has a hold on me and won't let me go until I feel I've done it justice." (Wannabeher, McPherson reveals, is the final version of a song that began 11 years ago.)
"I will say," Gavin adds, "one random tip is writing in motion - walking, driving, rollerblading, anything like that."
That explains why Muna's music always feels propulsive. "If you're not sweating after the first song, come on," laughs McPherson.
With an ever-growing fanbase, they'll play their biggest ever tour this autumn, titled the Gets So Hot Tour after the album's opening track – although the band previously joked it would be called "The Midwest Princess, Midnight Sun and the Eras Tour as Well", before abandoning the idea for copyright reasons.
A decade into their career, they're playing to "crowds we could never have imagined", while witnessing the genre labelled as "queer pop" expand into the mainstream, with artists like Chappell Roan, Renée Rapp, Lil Nas X and Troye Sivan all achieving crossover success.
"I do feel we were at the cusp of the reclamation of the word 'queer'," says Maskin.
"To us, it's actually a celebratory term, because it's inclusive, it includes everybody in the LGBTQI+ community.
"It came from academia first, the idea of queer theory," says McPherson, who admits the band were initially divided on whether to be open about their sexuality.
"We were reticent to come out of the closet in the hipster Pitchfork era of 2010 and 2011. We wanted to be mysterious and be closeted, and Katie was the one who encouraged us not to, and to just be ourselves. And we've only become more ourselves."

title: Long overdue, life-changing or frivolous? Your thoughts on wedding rule changes
summary: The government wants to relax wedding laws so couples can get married almost anywhere.
full_text:
Long overdue, life-changing or frivolous? Your thoughts on wedding rule changes
- Published
The day Sam and Courtney Scholey became husband and wife didn't feel like their wedding day.
There was no walking down the aisle, no rings exchanged, no wedding dress, and no music.
That all came several days later, when the pair had a bespoke ceremony led by a celebrant who knew them, at a venue in the Oxfordshire countryside. It was their dream wedding - but it wasn't legal in England and Wales.
And so in April, they forked out hundreds of pounds to quietly sign papers at a library in Buckingham.
"For us, that day was as insignificant as possible," Courtney told the BBC. "It was just the words we had to say to make it legally binding."
The Scholeys are one of a growing number of couples who feel the rigid rules around weddings are making getting married more stressful, more expensive and less meaningful.
But under new proposals announced this month - described by the government as the biggest shake-up of wedding laws in 200 years - couples in England and Wales could have the freedom to hold official marriage ceremonies in a wider array of unconventional locations, from forests to beaches, as long as the location is approved by a registered officiant.
It's welcome news for Nicky Brown, who said she wants to exchange vows in a wildly picturesque corner of Wales, with just her mum and her partner's mum as witnesses.
"I'd be quite happy to get married in a field full of sheep," the 57-year-old told the BBC.
But some say the sacred tradition of marriage is being perverted.
Currently, a marriage or civil partnership ceremony in England or Wales must take place at an approved venue to be legally binding – and many exert control on elements of the wedding such as vows, headcounts or music.
There are also tight restrictions on who can officiate a wedding and how. Authorised religious figures can, but – with few exceptions – only in places of worship.
Registrars can conduct a wedding, but it can't have any religious content. And celebrants can't legally marry people at all.
A Law Commission report in 2022 concluded that these marriage laws, which date back to the 18th and 19th Centuries, were "complicated, inefficient, unfair and needlessly restrictive".
David Lammy, then deputy prime minister, said marriage laws in England and Wales had "not kept pace with the social and cultural changes that have shaped modern Britain".
He added: "Some feel forced to pay for two different ceremonies, one legal and one belief based. Some enter into a marriage that isn't legally recognised. Others feel they have little choice but to marry in a way which doesn't reflect their beliefs, marring what should be a joyous occasion."
Scotland and Northern Ireland relaxed their rules years ago.
Though the exact shape of the new rules is still under public consultation until September, these changes will take regulations from a "buildings based" regulation model to an "officiant based" one.
'The laws are now, what, 200 years out of date?'
Brown said she and her partner had put off getting married because there was no legal and affordable version of a wedding that reflects them.
She said she didn't want bells and whistles - or even a wedding dress. "I just want somebody to marry us and in a beautiful setting that isn't just going to cost the earth."
Brown went on to explain that she'd been scared her mum - who is 86 and unwell - would miss out on her wedding day. But these changes had given her hope: "The laws are now, what, 200 years out of date?"
Miranda Allard, 66, also agreed that change is long overdue.
When she got married 40 years ago, she had to jump through hoops to get permission to hold an interfaith ceremony in her parent's garden - and finds it astounding couples today face the same obstacles.
"We applied for a special licence... [and] explained how we did not want to put my Jewish mother-in-law through a church wedding," she said.
"I, on the other hand, was brought up in a Christian family and would not 'feel married' if doing so in a registry office."
It took letters from the couple, their parents, the local bishop, the village vicar and more to convince authorities to allow the ceremony.
"We also combined our legal Christian service with Jewish prayers and tradition, like breaking the glass. Totally unheard of then and ever since," she said, adding the nuptials even made the paper.
Father John, who didn't provide his last name, wrote in to BBC Your Voice to say he'd like to be able to perform ceremonies like this too.
"Marriage is about the lifelong commitment made before God for me, and for some couples the setting can make that sacred moment even more personal and memorable."
Brian Bracher, 65, from Chichester in West Sussex, said he cannot believe the UK is still debating these changes.
"It is ridiculous that, in this modern era, a small minority are still trying to exert control and make decisions about what is frivolous and not acceptable. Just let people, that love each other, marry in a way that suits them."
The proposals will be a welcome change for Christians from the LGBT community, said 33-year-old Isabel Sinagola.
She added: "[They] currently cannot have the wedding they might want, as they cannot marry in the Church of England, but also cannot have religious content in the only option available to them: a civil ceremony."
Others are hopeful this provides more affordable wedding options.
'We want to get married but won't, as it costs too much'
Carl Jones said he and his partner of 20 years haven't wed because even the simplest weddings are too expensive.
"We want to get married but won't, as it costs too much. It's cheaper if we just have two witnesses, but why should our [12-year-old] daughter not be allowed to attend... It's wrong."
But sceptics say this will do little to lower the cost of weddings, which according to wedding planner app Hitched has jumped to £21,990 on average.
Reverend Tom Kennar said it isn't marriage that is expensive, it's the extras most modern couples like to add.
"[It] is the costs of the reception, vehicles, booze, photographers, clothing, food, cars etc," he said.
Other critics of the proposal say they fear it will dilute the significance of marriage.
"Marriage is a gift from God to secure society. Not an opportunity to set new standards and styles," said Donald Tosh, from Glasgow, who wrote to BBC Your Voice.
"It's now not a life decision, it's a temporary decision. And now with this, a very temporary frivolous decision," said Oliver, from Kent.
However, celebrant Zadie Ward told the BBC the changes could enhance the meaning of a wedding for many couples.
"[Critics] are saying it's a solemn promise and it's about the serious commitment, but how can you ask someone to make a serious commitment in words that mean nothing to them and ways that are meaningless to them?"
She says the changes won't take anything from those who still want traditional weddings – it simply gives couples who don't more options.
"You've got blended families, mixed cultures, traditions that are changing even within those cultures.
"Modern relationships deserve modern ceremonies."
The government has stressed there will be safeguards to guarantee the dignity of marriage is preserved.
Ceremonies deemed to be "gimmicks" that risk trivialising the legal act of marriage would not be allowed. Activities "such as skydiving, white-water rafting, roller coasters or other amusement rides" would "fall short of the standard".
"Every couple deserves to start their journey together with an unforgettable day that reflects their beliefs, their personalities and the lives they plan to build together," Lammy wrote.
"This Government's changes will bring weddings law into the twenty-first century."
Additional reporting by Mary Litchfield and Rozina Sini

title: Students tell us how to keep graduation outfit costs down
summary: Four newly graduated students tell us how they kept the cost of their dresses and suits down.
full_text:
Students tell us how to keep graduation outfit costs down
- Published
"From the beginning of my course, I've been thinking about what my graduation dress was going to be," says Keerthana Krishnadas. "I had to make sure I looked 10 out of 10, I couldn't compromise on that."
She is one of hundreds of thousands of university students graduating this summer and, like many, has been figuring out what to wear for a photo marking one of life's milestones - without breaking the bank.
"You can save some bucks if you thrift your outfit because you're only going to wear it once," says Keerthana. She bought hers second hand. "It was about 80 quid - a bargain."
The expense of graduation is keenly felt by many students and their families with costs ranging from transport and accommodation to clothing and photographs, says Tom Allingham of budgeting advice site Save The Student.
"For those who are the first person in their family to go to uni, it's a big deal for the family and there's a pressure to celebrate it - even though those students often come from a lower income background," he says.
The total cost can be hundreds of pounds with savvy students renting, making or thrifting their outfits to save money. Some have taken to social media to share their tips, vent their frustrations and break down the costs of their outfits.
BBC News spoke to students posing for photographs in Salford Quays to find out how they saved money on theirs.
Instead of scouring the internet like Keerthana for a bargain, Ehis Oboh asked his younger brother for help.
He is a tailor in Nigeria who designed and made the suit Ehis wore for his ceremony. Ehis now has a master's degree in international business and says it was important to mark the occasion properly attired, even if it can be financially difficult.
"When you have the funds, there's no pressure," he tells me. "But if the funds are not there - let's say, there's pressure."
The cost of renting a cap and gown for the day varies. Undergraduates and postgraduates at the University of Salford pay £42, while PhDs pay £45.
Across the river at the University of Manchester, the price increases by a pound for undergraduates and postgraduates, but those with a doctorate pay £57.
Ehis is not the only one who opted for a tailored outfit - Wendy Adu Amankwah wanted to create her own look for her graduation.
"My mum is a designer so she made this for me," says Wendy. "It took her a week… I'm her daughter, so she had to put in every [effort]."
Wendy says the significance of graduation inspired her to create a custom look. "I feel like you have to because it's your day. We go through a lot to get a master's degree so you have to look your best on the day."
Graduation also comes at a time when students are "the least financially resilient", says Allingham, as they have been absorbing the costs of studying all year.
The maintenance loan falls short of living costs by an average of £502 per month, according to analysis by Save The Student, external. This gap is plugged - sometimes only partially - by parental support, part-time jobs and debt.
Another factor that can increase the cost of graduation is buying an official photograph, with providers specified by your university, adds Allingham. "The price of photography on the day - it's extortionate."
Professional packages at the University of Salford start at £30 - an image of the graduate is sent digitally - and the most expensive is £350. For that you receive about 20 prints with various mounts and frames of two images, one of the graduate and another with friends and family.
Like Keerthana, Alicia Munhupedzi used the internet to find her dress - though it was a bit last minute.
"I thought, 'Where can I get a nice dress really quickly and cheaply?'"
The answer? Depop, the second-hand clothing app popular among Gen Z shoppers that sold for $1.2bn (£890m) earlier this year.
Like others, Alicia felt her outfit was important.
"Graduation, it's a milestone thing, especially if you're not planning on doing a master's," she says. "So, to me, there was a pressure."
So much so she couldn't sleep properly the night before her ceremony and woke at dawn to get ready. "I made it through today off two hours of sleep, water, good vibes, energy and a coffee."
Knowing all eyes would be fixed on her when she was handed her degree, Keerthana says she was nervous for her graduation ceremony - but it passed more quickly than she thought it might.
"This is the only moment you get for yourself," she says.
And was the 05:00 wake-up and two hours of getting ready worth it?
"Yeah," Keerthana says, "I couldn't compromise on that."

title: It's the cocktail taking young drinkers by storm - but the packaging is 'unrecyclable'
summary: BuzzBallz cannot be recycled because the metal lid and plastic body are attached, say experts.
full_text:
It's the cocktail taking young drinkers by storm - but the packaging is 'unrecyclable'
- Published
Cleaning up after pre-drinks, Aédén Rooney puts his empty BuzzBallz in the recycling.
"It's plastic and metal, so I'd just assume it's recyclable," he said.
The company behind the bright, pre-mixed cocktails that have taken Gen Z by storm said they were recyclable on its website, but experts say this is not true.
BuzzBallz cannot be recycled as the PET plastic ball cannot be separated from the aluminium lid, global environmental action body WRAP said.
"It's greenwashing. I'm shocked," Aédén said.
BuzzBallz blamed a website error for claiming they were recyclable via Terracycle, a US-only scheme, but did not comment on its now-deleted FAQ that said they were recyclable where UK councils allow.
Rooney, 21, is a student at Cardiff University and drinks at least two to three BuzzBallz every week during term time.
He's far from the only one.
BuzzBallz was named the fastest-growing alcohol brand in The Grocer's Britain's Biggest Alcohol Brands 2026 ranking.
Rooney thinks they are popular because they are "strong, they're cheap for the amount of alcohol and the price you're paying - it's a no brainer".
BuzzBallz was founded by teacher Merrilee Kick, but was bought by the Sazerac Company, whose CEO is Jake Wenz, in 2024.
BuzzBallz's UK's mission statement, which was deleted after the BBC contacted the company about this story, said it "loves our planet as much as we love a good cocktail" and partnered with TerraCycle to ensure its packaging gets recycled.
However, TerraCycle, which involves consumers collecting packaging and sending it to be recycled, only runs the BuzzBallz scheme in the United States.
BuzzBallz's UK FAQs, now also deleted, stated: "Yes, our packaging is recyclable. Please recycle your empties where local facilities allow."
But no local facilities anywhere in the UK allow BuzzBallz to be recycled, said Adam Herriott, the head of packaging at WRAP.
"They're a mix of two very recyclable materials that put together makes an unrecyclable format.
"No local authorities will accept these at the kerbside.
"If they end up at a sorting facility, they could end up contaminating the plastic stream because of the metals in there and that could be very problematic for plastics recyclers that get into the machinery."
But why should people care if their drink packaging is not recyclable?
"Plastic is a finite resource, and it's traditionally from a fossil-derived product as well, it comes from oil," Herriott said.
Recycling aluminium, which can be done infinitely, means less is being extracted from bauxite mines, which have huge impacts on communities and the environment from habitat destruction, contamination of soil and harm to human health.
Even the shape of the BuzzBallz make it harder to be recycled because they can roll on the conveyor belts at the sorting facilities, said Herriott.
Among the machinery used, scanners can identify it in one position, but by the time air jets are used to separate it into the right recycling stream, it could have moved, meaning it could contaminate other streams.
"It's definitely one of the villains of recycling," said Ambarish Mitra, co-founder of Greyparrot, a waste analytics company which helps recovery facilities.
He said BuzzBallz have "have no recovery route in the current system" and "is a huge pet peeve for our customers and us".
After analysing a plastic recover facility in Manchester with a processing capacity of 35,000 tonnes of plastic a year, for six months, the company found that BuzzBallz contaminated recycled plastic 66% of the time.
"Once in the plastic stream, the aluminium reduces the quality of the recycled plastic, while the colour pigments can lower the recycled plastic bale's value.
"This isn't a recycling problem. It's a packaging problem."
BuzzBallz refused to comment.
Environmental scientist and campaigner Laura Anderson, known online as LessWasteLaura, said most people would assume Buzzballz could be recycled.
Anderson said consumers were unlikely to find clear advice, even if they tried: "When you go to your council's recycling website there isn't a drop-down option for a plastic-metal can. How am I supposed to figure that out?"
Anderson described the company's messaging as "misleading" and "greenwashing".
"I would rather they just said, 'this can't be recycled widely, please just put it in the bin'. Because actually that is really probably what most people should be doing with them.
"If a company cared about sustainability, they could make these products in a fully aluminium can and still have the colours, the branding and the quirky design."
James Piper, co-host of the Talking Rubbish podcast, co-owner of Ecosurety, said he dislikes BuzzBallz because of how difficult they are to recycle.
"Every stage of the recycling journey has been designed around predictable packaging," Piper said. "When people come along and say, 'I'm going to make something different for marketing reasons', they are automatically making it more difficult for the recycler."
"There's nothing environmentally positive about mixing packaging types."
He said the BuzzBallz 'biggies' which have a plastic screw top lid is completely recyclable.
"Anyone can say on their website 'this is recyclable where your council allows'. But if no council allows it, then it doesn't mean anything," he said.
BuzzBallz said: "We very recently went through a global website update and the information pertaining to TerraCycle recycling for BuzzBallz was incorrectly copied and does not apply to the UK market as of today.
"We apologise for the oversight and have since updated our website to reflect the correct position for UK consumers."
The company refused to comment on the now-deleted UK FAQs stating its packaging was recyclable.

title: Wildfire burning one month on is 'the size of a small town'
summary: More than a month on, and firefighting shows no sign of immediate end at Tintwistle Moor.
full_text:
Wildfire burning one month on is 'the size of a small town'
- Published
As darkness set in over the Peak District one Wednesday night in June, calls started to come in to Derbyshire's fire service over smoke starting to rise from the moorland overlooking the town.
More than a month on, the Tintwistle Moor fire is now a sprawling, smouldering blaze the size of a small town, which can be seen from space.
Declared a major incident on 13 July, it has come in tandem with a prolonged spell of hot, dry weather that shows little sign of easing soon, pushing the country's firefighting resources to their limits.
Now Dr Kirsten Lees, environmental sciences lecturer, specialising in zero carbon at the University of Derby, has told the BBC Tintwistle is on a par with the biggest wildfires ever seen in England - and it's still burning.
When questioned about her assertion the fire could be one of the largest in recent memory in England, she said: "It may well be, yes."
She added: "Honestly, it's upsetting and it's really scary.
"In the most recent years, we had Saddleworth in 2018. We had Fylingdales up in the North York Moors last year. And this is comparable in scale to both of those.
"My estimate is that it is about the size of a small town. As this is not out yet, we don't know how much bigger it's going to get."
Analysis of data from the European Forest Fire Information System (Effis) by BBC Verify estimates the fire, which first began on 24 June, has burned 606 hectares (1,630 acres) - equivalent to 900 football pitches.
This is larger than the footprint of Hadfield, one of the nearest towns to the wildfire and home to about 6,700 people.
Lees - who has been monitoring the wildfire using satellite imagery - added: "In Wales we tend to have some large ones. In terms of being the largest fire that we've seen in the Peak District, it probably would need to grow another 25% or so to overtake the Saddleworth fire, and obviously Fylingdales was bigger again."
A further wildfire at Dovestone Reservoir, north of the Tintwistle blaze, covers about 90 hectares (220 acres).
Lees added: "At the moment the fire services have been doing a fantastic job keeping it under control as much as possible. We probably won't see this being completely out until we get some good rain."
Clive Stanbrook, deputy chief fire officer for Derbyshire Fire and Rescue Service, said on Thursday the operation was "complex and challenging", which the brigade and partner agencies were working to bring to a "safe conclusion as quickly as possible".
Firefighters said due to its vast scale, the ground affected had been divided into four sectors - Didsbury Sector, Crowden Sector, Arnfield Sector and Featherbed Moss Sector - to allow teams to focus resources on specific areas.
Stanbrook said: "Around 65 firefighters from Derbyshire and across the UK, supported by partner organisations including the Fire Operations Group, are actively supporting the response to the Tintwistle Moor wildfire, with many more being rotated and mobilised when required.
"Thanks to their hard work, and the support of many colleagues behind the scenes, significant progress has been made."
But a huge issue for those on the ground - or in the skies, with helicopters providing support by dropping loads of water on to the wildfire - is what is actually burning.
Lees said: "In the summer, we tend to get different types of vegetation igniting - woody shrubs, things like heather, and they burn much more intensely, which means that the fires can be not only large, but also severe as well.
"Once the wildfire gets into the peat, peat is a fuel, burned historically particularly in Scotland and Ireland, so it does burn incredibly well.
"Once the fire gets into that, it is incredibly vulnerable. We're struggling with ways to prevent the fire spreading once it gets into the peat and prevent it reigniting."
Peak District National Park Authority ranger Kate Wilson, 40, from Buxton in the county, has been just one of those searching for hotspots in the peatland, and helping to keep the flames from spreading.
She said: "You've got your full firefighting kits, you've got all your tools, you're carrying water and you're trying to put out flaming moorland.
"It's really hot, really hard work, you get really dirty, but also you feel like you're doing good work and really helping the environment.
"You get competing emotions, you're frustrated that the fires happen, really sad to see the devastation, there should be heather and shrubs and grass and bilberries, you can walk past a nest of eggs that have been completely burnt out.
"But there's a real sense of camaraderie. We're a very small cog in a massive firefighting machine, everyone is working really hard in hard conditions."
The fire can be devastating for wildlife. The flames destroy nests, kill fledglings, mammals, and insects unable to escape the fast-moving flames.
Dr Kirsten Lees added: "It's really upsetting to see the impact that it's having on the vegetation, the plants and the wildlife.
"This is going to have a really, really devastating impact on the wildlife particularly our ground nesting birds so curlews, skylarks... things like that are really vulnerable to wildfires because they nest literally on the ground - they can't escape the flames so their chicks, their eggs, particularly late spring, early summer, they're really vulnerable."
And once the fire is dampened down, the habitats needed to support fragile ecosystems are lost, sometimes for decades, Craig Best - National Trust general manager for the Peak District - said.
"These peatland habitats are vitally important for all of us," he said.
"They provide our drinking water, they store carbon, they're a great place for people to walk, and obviously they're essential for nature, but these fires can have a huge impact on these landscapes and it's particularly the peat soils we get concerned about.
"Every millimetre of peat takes approximately 100 years to accumulate."
Wildfires come with a human impact too, above and beyond the obvious physical damage they cause to land and sometimes property.
All smoke is potentially harmful to your health, according to advice from the UK Health Security Agency.
Fine particles in the smoke, which can vary depending on what is being burned, can penetrate deep into your lungs and even enter your bloodstream causing illness.
While short-term exposure is not usually an issue for healthy people, people with health conditions are more likely to be affected.
Nicola Naylor, a farmer whose land sits near to Tintwistle, said: "The fire itself has been one of the most dramatic ones I've seen in the last 20 years, and the fire service's response is amazing.
"People are shocked at how much smoke there's been. People with health conditions, people that were older, children, were distressed by it."
And Lees added: "When we do eventually get some rain, that run-off is going to go into our reservoirs and our water supply, and it's going to cost more to treat that to make sure it's clean for us."
Rob Kenning, ranger team manager for the Peak District National Park Authority, said it was trialling using a seasonal ranger to patrol in the evenings to help prevent wildfires in the lighter, warmer summer months in areas likely to attract lots of tourists.
He said council public spaces protection orders have also begun to be enforced, which can see people starting fires or using barbecues fined up to £1,000 in parts of the Peak District.
He said: "Unfortunately, having many more visitors coming out to the park, we're pretty clear that this is going to be an ongoing problem and potentially an increasing problem."
And it's not just the Peak District that is seeing a rise in wildfires.
The Fire Brigades Union (FBU) said more than 40,000 hectares burned last year in more than 1,000 incidents, while in 2026 fire and rescue services in England and Wales have responded to 342 wildfires up to 6 July, according to data from the Na

title: From palava huts to TikTok: How Liberians are preserving their past
summary: From podcasts to TikTok, young Liberians are using digital platforms to keep history alive and challenge old narratives.
full_text:
From palava huts to TikTok: How Liberians are preserving their past
From podcasts to TikTok, young Liberians are using digital platforms to keep history alive and challenge old narratives.
Monrovia, Liberia – For generations, Liberia’s history lived in the voices of its elders, carried through conversations, ceremonies and community gatherings.
Today, those stories are finding new audiences across TikTok, Facebook, YouTube, podcasts and digital archives.
Young Liberians are documenting their history, exploring their culture and reaching audiences at home and across the diaspora. Rather than replacing traditional storytellers, they are carrying an age-old tradition into the digital age.
Across much of West Africa, griots, or oral historians, preserved history through storytelling, music and oral tradition. Liberia never developed the formal griot tradition found across the Sahel, but its elders fulfilled a similar role, preserving family histories, cultural traditions and the stories that bound communities together.
Over time, however, that tradition has come under growing pressure.
Among those leading efforts to preserve Liberia’s past is Bilphena Decontee Yahwon, founder of Archive Liberia, a memory and political education project that explores Liberian history through research, archives and public storytelling.
“I didn’t originally set out to tell Liberian stories. I wanted to tell my own story,” Yahwon says.
“Within my story was also a story of war and migration, one that I felt I could only contextualise by understanding the story of Liberia, who we were before the 1800s, what happened afterwards, and what we became. I realised I was inside a web of stories, and that is ultimately what brought me to the work I do now,” she tells Al Jazeera.
Her personal search has become part of a wider movement of young Liberians using digital platforms to reclaim the country’s past and reshape how it is remembered.
A history interrupted by war
Elders passed down the memories of families, communities, cultural traditions and the events that shaped Liberia for generations, but the country’s civil wars severed that chain.
Liberia’s two civil wars, fought between 1989 and 2003, killed an estimated 250,000 people, displaced hundreds of thousands more and disrupted the transmission of history, culture and family memory.
“Liberian societies in the forest belt lacked the professional caste of griots that existed in the Sahel. But our elders did their best to transmit historical and cultural knowledge, albeit on an unpaid basis,” says Patrick Burrowes, a Liberian historian and author.
“The chain of transmission across generations continued in an unbroken fashion for centuries until the war. That is why we are seeing less and less transmission of accurate historical and cultural knowledge,” Burrowes tells Al Jazeera.
The effects of that disruption are still felt today.
As Liberia has become more urbanised, many young people have moved away from the communities where oral histories were traditionally shared. According to a 2022 report by the Liberia Institute for Statistics and Geo-Information Services, internal migrants account for 46.7 percent of the urban population, compared with 13.6 percent of the rural population.
The places where stories are shared have changed. The need to preserve them has not.
The new palava hut
For many young Liberians, the new gathering place is online.
A historical photograph shared on Facebook, a TikTok video explaining a cultural tradition or a podcast exploring Liberia’s past can now reach audiences far beyond a single community.
Stories once shared between elders and younger generations now travel across cities, continents and the Liberian diaspora in seconds.
Zuleka Dauda, chief programme officer at the Center for Integrated Solutions, a Liberian-owned research and strategic planning organisation, says the shift reflects evolution rather than loss.
“Culture should never stand still,” she tells Al Jazeera.
“Young Liberians are consuming culture differently, but it’s still being taught and shared. Instead of gathering around the palava hut, they gather around TikTok, Facebook, podcasts and YouTube. We didn’t lose storytelling. We changed the stage.”
For many creators, these platforms have become spaces to document traditions, preserve family histories and challenge narratives about Liberia that have often been shaped from outside the country.
Historical photographs, forgotten traditions and family memories are reaching new audiences as Liberians use technology to reconnect with their past.
But taking storytelling online has also brought new challenges.
Truth and memory
Access remains one of the biggest barriers.
According to World Bank figures, just over one in three Liberians uses the internet, limiting who can participate in this growing digital archive.
There is also the challenge of misinformation.
Traditional storytellers learned over many years, with elders responsible for correcting inaccuracies and protecting the knowledge passed between generations.
Social media has opened storytelling to everyone, but it has also removed many of those safeguards.
“Historically, African griots underwent rigorous training, and the recitation of knowledge by young acolytes was fact-checked by their elders,” says Burrowes.
“But social media is a brave new world. Individual users do not undergo training in sifting fact from falsehood. Many users post information without vetting. They often use their platforms to gain followers and influence, without regard to social responsibility.”
Limited literacy and restricted access to archives also make it harder for many Liberians to verify historical claims. Government figures estimate literacy among Liberians aged 15 and above at 58.6 percent.
For Yahwon, however, the challenge is not only about accuracy but also about who gets to shape Liberia’s historical narrative.
“For me, one of the biggest challenges in telling Liberian stories, culture and history is undoing the ahistorical account of our past that has dominated for so long,” she says.
“So much of what has been written about Liberia is shaped by narratives that lack an anti-colonial and anti-imperialist perspective.”
Who gets to tell Liberia’s story?
As more Liberians turn to digital platforms to preserve the past, the challenge is ensuring those stories remain rooted in evidence as well as memory.
The Liberia Tourism Authority says it is working with historians, cultural institutions and content creators to improve access to historical resources and help produce accurate, engaging stories about Liberia.
Dauda believes the answer is not to discourage young people from telling stories online, but to help them tell better ones.
“Silence is a far greater threat than conversation. We need to find ways to encourage young Liberians to tell better stories,” she says.
The voices have changed. The responsibility has not. Whether stories are shared beneath a palava hut or uploaded to TikTok, the task remains the same: ensuring Liberia’s past is preserved for the generations that follow.
“Our generation doesn’t just inherit history. We are creating it and sharing it,” Dauda says.
“Think about it. The future of Liberian history may not be written first in textbooks. It may be uploaded.”

title: Sons of immigrant killed by ICE in Texas share grief, demand accountability
summary: Lorenzo Salgado Araujo's sons tell lawmakers their father worked hard 'to protect and provide' for his family.
full_text:
Sons of immigrant killed by ICE in Texas share grief, demand accountability
Lorenzo Salgado Araujo’s sons tell lawmakers their father worked hard ‘to protect and provide’ for his family.
Two sons of a man shot dead by US immigration authorities have demanded a transparent investigation into the incident in an emotional hearing with legislators.
Speaking at a Houston hearing with Democratic members of Congress on Friday, the sons of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo described the “Kafkaesque nightmare” they have experienced since learning on Facebook that their father was the victim of a fatal shooting.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items- list 1 of 3Trump urges ICE to keep using traffic stops after deadly incidents
- list 2 of 3ICE agent behind fatal shooting in Maine reportedly had troubled history
- list 3 of 3Protests continue in Houston over ICE killing of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo
“He worked hard to protect and provide for our family … He taught us that good things come to those that work hard,” the sons said in a pre-written statement, The Associated Press news agency reported.
Salgado Araujo, 52, was killed during a traffic stop by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents, prompting thousands of Houstonians to take to the street in protest and to demand justice.
Salgado Araujo was a Mexican immigrant who had lived in the US for more than 30 years without legal status, according to his family. He was not the intended target of the ICE operation that resulted in his killing.
“I learned again from a Facebook post that our dad had been shot,” one son, Ronaldo Salgadok, told the hearing. “Not because I could see him, but because I could hear his voice on videos posted online crying for help.”
Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare told the hearing that the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE, has ignored his requests for information and evidence surrounding the case, including the name of the officer who fired the fatal shot.
Three other passengers, including Salgado Araujo’s brother, were detained by ICE during the traffic stop. Officials originally claimed that Salgado Araujo had weaponised his vehicle against officers, but the ICE agents were not wearing body cameras at the time and witnesses have disputed this version of events.
Democratic members of Congress are signalling they plan to investigate ICE and enact changes if they regain control of Congress in this November’s midterm elections.
Speaking at Friday’s forum, Democratic Congressman Christian Menefee said ICE needs to be “torn down to the studs” and rebuilt as an agency that recognises the “dignity of the people that it encounters”.
“But we all know that that will not happen under this administration,” he added.
Less than a week after Salgado Araujo was killed, ICE agents fatally shot Joan Sebastian Duran Guerrero, a Colombian immigrant, in Biddeford, Maine.
Earlier this year, federal immigration agents killed two US citizens in separate incidents in Minneapolis, prompting nationwide outrage and protests.
