title: EU adds HTX to Russia sanctions list, barring transactions starting Aug. 23
summary: Other crypto platforms listed alongside HTX include EXMO, Rapira, BitPapa, Aifory Pro, WhiteBird, NoOnecrypto and Exnode.
full_text:
EU adds HTX to Russia sanctions list, barring transactions starting Aug. 23
Quick Take
- The European Union added HTX to a list of third-country financial and crypto service providers accused of helping Russia circumvent sanctions, with a transaction ban set to take effect on Aug. 23.
- The measure does not impose an asset freeze, but generally bars people and companies in the EU from dealing directly or indirectly with the exchange.
- The bloc also created a broader mechanism to prohibit dealings with crypto platforms based in countries that repeatedly fail to prevent Russian sanctions evasion, although no countries have yet been added.
- Other crypto platforms listed alongside HTX include EXMO, Rapira, BitPapa, Aifory Pro, WhiteBird, NoOnecrypto and Exnode, among others.
We'd love your feedback.
The European Union has added crypto exchange HTX to its Russia sanctions regime, prohibiting people and companies in the bloc from transacting with the platform beginning next month.
The EU identified "HTX (HUOBI GLOBAL SA)" among a group of third-country financial institutions and crypto service providers that it said were significantly frustrating restrictions imposed over Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, according to a regulation published in the bloc’s Official Journal. The restriction takes effect on Aug. 23.
Under the applicable rules, EU operators will be barred from engaging directly or indirectly in transactions with HTX. The measure stops short of a full designation or asset freeze, Reuters reported. Eligible EU, European Economic Area and Swiss nationals and residents may seek authorization to withdraw funds or close accounts, but must apply within three months of the ban taking effect.
The legal document’s identification of the exchange as "HTX (HUOBI GLOBAL SA)" contrasts with a statement an HTX spokesperson gave The Block after the United Kingdom sanctioned Huobi Global S.A. in May. The spokesperson said at the time that Huobi Global S.A. was distinct from HTX.
Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, first announced the sanctions package in June and said it would extend to 20 non-EU entities, including banks, crypto platforms, and oil traders that have been servicing sanctioned Russian entities and individuals, but did not name HTX at the time.
The UK said it had reasonable grounds to suspect that Huobi Global S.A. supported the Russian government by providing financial services or making funds and other resources available to A7 Limited Liability Company, a Russia-linked cross-border payments firm. HTX said following the British action that regulatory compliance remained an "absolute top priority" and that it adhered to the rules in jurisdictions where it operated.
The EU action also comes two days after blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs alleged that HTX had been rotating hot wallets and funding addresses across TRON, Ethereum, BNB Smart Chain and Solana following the UK sanctions. TRM said addresses were rotated and retired within hours, making screening systems built around static sanctions lists less effective.
HTX rejected TRM’s characterization, telling The Block that the wallet movements reflected "routine, security-driven platform operations common across the industry."
The HTX restriction forms part of the EU's 21st sanctions package against Russia, which was adopted on July 23. The package designated 218 individuals and entities, the largest batch of listings in four years, while separately expanding transaction restrictions covering banks, crypto platforms, oil traders and other entities. The Council said it also added four designations tied to the A7 network and extended its transaction ban to 14 crypto-related service platforms.
Other crypto platforms listed alongside HTX include EXMO, Rapira, BitPapa, Aifory Pro, WhiteBird, NoOnecrypto and Exnode. The restrictions against those platforms are also scheduled to take effect on Aug. 23.
The package goes beyond targeting individual exchanges. A new provision allows the EU to prohibit transactions with crypto service providers established in a country that has "systematically and persistently" failed to stop platforms from undermining the bloc’s sanctions. The accompanying annex naming countries subject to that restriction is currently empty, meaning the EU has established the mechanism without yet applying it to an entire jurisdiction.
HTX did not immediately respond to The Block's request for comment on the EU action. The exchange was founded as Huobi in China in 2013 and is closely associated with Tron founder Justin Sun, whom HTX has described as an adviser.

title: SDCC teaser gives us our first good look at Blade Runner 2099
summary: Also: Forging the One Ring in Rings of Power S3 teaser; new Lanterns trailer; Spaceballs: The New One panel.
full_text:
It’s been nearly five years since Ridley Scott first announced his plans for a TV spinoff of his sci-fi masterpiece Blade Runner (1982) and the 2017 sequel Blade Runner 2049. It’s finally here—or almost, anyway. Prime Video debuted the first teaser for the new ten-episode series, Blade Runner 2099, at San Diego Comic-Con on Friday. We also got a teaser for the third season of Prime Video’s Rings of Power and a new trailer for HBO’s Lanterns.
Yeoh and Schafer joined show runner Silka Luisa (Shining Girls) onstage for the big reveal, which also included an exclusive clip shown to the audience. Luisa told Entertainment Weekly that the series stays true to the original’s “noir principles… and there’s a mystery at the heart of the show that looks both forwards and backwards in terms of mythology.” An uprising has occurred and the humans lost, which means they are now the hunted second-class citizens. “The show is really imagining what comes after us, and what does it mean to be human in a world where humanity is no longer relevant,” said Luisa.
Per the official synopsis:
Fifty years after the events of Blade Runner 2049, Los Angeles has been reborn, just not by humanity. Cora, a fugitive in a final bid to stop running, takes on one last identity: a Blade Runner. Forced to partner with Olwen, a Replicant days from dying, she hunts down a runaway hiding a truth that could collapse their fragile city.
The incomparable Michelle Yeoh stars as Olwen, the dying Replicant, along with Hunter Schafer (Euphoria) as Cora. The cast also includes Hugo Hamlet as Buster Friendly, as well as Dmitri Abold, Lewis Gribben, Katelyn Rose Downey, Daniel Rigby, Johnny Harris, Amy Lennox, Sheila Atim, Matthew Needham, Tom Burke, and Maurizio Lombardi—all in as-yet-undisclosed roles.
Blade Runner 2099 will premiere on November 25, 2026, on Prime Video.
Rings of Power S3
Prime Video made a major investment in The Rings of Power when it acquired the rights to the source material from the Tolkien estate, even committing to multiple seasons upfront. We’re now coming up on S3 and based on the teaser the streaming platform unveiled at SDCC, we’ll finally get to see Sauron (Charlie Vickers) forging the One Ring.

title: Littler sets up Price final at World Matchplay
summary: Luke Littler is on course to beat Phil Taylor's tournament average record after another impressive victory saw him reach the final.
full_text:
Littler sets up Price final at World Matchplay
- Published
Defending champion Luke Littler strolled into the World Matchplay final with a 17-5 demolition of unseeded Dirk van Duijvenbode in Blackpool.
The world number one raced in an 8-2 advantage and was averaging 117.10 and on course to beat Phil Taylor's tournament match average record of 114.99
Littler admitted afterwards that distracted him and his level did drop slightly as he finished with an average just below 111.
However, that leaves him well placed to beat Taylor's tournament average of 106.31, with Littler's currently at 110.88.
The teenager's victory also means he has now amassed more than £3m in the PDC's order of merit, and is more than £2m clear of world number two Luke Humphries.
Littler will face Wales' Gerwyn Price in Sunday's final after he beat Netherlands' Gian van Veen 17-10.
Sunday's final gets under way at 20:05 BST, with the Women's World Matchplay taking place in the afternoon session from 13:00 – Beau Greaves and defending champion Lisa Ashton the top two seeds.
Price replaces Clayton as Welsh number one
Price broke in the opening leg of the game and charged into a 4-1 lead, before a scrappy run of legs saw both players break throw regularly to leave Price leading 11-9 at the final mini-break.
From there, the seventh seed powered on and stretched away from Van Veen in scoring and finishing to seal a comfortable victory.
Both players missed 23 darts at a double across the match, while Van Veen was broken nine times in 14 legs throwing first on what was a difficult night for the world number three.
The victory sees Price climb to fourth in the order of merit, above Jonny Clayton, and in turn becomes Welsh number one.
Price told Sky Sports he was "happy" to reach the final, but "getting one up" on good friend Clayton was his main focus going into the tie.
Follow live text coverage of the men's World Matchplay on the BBC Sport website and app from 19:30 BST on Sunday.

title: 'He'll go right through this guy' - Joshua v Prenga predictions
summary: Figures from the boxing world give their predictions for Saturday's heavyweight fight between Anthony Joshua and Kristian Prenga.
full_text:
Joshua v Prenga - heavyweight predictions
- Published
Anthony Joshua returns to the ring on Saturday against the relatively unknown Kristian Prenga in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, knowing that victory would set up a long-awaited showdown with Tyson Fury.
Joshua, a two-time world champion and Olympic gold medallist, has won 29 fights - 26 by stoppage - and lost four.
Albanian Prenga enters the fight with an impressive record of his own, having achieved all of his 20 victories with stoppages while suffering only one defeat.
However, the 35-year-old has never faced anyone close to Joshua's level.
After Fury comfortably dispatched Polish veteran Mariusz Wach in Thailand on Friday, can Joshua can come through his own warm-up bout?
This will be Joshua's first fight since he was involved in a car crash in Nigeria that claimed the lives of two close friends, Sina Ghami and Latif 'Latz' Ayodele.
The Fury-Joshua fight has been a decade in the making. Contracts have been signed, with the blockbuster bout expected to take place later this year.
But could Prenga spoil the party and pull off a huge shock to go down in boxing history as the man who got in the way of Joshua-Fury happening?
Radio commentary from Jeddah will begin from about 20:30 BST on BBC Radio 5 Live, BBC Sounds, and the BBC Sport website and app.
Live text commentary will begin at 19:30 on the BBC Sport website and app.
BBC Sport spoke to figures from the boxing world to get their predictions for Saturday's fight.
Natasha Jonas - former two-weight world champion
"I think AJ will win by a stoppage late. He has to be careful at the beginning of the fight because a lot of Prenga's stoppages have come in the first couple of rounds - he rarely goes past six rounds, so that's uncharted territory."
Prediction - Joshua
Carl Frampton - former two-weight world champion
"I think AJ will have a look in the first round but it will be over round three or four. I think he'll go right though this guy. I hope he does and we see him and Fury."
Prediction - Joshua

Do your job, get in and get out."

Adam Smith - DAZN commentator
"Obviously it's been an incredibly difficult time for AJ but he seems mentally and physically in a good place, training under Team Usyk.

Adam Booth - trainer

We saw with Rico Verhoeven against Usyk that these kickboxers can make it tough. I expect AJ to look fresh, establish a quick jab early and have attention to detail.
"He looks very lean, I think he'll be quicker than before and I think he's going to get a clean win. Prenga will try but I think AJ will walk him on to a shot."

Prediction - Joshua
Tony Bellew - former cruiserweight world champion
"You will not see a third round. Joshua will win by a brutal, nasty and vicious knockout."
Prediction - Joshua

"AJ will win by knockout between rounds three and five."
Prediction - Joshua

title: The West is debating AI’s future with half the world absent
summary:
On July 13, more than 200 leading economists and AI researchers, including 16 Nobel laureates, signed an open letter organised by the Stanford Digital Economy Lab. Its warning was stark: artificial intelligence may drive an economic transformation “larger than the Industrial Revolution” compressed into a fraction of the time, and that we “must act now” to build the institutions to steer it.
We agree with every word. Then we scanned the signatory list. Four in five signatories come from the...
full_text:
On July 13, more than 200 leading economists and AI researchers, including 16 Nobel laureates, signed an open letter organised by the Stanford Digital Economy Lab. Its warning was stark: artificial intelligence may drive an economic transformation “larger than the Industrial Revolution” compressed into a fraction of the time, and that we “must act now” to build the institutions to steer it.
We agree with every word. Then we scanned the signatory list. Four in five signatories come from the United States and Canada, and the rest almost entirely from Europe. Not one name comes from China.
The letter writes about a global economic transformation, but its signatory list suggests half the AI world does not exist. China is home to roughly half of all frontier model development and has arguably the world’s fastest AI adoption. Trying to understand this transformation while excluding China is like studying the Industrial Revolution while ignoring the country with the most factories.
No one intended the omission. It reflects a two-level information gap that runs deeper than most Western observers realise.
The first level is of the AI models themselves. Western businesses are already ahead of Western discourse here. DoorDash, Siemens and Airbnb have adopted Chinese models from DeepSeek, Z.ai (Zhipu AI) and Moonshot AI alongside, and sometimes instead of, their American counterparts.
For cost-conscious companies and governments, the sensible choice is often an open-weight model that runs cheaply on local hardware. Today, that choice is a Chinese model. With the recent release of Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3, which matches leading US models on many benchmarks, that trend will only accelerate. Investors grasped this immediately: US chip stocks fell on the news.

full_text:
Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels claimed a missile attack on the southern Saudi city of Jizan on Saturday, after vowing retaliation against the kingdom for attacks this week.
Iran, meanwhile, reported no strikes overnight on Saturday for the first time after two weeks of US attacks. The Iranian health ministry spokesperson, Hossein Kermanpour, said: “Iran had a peaceful night” in a post on X. Tensions, however, remain high.
A memorandum of understanding (MoU) signed between the US and Iran in June seemed to break down two weeks ago, after Iranian attacks on tankers in the strait of Hormuz prompted US strikes on Iran, which led to Iranian retaliation against US allies in the region. 
 The MoU was meant to reopen the strait after its closure by Iran during the war and pause hostilities for 60 days to give room for negotiations, but active fighting has prevented progress in talks. Much of the current fighting has centred on the strait, a transit point for a fifth of the world’s oil and gas prior to the war.
The US president, Donald Trump, threatened expanded strikes on Iran, meeting top national security advisers on Friday to decide whether the administration should escalate attacks.
He has warned he could widen the scope of targets in Iran to include civilian infrastructure such as Iranian energy plants and bridges, as well as launch a ground operation to seize Kharg Island, one of Iran’s largest oil export terminals.
“There’s a military exit where we just keep going just the way we are, and we can even make it a heavier dose, and it’s knocking out everything they have. Or there’s a smarter strategy that you make a deal,” Trump told reporters on Friday.
Iran issued warnings to citizens of Gulf countries hosting US military sites to stay away from bases to protect themselves from future attacks.
On Saturday night, a spokesperson for Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said that Britain would become a “definite and legitimate target” if it supported the US in any war with Tehran, according to the Iranian state broadcaster, Irib.
The spokesperson said any country, including Britain and Gulf states, that backed the US in a conflict would be considered a legitimate target, adding that US bombers had recently used British airfields.
Trump insisted on Friday that, despite the fighting, negotiations with Iran were going well, calling them “by far the most serious that we’ve seen”.
The Iranian foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said the “American approach” was preventing peace talks from proceeding, while vowing Iran was “neither intimidated by threats nor will we yield to pressure”.
Tensions over the strait continued, with the US firing on a merchant vessel in the Gulf of Oman which it said was violating its blockade of Iranian ports, while the UK maritime agency reported an incident between a tanker and military forces on Friday, without specifying the responsible parties.
Air defence systems in Saudi Arabia intercepted two ballistic missiles from Yemen on Saturday, Reuters reported. The attacks targeted oil refineries in Yanbu on the Red Sea, while the Saudi civil defence also issued warnings for the port city of Jizan, close to the border with Yemen.
A video circulating on social media showed dark clouds rising above a refinery in Jizan belonging to Aramco, the Saudi oil giant. A Yemeni security source told Agence France-Presse a naval base in Hodeida and a military camp on Kamaran island were targeted by Saudi Arabia on Friday. The Houthis said the attacks were a “dangerous escalation”.
The Iran-aligned Houthi movement, which controls northern and western Yemen, declared a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia in the Red Sea last week after the kingdom struck the airport in Sana’a. The Houthis struck two Saudi tankers in the Red Sea on Thursday, prompting Trump to threaten a “major military punishment” for Tehran and the Houthis.
The naval blockade threatens to further upend global energy markets, as Saudi Arabia has been avoiding the closure of the strait by diverting millions of barrels of oil to the Red Sea. Oil prices pushed past $100 a barrel on Thursday for the first time since May, while the cost of shipping insurance through the southern Red Sea doubled for some companies.
Araghchi said on Saturday that there was no military solution to the Saudi-Houthi conflict and that it was “rooted in old disputes”.
“We believe that there is no military solution to the issue of Yemen, Bab al-Mandab and other regional issues,” Araghchi said in an interview with an Iranian newspaper. He called for further dialogue between the two sides.
Mediators have tried to keep talks alive amid the escalating fighting, Pakistan and Qatar delivering messages between the US and Iran over the last two weeks. The New York Times reported that Iraq had delivered a ceasefire proposal to Tehran, which was promptly rejected – a report disputed by Iraq.
Pakistan has also reportedly been pushing for fresh talks between the two sides after a diplomatic initiative by China explored new dialogue. Iran’s interior minister, Eskandar Momeni, visited Istanbul this week to discuss the topic, reports said.

title: What Love Island tells us about the changing face of dating
summary: From women making the first move to shifting relationship dynamics, Love Island has become a window into Britain's evolving dating culture
full_text:
On the fourth series of Love Island UK in 2018, Megan Barton-Hanson pulled fellow Islander, Wes Nelson, for a chat.
Just moments earlier, she had ended her relationship with Eyal Booker after admitting the pair had little more than physical chemistry. Now, sitting opposite Wes, who had been coupled up with Laura Anderson since the start of the competition, she decided not to wait for him to make the first move.
"I think it's pretty obvious that I do really fancy you," she told him. "And I just felt like, if I didn't say something, I'd regret it massively."
By the end of the episode, viewers had a new nickname for her: "Muggy Megan". Critics accused her of moving too quickly between relationships and breaking "girl code". Others admired her honesty.
At the time, Barton-Hanson argued that she had been treated differently to her male counterparts. "People definitely do give girls a harder time than men… It's sexist."
But eight years later, scenes like Barton-Hanson's no longer feel quite so out of the ordinary. Until this series, the opening coupling had always seen the men choose first. This year, the shows rules were changed, with the women making the first choice.
Alicia Denby, a sociologist at Manchester Metropolitan University, argues the show's tweak is reflective of a broader societal change where "women may now be more likely to approach someone first".
At its peak, around five million people tuned in to Love Island every night. Live audiences are not what they were, but it remains ITV's biggest programme among 16 to 34-year-olds.
For Prof Kitty Nichols, who researches relationships and popular culture at the University of Sheffield, Love Island has become "an important cultural vehicle" allowing us to "reflect on the dating scene and culture at the moment".
Former PE teacher Kai Fagan met his now wife, Sanam Harrinanan, when he won the 2023 series, an experience he says transformed his life.
"My life ever since then has been a fairytale. The whole show is about love. That's the point of it. You're put in a situation to fall in love."
For Fagan, the show delivered exactly what it promised: love. Meanwhile, for thousands watching at home, it has become a window into how modern relationships are formed, tested and understood.
As another series of Love Island approaches its end, what do Love Island's changing dynamics tell us about dating culture beyond the villa? And does women making the first move really represent genuine progress towards equality?
The forever changing rules
For much of the 20th Century, heterosexual dating followed a script that would have felt familiar to the characters in Pride and Prejudice. Men were largely expected to make the first move. They asked women out, paid for dates and, in many cases, took the lead in deciding when the relationship moved forward.
By the 1960s, the women's liberation movement began challenging many of those norms. As Aretha Franklin's Respect became an anthem for a generation demanding greater equality, the widespread availability of contraception changed the ideas about sex. Then with the rise of online dating in the 2000s, millions of people began meeting through websites and, later, dating apps.
But whether these changes have really done anything to shift gender expectations is unclear.
As recently as 2021, sociologist Ellen Lamont reviewed more than 100 studies on heterosexual dating and found traditional dating scripts still remained, with men still expected to make the first move.
For cultural commentator Coco, who goes by her first name and has amassed more than 100,000 followers on TikTok analysing Love Island, this reflects an important distinction.
She argues women aren't replacing men as the pursuers, they simply have greater freedom to act on what they want.
"Women haven't flipped the roles," she says. "Women have just been allowed to exist." She believes women now have "more choice, freedom and opportunity than we've ever had in history".
Love Island's contradiction
But even if women are becoming more comfortable making the first move, Denby argues that this does not mean gendered power relations have disappeared.
She argues that women on Love Island are often praised for their patience and loyalty while male contestants explore connections with other contestants. But she says when women take a more active role in pursuing relationships, they are judged differently.
"It's almost as if women are praised for being submissive in the villa, because when they do take on more of an active or expressive role, they are criticised for it."
On this year's Love Island, in a move that may have reflected the growing trend of women on the show taking the lead, Elicia Bailey took both Aidan Murphy and Finley Maddock to the Hideaway, the villa's private romantic room.
But she faced criticism for it and Denby points to what she sees as a sexual double standard around women's sexuality. Another female contestant on this year's show, Priya Jaswal, was labelled a "sexual person" by a male contestant and accused of "pouncing" on Murphy, comments that Denby argues, suggest "women are judged for taking an active role" in dating.
Nichols sees similar patterns.
She believes Love Island has what she describes as "pockets of diversity" and "little moments of change", where contestants challenge conventional gender roles.
Yet she argues those moments are often temporary, with Islanders reverting "back to the expected gender roles".
According to Nichols, double standards persist. "If a woman behaves in the same way that a man behaves, they get reprimanded."
That reaction can be seen in the programme's history.
For example, Ekin-Su Cülcüloğlu's pursuit of Jay Younger divided viewers during the 2022 series. Some accused her of betraying Davide Sanclimenti, who she later won the show with, while others praised her confidence.
For Nichols, those responses reveal something about British attitudes to dating.
"I think audience members receive more positively men diverging from their expected roles," she says.
She said it may be because viewers "don't anticipate" behavior like that, But adds that, "sometimes women doing so is sort of seen less positively."
What happens when the rules change?
For Tareq Ferguson, a long-time Love Island viewer and TikTok commentator with more than 50,000 followers, one of the biggest changes in recent series has been watching male contestants become more passive.
"The men want to be passenger princesses," he says. "They want to sit back, kick up their feet, while the women do the grafting and do the work."
On this year's show, Lorenzo Alessi was reluctant to make Julia Majchrzak a morning coffee, something many contestants see as an act of care for the person they're coupled up with. It become a flashpoint on the show and sparked debate among viewers.
For Ferguson, moments like those reflect a wider shift in modern dating, with some men appearing increasingly hesitant to take the lead.
But some research suggest that men's reluctance may stem less from disinterest and more from uncertainty about how to navigate dating today.
In a recent Cosmopolitan survey, men said online dating had made then feel judged on their appearance. While others said repeated rejection and lack of matches had damaged their confidence.
Research like this echoes what Coco believes is happening both inside and outside the villa.
"Society has rightly expanded what's possible for women," she says. "But we haven't spent the same amount of time helping young men understand what their role looks like in this landscape. The cultural conversation hasn't kept pace with the social change."
She also believes online conversations have contributed to that uncertainty.
"I think the manosphere content we're seeing has done something to women," she says. "It's put their guard up."

title: Ramsay-Peaty in tears after missing out on gold again
summary: An emotional Adam Ramsay-Peaty questions how his future looks after missing out on gold at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.
full_text:
Ramsay-Peaty in tears after missing out on gold again
- Published
After tears in Paris, tears again in Glasgow.
It leaves even the great Adam Ramsay-Peaty wondering how much of this is worth it.
"I work a lot harder than what it says on the scoreboard," the Englishman said after taking 100m breaststroke bronze at the Commonwealth Games, his eyes and cheeks red with emotion.
"It hurts too much. I have got to approach training differently now because it hurts too much."
Ramsay-Peaty has done it all in this sport.
Three Olympic gold medals. Eight world titles. The 14 fastest times in history.
But after taking a break from swimming amid a wave of mental health issues in 2023, he is still searching for that winning feeling again on the big stage.
He was pipped to Olympic gold in Paris two years ago. In Glasgow, despite coming into the final as the fastest qualifier, he had to settle for bronze.
He was beaten by Australia's Sam Williamson but also Jersey's history-maker Filip Nowacki, the 18-year-old he has taken under his wing.
Ramsay-Peaty was third at halfway and could not close the gap. His time - 59.65 seconds - was more than four-tenths slower than his semi-final swim and three seconds off his personal best from seven years ago.
"It took a lot of courage to get back into the sport, so we should be happy with everything we get, but then that contradicts the athlete inside me and what I work for," he said.
"I just think I deserve more. I know sport isn't about what you deserve or even what you work for - it's who gets it on the day.
"I just know I'm a better athlete than that. It's very disappointing."
Ramsay-Peaty has spoken about the difficult decisions that come with being an elite athlete. The time away from his son, whom he held in his arms after the Paris silver. The events at home he has to miss.
"They are not even sacrifices; they are choices," he said.
"It's like getting knocked out in the group stages in the World Cup for a very good team. You know you're better and it hurts because you know you have to wait for a very long time for the next championships.
"This is probably - realistically - my last Commonwealth Games and I thought I'd trained for better. I could do better. I've been faster this season. That's where the frustration is."
Ramsay-Peaty has made no secret of the fact he is still competing in the quest for Olympic gold.
He considered retirement again after Paris, but committed to another four years when the 50m race was added to programme for Los Angeles 2028.
This 100m breaststroke is his event - the one in which he went unbeaten in eight years - but there may be a time when he has to let it go.
The 50m race - a dash down one length of the pool - would be less taxing on the body, and Ramsay-Peaty is due back in the pool for that event on Sunday morning.
"Is the 100 even viable any more? I don't know," he said.
"When it hurts like this, the 50 is probably my super strength with my power.
"With the Olympics, that's probably going to be more realistic, but it's too early to tell.
"I just feel like I couldn't have given more this cycle. If I had given less, would it have even equalled more?"
Given the emotion, there are times you wonder how close Ramsay-Peaty is to walking away entirely.
He appeared to walk to the edge but always turned back, insisting the drive for LA remains.
"Of course," he said.
"I know I'm a sprinter. I know I can do very well because I've done it. It doesn't disappear overnight.
"It requires me to look at the formula and see how I can get to that speed again."

title: I thought the Lockerbie bombing was a closed case until I started asking questions
summary: The deeper I dug, the more complicated Lockerbie became and there have been times that I don't know what to believe.
full_text:
I thought the Lockerbie bombing was a closed case until I started asking questions
- Published
I was only a year old when the UK's deadliest terror attack shocked the world.
In December 1988, Pan Am flight 103 exploded over the Scottish town of Lockerbie, killing all 259 people on board as well as 11 on the ground.
I was a teenager by the time Libyan intelligence officer Abdelbaset al-Megrahi was convicted of the bombing in 2001 and, when he later died, I thought that was largely the end of the story.
It wasn't.
The case still rumbles on and, later this year, a man suspected of making the bomb which blew up the plane, Abu Agila Masud, goes on trial in Washington DC.
As part of a Radio 4 Intrigue podcast series, I had an opportunity to delve into this complex case with fresh eyes.
The deeper I dug, the more complicated Lockerbie became and there have been times that I don't know what to believe.
Jim Swire, on the other hand, is sure what he believes - and it is not the official story.
His daughter Flora died in the bombing, but he is convinced that whoever killed her got away with mass murder.
Swire believes Megrahi is innocent, even befriending the convicted bomber up until his death in 2012.
"The burning issue was to get to the truth," he says.
"Always has been, always will be and I will not shut up about what I know to be true."
Swire's doggedness has made him a prominent voice but most of the Lockerbie victims' families don't agree that Megrahi's conviction was a miscarriage of justice - and the bomber’s own appeals against the verdict either failed or were abandoned.
For Swire, the simplest explanation is that Iran was behind the attack - not Libya.
The Lockerbie bombing came five months after 290 people were killed when an Iranian commercial airliner was shot down by a US battleship.
Iran swore revenge and months later Pan Am flight 103 exploded on its way to New York.
And there's more.
Iran - much like they do now - used proxy militant groups to pursue their ends.
Before the Lockerbie bombing, a militant cell based in Frankfurt, part of the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine - General Command (PFLP-GC), was foiled by German police.
Police arrested suspects and seized explosive devices, concealed in radio cassette players, that were designed to trigger at altitude.
The bomb that brought down Pan Am 103 was in a radio cassette player hidden inside a samsonite briefcase.
Because of this, Swire believes the device that brought down Pan Am 103 was loaded at Frankfurt, and not Malta as the court had concluded.
And, for Swire, this is only the tip of the iceberg.
He also questions much of the evidence presented at the 2001 trial, discredits witnesses, and is extremely suspicious of the involvement of intelligence agencies - like MI5, MI6 and the CIA - in the aftermath of the bombing.
Combine these suspicions with his all-consuming grief and you can see why Swire is such a force to be reckoned with on his quest for a truth he believes has been denied to him.
"Discovering the truth became my way of handling the consequences of the grief reaction," Swire says.
"And it was very tough for other people to understand that but that's just the way I'm made, I suppose."
Intrigue: Lockerbie
On 21 December 1988, a plane explodes over Lockerbie, Scotland, killing 270 people. Almost four decades on, there's fresh evidence. Who was really behind the bombing?
Dick Marquise, who led the FBI's Lockerbie task force, says that in the early days of the case he too believed the PFLP-GC were the "number one suspect", but years of investigation found nothing to prove it.
"There was not one shred of evidence that could be taken to court and get a conviction," he says. "You couldn't do it. There was nothing."
However, there are others, besides Swire, who still question the "official narrative" - including former CIA agent John Holt who also believes Iran was behind the bombing.
Holt worked with Libyan intelligence assets in the 1980s and was the handler of double agent Abdul Majid Giaka, whose information became central to the investigation into the Lockerbie bombing.
Holt now believes Giaka was a "BS artist" who was out for money and was feeding the CIA fake stories to get paid.
"I didn't think much of him at all," he says.
"He gave us some little tidbits about what was going on, but he never knew anything about the Pan Am bombing. And he knew a lot about Megrahi," Holt says.
Holt believes the fact the CIA bankrolled Giaka devalues him as an informant.
"It makes it easier for somebody to say whatever the person who's giving them money wants them to say," Holt says.
I managed to get a hold of the CIA papers - known as cables - from the time, which showed what Giaka had told the Americans.
The cables date back to the months before Lockerbie and include notes of conversations between Giaka and Holt and two earlier CIA handlers.
Within the cables, Giaka places Megrahi in Malta - where the bomb was said to have been planted - at a key time in the Lockerbie plot.
Megrahi is also said to have visited a Maltese clothes shop, buying shirts and baby grows - which were placed in the suitcase with the bomb and later found at the plane crash site.
Giaka had even talked to the CIA about eight kilos of orange-coloured explosives stored at the Malta airport offices. Semtex, the explosive used in Lockerbie, is orange.
In the 2001 trial, Giaka was to be a "key" witness in the prosecution's case but the four judges described some of his evidence as "at best grossly exaggerated and at worst simply untrue".
The Senussi files
Decades on from Megrahi's conviction, new intelligence documents have been recovered allegedly from the heart of Libyan intelligence.
They are believed to have come from Libyan leader Colonel Gaddafi's notorious intelligence network run by his spy chief Abdullah Senussi.
These leaked Libyan intelligence documents contain information that could potentially put an end to the doubt, theories and countertheories that have tied so many, including me, in knots.
The original 'Senussi Files', as they are now known, were shown to French journalists who later published a book, The Murderer Who Must Be Saved.
I travelled to Paris to meet one of the authors, investigative journalist Vincent Nouzille.
He brought piles of documents, enough to cover the whole bed and the hotel room desk.
You can tell he loves his work and despite having pored over these documents for years, he's still awestruck by their content.
Some of the Senussi files date back to autumn 1988, in the months before Lockerbie, and contain documents apparently detailing plans to target aircraft on multi-stop flights using a 11-hour long-delay timer bomb concealed in luggage much like the Lockerbie bombing.
It even mentions tests on concealing a device inside a tape recorder.
As we go through each document, my head is spinning.
There are references to dry runs, apparent weaknesses in airport security, and enough detail about the movements of Megrahi and others for Nouzille to crosscheck dates and places against other sources.
Nouzille says he spent three years carefully verifying everything in the files.
He shows me another file which details the apparent movements of Megrahi and Masud, coming in and out of Malta.
This account lines up with the information provided in the CIA cables from the previously discredited Giaka.
"We know from the CIA cables that Giaka reported the same people, the same dates, the same false passport, at the same date," Nouzille says.
"So two sources, independent, which match."
The Senussi Files seem to corroborate several details first mentioned in the cables, including the presence of semtex at Luqa Airport in Malta.
Nouzille shows me a translated document, signed by Megrahi, dated January 87, which mentions "10 kilos of explosive material" stored at the airport by Lamin Khalif Fhimah, the man who stood trial alongside Megrahi in 2001 but was acquitted.

title: Pizza, pasta, potatoes, protein - how Italian children became so overweight
summary: The Mediterranean diet was a blueprint for healthy living, yet Italian children are among the most overweight in Europe according to WHO.
full_text:
Pizza, pasta, potatoes, protein - how Italian children became so overweight
- Published
Daily life is not easy for Salvatore. At 17, he weighs 170kg (26st 10lb) and struggles to walk.
He can't tie his own shoelaces and his Vespa scooter strains to bear his weight - in one week, its wheels broke seven times.
"He eats constantly," says his mother Anna.
Salvatore is among a growing number of Italian children and teenagers living with obesity. The problem is particularly acute in the south: in parts of the Campania region, more than 40% of eight and nine-year-olds are overweight. The town of Ponticelli, on the outskirts of Naples, has earned the unenviable reputation as one of the world's child obesity capitals.
It is a striking development in a country long regarded as the spiritual home of the Mediterranean diet. Yet today, Italian children are among the most overweight in Europe, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).
Salvatore is waiting for life-changing surgery at the Betania Hospital in Ponticelli, where Dr Sonja Chiappetta has spent 15 years treating patients with severe obesity.
Until recently, she says, most of her patients were in their fifties. "Now I see those same patients when they're teenagers, as young as 16. They are getting younger, and it's frightening."
The surgery she carries out removes up to 90% of the stomach - meaning people are unable to eat large quantities of food. Demand has risen sharply in this part of Italy.
But Salvatore has been told he cannot get the operation. His weight is so excessive it makes the surgery too dangerous.
Instead, Dr Chiappetta has prescribed him a GLP-1 weight-loss injection to reduce his appetite and help him lose enough weight for the operation.
For decades, Italy was held up as a model of healthy eating.
The Mediterranean diet - rich in vegetables, legumes, olive oil, whole grains and fish - became famous after US physiologist Ancel Keys and his wife, biochemist Margaret Keys, studied communities in southern Italy in the 1950s and linked their habits to remarkably low rates of heart disease.
Their research transformed a regional way of eating into one of the world's best-known diets; a blueprint for healthy living.
But the Italy that inspired those studies no longer exists.
"The traditional Mediterranean diet has been lost," says Doctor Valter Longo, director of the Longevity Institute at the University of Southern California. "Only 10% of Italians really follow it."
Dr Longo sums up the modern Italian diet with what he calls the "five Ps": pizza, pasta, potatoes, protein and pane - the Italian word for bread.
The transformation is visible everywhere: from supermarket shelves stocked with ultra-processed foods to pizzerias selling slices piled high with chips, sausages and fried snacks.
Doctor Roberto Berni Canani, a paediatrician and obesity specialist at the Federico II University in Naples, sees the consequences every day.
"I've treated children who are just two or three years old and already weigh 25kg," he says.
He says most parents don't recognise their children are overweight. "They come to see me because of other problems - a cough, stomach pain, diarrhoea. They don't realise their child's weight is what's causing it."
Italy’s child obesity time-bomb
Italian children have become some of the most overweight in Europe, despite the country being famous for the so-called Mediterranean diet. What can be done to help them?
Ten-year-old Francesca has a persistent cough and struggles to swallow. Doctors suspect an inflammatory condition of the oesophagus.
She weighs 60kg (9st 6lb) - but that's not why her parents have sought medical help.
Francesca says she eats bread with Nutella for breakfast, a chocolate-filled sponge cake as a snack, pasta with lentils for lunch and usually chicken for dinner.
"But she doesn't eat vegetables," her mother, Carmen, interjects. "I put them in front of her, but she won't touch them."
Francesca's parents insist she is active. She does artistic gymnastics and Latin dance, and doesn't get tired. They have never considered her weight as a problem.
Dr Berni Canani reaches a different conclusion.
The problem, he explains, is the overall pattern rather than any single meal. Small, calorie-dense foods consumed throughout the day, sugary drinks, too few fruit and vegetables and little understanding of how these habits accumulate over time.
"This is a very good mother," he says. "A very good father. They simply don't recognise the importance of diet quality and body weight."
By the time many families arrive at his clinic, unhealthy habits have already become deeply ingrained. They begin at home and are reinforced at school.
And in Italy, encouraging children to be more active can be surprisingly difficult.
Many schools are housed in beautiful old palazzi - they were never designed with modern physical education in mind.
The Ugo Foscolo primary school is no exception. Its gym has barely enough space for a class of children to move around.
"I have one pupil I'm particularly concerned about," says Francesca Pecce, who teaches at the school. "He's 10 years old and weighs around 60 kilograms."
She has tried raising the issue with his mother.
"But she is not worried," Pecce says. "In Neapolitan culture, if a child is a little chubby with rosy cheeks, people often think they're healthy."
Schools, she believes, can help change that, especially if children "take home" lessons about healthy eating.
"Sometimes it's easier to educate the parents through their children than the other way round."
At a secondary school in Naples, students file into a classroom for a nutrition workshop run by the Valter Longo Foundation.
The programme is part of a regional initiative to tackle childhood obesity. Over the coming months, more than 17,000 students across 25 schools will take part. Families will receive support to help change eating habits at home.
But not all of the students are convinced.
Eighteen-year-old Ciro doubts that information alone will change behaviour.
"My classmates already know what's healthy," he says. "They just don't care."
Carmen, 19, is more optimistic.
"I thought it was actually really helpful because teenagers today are really big into junk food, and don't exercise as much."
She says the problem is that temptation is everywhere. Even foods traditionally associated with Italy have changed.
"When we go out for pizza, people don't just order a Margherita. They put chips, sausages and fried food on top."
Add to that the centuries-old cliches of Italian mothers and grandmothers showing their love through food, and it's a perfect storm.
Obesity is an "escalating global epidemic", says the WHO. More than one billion people worldwide are now obese, and childhood obesity has quadrupled since 1990.
In 2025, Italy became the first country to pass a national law recognising obesity as a chronic, progressive and relapsing disease.
Rather than treating obesity simply as the result of poor choices, the country's new law recognises it as a chronic disease influenced by biology, environment and social circumstances.
The Campania region has become a testing ground for putting that philosophy into practice, implementing a series of ambitious interventions - including a controversial trial of a "fast-mimicking diet".
Researchers are recruiting 300 overweight adolescents who will spend five days every three months on a controlled diet of 1,100 calories on day one and 770 calories on following four days - so restrictive it resembles a fast.
The goal is to trigger a "metabolic reset".
"Fasting, or controlled deprivation of food, is linked to a longer and healthier lifespan," says Dr Longo, who has spent three decades studying the effects of fasting.
But not all obesity specialists are persuaded that fasting is the right approach for children.

title: What a week's work experience taught these Year 10s about their futures
summary: Three 15-year-olds tell the BBC how their outlook changed after one week in the world of work.
full_text:
What a week's work experience taught these Year 10s about their futures
- Published
When Kelsey first arrived at secondary school, she said she wanted to be almost anywhere else but there.
She struggled with friendships, clashed with teachers and often tried to avoid coming into school.
But after a week's work experience placement at Whipsnade Zoo, in Bedfordshire, her outlook could not be more different.
She said it made her a "completely different person" - more confident, with a "good group of friends" and a greater sense of purpose about where her education could lead her.
Children across the UK are strongly encouraged to do work experience while at school. In England, the government published new legal guidance in June for schools to deliver two weeks of "in-person and immersive" work experience in future, one between Year 7 and Year 9, and one between Years 10 and 11.
But not all work experience placements are equal, and finding the right one can be tricky.
Organisations like the Sutton Trust and the Social Mobility Foundation said some students could be limited by the availability of placements in their area, or a lack of family connections with local employers.
BBC News spoke to three Year 10 pupils, one year ahead of their final GCSE exams, about how they decided what areas of work they were interested in, their experiences of trying to find the right placement, and what it taught them about their future education and ultimate career goals.
Before her placement, Kelsey said she had no clear idea what she wanted to do after school. It was part of the reason why she struggled to commit to her education.
She had always loved animals, but spending time at the zoo helped her understand the range of careers available - and the qualifications she would need to pursue them.
"I realised why school matters, and how it links directly to the career I want," she said.
"I've started revising properly and putting much more effort into my education because I know it's the route to my future."
The practical nature of the placement also helped Kelsey build her confidence.
She worked alongside other students to design enrichment activities for a tiger, for example, before presenting their ideas to members of the public - something she said she would previously have found intimidating.
"I wasn't treated like a child, and I was trusted to do meaningful work," she said.
Kelsey now plans to study animal care at college after her GCSEs, before pursuing a career as an animal behaviourist.
For Maddison, her goal to end up in office-based work was clear to her from the beginning, so she approached Central Employment North East, a recruitment firm in Newcastle where her uncle was a partner.
"I'm quite a shy person," she said. "Before I left, my mum told me: 'Confidence is key.'"
She quickly settled in as colleagues made her feel part of the team.
By the end of the week, she felt her confidence had grown and she could see herself pursuing the career she had imagined.
It left her eager to return to school to gain the qualifications she needs for an office-based career.
"When I got home on Friday I told my mum I couldn't believe it was already over," she said.
"I wished I could leave school and start working there straight away."
For Azhe, a placement at Kwick Fix Auto Care, also in Newcastle, proved valuable for a different reason to Kelsey and Maddison.
Rather than confirming a future career, it helped him realise mechanics probably was not the right path for him.
Like other students, Azhe was responsible for arranging his own placement, and with no clear career path in mind, he chose an opportunity that would allow him to explore a completely different environment.
"I decided to choose something I knew nothing about," he said.
Although he said staff explained processes clearly, he said his lack of prior interest in the field meant he sometimes felt "overwhelmed" with information.
He had hoped to spend more time on repairs himself and said that sometimes felt frustrating, but that he understood why safety and experience meant students could not simply be handed tools and left to work.
The placement also challenged his understanding of what the job would be like, and that being a mechanic "isn't just about fixing cars".
"It involves problem-solving, teamwork, communication and taking responsibility for people's safety," he said.
He also found the work much more physically demanding than he had expected, with long hours on his feet and the need to remain focused throughout the day.
The experience has left him thinking carefully about his future and the alternative careers he might enjoy.
'Opportunities remain unequal'
Erica Holt-White, research and policy manager at the Sutton Trust, said the experiences of these students, and thousands of others like them, show why meaningful work experience can be so beneficial.
It can be particularly valuable for young people who do not have family or friends working in the industries they are interested in.
"It gives them exposure to professional environments and the chance to meet people in careers they might otherwise never encounter," she said.
But access to those opportunities remains unequal, according to Sarah Atkinson, chief executive of the Social Mobility Foundation.
"Many schools now ask students to find placements themselves," she said.
"That creates significant inequalities, because young people without family or professional networks are far more likely either to miss out altogether, or to end up in placements that aren't relevant to their ambitions."
Both said work experience does not need to lead directly to a future career to be valuable.
For Kelsey, the lessons from Whipsnade Zoo continue to shape both her ambitions and her approach to education.
Her advice to younger pupils is simple.
"Take the opportunity when it's offered - talk to people, ask questions and enjoy it because you'll learn far more than you expect."

title: Another UK heatwave looms after cooler end to weekend
summary: Temperatures are forecast to surge next week as another UK heatwave begins.
full_text:
Another UK heatwave looms after cooler end to weekend
- Published
Another UK heatwave could be declared next week as temperatures are once again forecast to intensify across England and parts of Wales.
Following some much-needed rain in the north and north-west of the UK this weekend, temperatures will rise back to heatwave threshold levels in many locations.
Maximum temperatures are forecast to climb as high as 35C (95F) in the hottest areas.
It comes as some parts of the UK will only have just seen an end to their third heatwave, after three consecutive weeks above the temperature threshold.
Temperatures to rise after cooler Sunday
Sunday will be a cooler day for all of the UK as it begins cloudy with a little bit of rain for southern and eastern areas.
As temperatures fall widely by a couple of degrees, a few locations will finally mark the end to their third heatwave of the year, including Usk in Monmouthshire and Exeter in Devon.
Both places are forecast to see temperatures drop beneath the heatwave threshold for the first time in 21 consecutive days.
A breezier and fresher day for all, temperatures will largely be in the mid-20s Celsius for the south-east of the UK and in the mid-teens Celsius further north.
For many, the relief from the heat will be short-lived as high pressure is set to build close to the south of the UK next week.
This will stall rain-bearing weather fronts and any wet weather will become confined to northern and western areas - especially north-west Scotland.
In southern parts of the UK, temperatures look set to climb once again.
Tapping into the heat over the near continent, the UK is likely to enter another heatwave, with temperatures in England and Wales likely to peak around 25-32C for much of next week.
The hottest weather will initially be focused on central and eastern England by Tuesday before spreading northwards and westwards.
Scotland and Northern Ireland will remain cooler with temperatures generally in the high teens or low to mid-twenties Celsius.
Wednesday is likely to be the hottest day of the week.
East Wales and most of England could see temperatures between 30-35C.
It will also become warmer in Scotland and Northern Ireland with temperatures reaching the mid twenties.
Some computer models suggest an even more intense surge of heat could arrive by midweek.
How long will the heat last?
By next weekend, the forecast suggests a return to cooler weather with Atlantic systems bringing some rain and westerly winds.
Unfortunately for southern areas, where the rain is needed most, it may remain dry.
How long the heat lasts depend on whether a southerly or westerly wind develops.
A westerly wind will bring an end to heatwave conditions, while southerly winds could signal a return to intense heat.
You can check the latest forecast for your area on the BBC Weather website and app.
Boiling Point: The Week of Extreme Heat
The last week of June 2026 saw record-breaking temperatures across parts of the UK and Europe. While some enjoyed the sunshine, the heat caused trains, schools and emergency services to buckle.

title: Joshua knocked down twice as dramatic win sets up Fury fight
summary: Anthony Joshua suffers two knockdowns before recovering to dramatically stop Kristian Prenga in the second round.
full_text:
Joshua knocked down twice as dramatic win sets up Fury fight
- Published
Anthony Joshua suffered two knockdowns - the first happening after just 20 seconds - before recovering to dramatically stop Kristian Prenga in the second round of his comeback fight in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia.
The British heavyweight was fighting for the first time since surviving the December car crash in Nigeria that claimed the lives of his close friends Sina Ghami and Latif 'Latz' Ayodele.
He was sensationally rocked by a huge uppercut from underdog Prenga in the opening round, and then hit the canvas again later in the round.
At that point he looked on the verge of one of the biggest shock defeats in heavyweight history, with the long-awaited Tyson Fury fight hanging by a thread.
But Joshua produced one of the greatest escapes of his career, and now that fight is on.
He unleashed his right hand in the second round, with the final shot sending Albanian Prenga crashing down and forcing the referee to halt the contest.
"It's more than punch power. That was spirit, that was Latz, that was Sina, that was the families. It hurts to even talk about it. It has been tough," Joshua, 36, said.
He choked up and stepped away from the microphone, before adding: "It's my brothers. I don't want to talk about it."
There had been speculation fellow Briton Fury might make a appearance despite insisting he would not attend.
But the master of mind games stayed true to his word, with Fury nowhere to be seen barely 24 hours on from his own warm-up win over Mariusz Wach in Thailand.
"I respect everything he has done and everything that he has achieved, but as a fighting person, we're here now. I hope the fans will be in for a lovely treat," Joshua said about the prospect of fighting Fury.
Contracts have been signed, but the venue and date for a fight more than a decade in the making are still unknown.
This chaotic night, however, belonged to Joshua in a victory forged through adversity during the most difficult months of his life.
Down but not out for AJ on emotional return
Given the circumstances, this was never going to be a straightforward return for Joshua. Few, however, could have predicted the drama that unfolded inside six minutes.
Joshua carried the names of Ghami and Ayodele on his chest and walked to the ring alongside his entire team in a quiet show of unity. The canvas carried their names too, alongside the words 'My Brother's Keeper'.
His comeback could scarcely have begun in any worse fashion. Just 20 seconds in, a right uppercut from Prenga sent Joshua crashing to the canvas and stunned the arena.
Joshua smiled as he climbed to his feet. Prenga, who arrived with 20 knockouts from his 20 victories but little profile even with boxing's hardcore followers, sensed an opportunity.
Promoter Eddie Hearn barked instructions from ringside, while Joshua stablemate Oleksandr Usyk watched on with a look of concern.
A left uppercut later in the round dumped Joshua on the canvas again. He was still unsteady at the start of the second round and appeared to be there for the taking, but Prenga surprisingly began to box off the back foot and let the Watford fighter off the hook.
Joshua capitalised and using his years of experience - and perhaps the emotion - he drew Prenga on to a jab before uncorking a crushing right hand. More rights followed as Prenga collapsed to the canvas and the referee had seen enough.
This was 35-year-old Prenga's second loss in his career.
It was Joshua's first test against a recognised professional opponent since Daniel Dubois stopped him in September 2024.
His only fight since had come against YouTuber-turned-boxer Jake Paul in December, 10 days before the fatal crash that left him injured.
Joshua passed the Prenga test, but not in the manner anyone expected. It was not the destructive, free-flowing champion who once swept opponents aside.
'Tonight wasn't about Tyson Fury'
After defeating 46-year-old Wach in Pattaya, the question of whether Fury would show up to watch Joshua became a subplot of fight night.
A Fury lookalike briefly fooled reporters when he stepped out of a taxi, while Fury's manager Spencer Brown insisted the 'Gypsy King' would be "there in spirit".
The fight between two of the most recognisable names in British boxing is understood to have been agreed for November.
Neither man is at the peak of his powers, but while the commercial appeal remains strong, Joshua's struggles are likely to leave Fury a clear favourite.
The bout is expected to stream on Netflix. British fans are hoping for a homecoming event, but it is understood Saudi organisers and broadcasters favour a venue in the United States to cater for American audiences.
"We've signed the contract. Everything is done," Hearn said.
"But tonight wasn't about Tyson Fury. It was about the strength Anthony Joshua has shown just to be here.
"No-one knows what he's been through over the last seven months. When he went down in the first round, I thought he'd come back too soon."

title: Residents allowed to return after Cairngorms wildfire evacuation
summary: The fire was declared a major incident on Friday, but that has now been stood down by Police Scotland.
full_text:
Residents allowed to return after Cairngorms wildfire evacuation
- Published
Residents of the village of Nethy Bridge, near the wildfire that has been burning in the Cairngorms, have been told they can return to their homes after being evacuated on Friday night.
The fire was declared a major incident due to a change in weather, but that has now been stood down by Police Scotland.
First Minister John Swinney said the government and emergency services will continue to treat the blaze with the utmost seriousness until the last flames are out.
Locals have criticised the handling of the wildfire, which has been burning for 10 days, saying the move to declare it a major incident came too late and the government had been slow in scaling up their response.
In a statement on Saturday night, Police Scotland said "after an extensive multi-agency response to a large fire within Cairngorms National Park, residents of Nethy Bridge are being advised that they can now return to their properties".
Police Scotland's deputy assistant chief officer, Kenny Barbour, said the decision to stand down the major incident followed a detailed assessment by emergency responders.
He added in a statement: "The extensive work carried out over recent days, including the creation of effective fire breaks, has significantly reduced the risk to nearby communities, allowing evacuated residents to safely return home."
Supt Judy Hill added that the "ongoing multi agency response remains a high priority, with significant partnership resources and volunteers working tirelessly and in challenging circumstances, to support our efforts to extinguish the fires".
Firefighters will continue to maintain a significant operational presence until the incident is safely concluded, with 75 remaining on the ground on Saturday, police said.
At a meeting of the Scottish government's resilience room on Saturday evening, the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service said there had been "good progress" in strengthening fire breaks to protect residential areas and said the number of fire hot spots was reducing.
First Minister John Swinney welcomed the lifting of the evacuation notice but stressed that "the Scottish Government, the emergency services and all relevant authorities will continue to treat this wildfire, as has been the case since its onset, with the utmost seriousness and necessary resources until the last flames are out."
Nethy Bridge residents said there had not been enough communication from the government about the wildfire, and also criticised the time that was taken to declare it a major incident.
Nethy Bridge community council leader Sandy McCook said too many decisions had been "taken from Edinburgh", while local resident John McGlinchey said the evacuation was "just not organised properly".
The Cabinet Secretary for Justice, Neil Gray, said: "Throughout this significant incident, the government and the emergency services have given everything to ensuring that the fire is being addressed."
The fire broke out near the village of Glenmore on Wednesday last week, and led to residents and campsites being evacuated.
It covered about six square kilometres of heather and small trees at its height, with more than 500 firefighters tackling it.
In an update on Saturday morning, Police Scotland said residents in a small area of properties north-west of Dorback Lodge (Lain Thatchan) had also been evacuated as a precaution.
Residents living in the affected areas and those impacted by the spread of smoke, including Aberdeenshire and Moray, have been advised to keep all windows and doors closed.

title: People call me the sex MP but we need to be educating
summary: Samantha Niblett officially launches her "summer of sex" campaign, as her educational bid ramps up.
full_text:
People call me the sex MP but we need to be educating
- Published
When Samantha Niblett launched the Yes Sex Please, We're British! campaign earlier this year, it did not take long for the jokes and criticism to start flying - and for her to be given a new nickname.
"Now in times gone by, being referred to as a 'sex MP' would've been something quite sleazy and seedy. But thankfully, and hopefully, I'm helping to change that," the Labour MP for South Derbyshire says.
The campaign was begun to push education around consent, respect and healthy relationships, with the aim of preventing abuse and violence.
The MP wants to remove the stigma around sex, and says the backlash and ridicule she has received in response to her campaign - including from sections of her own party - is "half the reason" for running it.
A launch event for the campaign, dubbed "summer of sex", was held in London this week and later in autumn, Niblett will display a number of sex toys and sex education aids in Parliament.
The Crime Survey for England and Wales found, for the year ending March 2025, that about 15.9% of people aged 16 or over (7.7 million people) had experienced sexual assault since the age of 16.
Of those, 1.9 million were victims of rape, and 1.8 million of rape victims were females, according to figures published by the Office for National Statistics.
Campaigners have long been calling to improve sex education in England. In 2017, the Local Government Association (LGA) said the lack of sex and relationships education in some of the country's secondary schools was creating a "ticking sexual health time bomb".
Another Labour MP, Alistair Strathern, has been calling for the government to make relationships and sex education mandatory for 16 to 18-year-olds.
He introduced the Relationships and Sex Education (Further Education Sector) Bill to Parliament in June.
That followed a petition by the survivor-led campaign group Make It Mandatory, which called for sex education to be mandated to 18 and gathered more than 106,000 signatures.
Niblett has partnered with sex educator Cindy Gallop, who wants to steer people from pornography as sex education.
In a TED conference, Gallop previously said access to online pornography, combined with a "society that is reluctant to talk about sex", had led to pornography becoming the "default sex education".
Niblett hopes the launch will "silence some critics, or at least make them think again".
Some of those critics Niblett shares the same side of the Commons with. She says earlier this year, she was asked not to do media by some in the Labour administration.
Asked on the BBC's Politics Live programme in April whether he thought the campaign was a good idea, fellow Labour MP Tom Hayes said he commended his colleague for taking it forward.
However, he added: "I represent Bournemouth East, which is a coastal town, and may be used to a bit of seaside racy joking, but I don't think my pensioners want to talk dirty - I think they want to talk defence.
"And for me it's not about a summer of sex, it's about an all-year-round, round-the-clock focus on the cost of living."
Liberal Democrat MP for Frome and East Somerset, Anna Sabine, said while her constituents "might be interested" in the topic, she believed they would "much rather" she was talking about potholes and the cost of living.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch also criticised the campaign during a session of Prime Minister's Questions earlier this year.
Badenoch said: "What are they [Labour] doing?
"They're promoting sex toys in Parliament. It gives a whole new meaning to 'fiddling while Rome burns'."
'It's absolutely political'
"I think if some of my colleagues - who should be some of the most progressive MPs that there are - are finding it amusing, then I look forward to seeing the goodness that will come off the back of the campaign," Niblett says.
And Niblett says while the matter of sex education and destigmatising sex is "absolutely political", it's not party political.
She says: "I would be doing this no matter what party I was sitting in, and I really hope the campaign itself is not diminished because people want to use it as a weapon to make it party political.
"It is absolutely political. There are things that we need to do within the system to offer better sex education and support that can only really happen from the top down from the government."
The MP is calling for "lifelong sex education" and says she hopes to target the Department for Education and the Department of Health and Social Care with her campaign.
The campaign will also aim to raise awareness about life stages such as childbirth, the menopause, stress and erectile dysfunction, as well as other health conditions.
Niblett has also recently become chair of the All-Party Parliamentary Group on Sex and Reproductive Health, allowing her regular contact with experts in the field as well as sexual violence campaigners to help guide her campaign.
The MP told the BBC that talking about sex toys as part of the campaign was not a mistake.
"A significant part of sex between people... is communication and it is pleasure. And one of the ways we can get pleasure is through the use of sex toys.
"Trying to take away the stigma or shame around even talking about them is why the campaign is absolutely talking about sex toys," she says.
Niblett adds people are expected to speak in court about "horrifying things that have happened to them, when we don't openly talk about good sex".
She says: "How can we talk about bad sex if we can't talk about good sex?"
Niblett says she has checked with Parliament's security team ahead of her event there in the autumn, and has confirmed that sex toys are not on the banned items list to bring on to the estate.
She believes while access to pornography was "ruining" experiences of intimacy, "we need something more than just blocking and banning".
"We need to be educating," she says.
Niblett says another reason people needed to talk openly about sex and pleasure was because "it can be used as a weapon".
"When it can be used as a weapon against us, we need to be able to take that weapon off people.
"And women are so frequently on the receiving end of those weapons," she says.
Going forward, she hopes the new Prime Minister Andy Burnham will be supportive of the campaign, including her calls for a ministerial post to be dedicated to the issue of sex education and wellbeing.
The MP added despite initial reluctance, a number of her colleagues on her own Labour backbenches were beginning to come around to supporting the campaign.
Niblett said she believed a lot of minds had "changed already" and added her backbench debate, due to take place in the autumn, had cross-party support.
She said: "An initial giggly response has turned into 'well, this is quite serious isn't it?'"
Niblett says she has also received support from people working within the NHS and the probation service, as well as high-profile figures like actress Emma Thompson.
In a video shared by the MP last month, Thompson said: "I'm backing Samantha and Cindy's campaign for lifelong sex education, which is not party political, but it is critical."
Reflecting on the fallout amid the launch of her "summer of sex" campaign, Niblett says more and more are starting to recognise her for this work.
"It's just been wonderful," she says. "People are now starting to recognise me... it's, 'oh, you're that sex MP, aren't you?'
"I think as it picks up support across the country, you'll probably find more of my colleagues feeling comfortable to put their head above the parapet and talk about it.
"It's really important - that when somebody else tries to grab the microphone and diminish what you're doing - you grab it back."

title: Rental searches for pet friendly properties drop after law change
summary: Agents say some renters wrongly believe permission to have a pet is guaranteed.
full_text:
Rental searches for pet friendly properties drop after law change
- Published
Rightmove searches for rental properties that allow pets have plummeted since law changes gave renters more rights.
Following the introduction of the new rules, pet searches dropped by more than 50% in May and June compared with a year earlier.
Landlords in England cannot unreasonably refuse pets in their properties under changes made in May in the Renters' Rights Act.
But agents say some renters wrongly believe permission to have a pet is guaranteed, and landlords say some homes remain unsuitable for multiple pets or large dogs.
"Landlords must consider requests fairly and cannot unreasonably refuse them, but they can still decline where there is a valid reason," said Megan Eighteen, immediate past president of lettings agents trade body ARLA Propertymark.
She said there was plenty of "potential for misunderstanding", among tenants about pet-friendly properties.
Power shift over pets
The Rightmove data suggests that fewer tenants are proactively filtering for pet-friendly properties when searching for a home. While pets remain the most common searched-for term overall - ahead of gardens, garages and furnishings, the lead at the top is shrinking.
Renter searches for properties that allow pets fell by 54% in May and 52% in June compared with the same months a year earlier, according to the figures shared with the BBC. Falls had accelerated through this year, as the changes got closer and were then introduced.
Marc von Grundherr, director of agency Benham and Reeves, said some tenants have only disclosed a pet after signing their tenancy agreement, while others have been discovered during property inspections.
"The reality is that tenants now understand the balance of power has shifted. Landlords can no longer rely on a blanket 'no pets' policy to deter applications and should instead expect conversations around pet ownership to arise much later in the letting process," he said.
Now, in England, landlords may still be able to refuse a pet if another tenant has an allergy, the property is too small for a large pet or several pets, the pet is illegal, or the landlord is a leaseholder and the freeholder does not allow pets.
Before the rules changed, Eve Williamson had to give up her American Bulldog, Khan, or face eviction from her home - despite having previously had a dog in the property.
The 41-year-old former hairdresser, from London, described the experience as awful, especially as Khan had brought comfort while she gave full-time care to her mum.
"Life can get tough, but pets bring unconditional love," she said. "They're family."
Khan has since been happily re-homed, and Eve said she was delighted with the law change.
Katie Smith, 29, from Swindon, has two cats - Pumpkin and Pippin - in her rental home.
The new mum said the family had shared "wonderful moments" with pets, which would also teach children about life and death.
But she said the choice of places to rent still dropped sharply on property portals when pets were part of the equation.
"Landlords should give them a chance," she said.
Yet, even under the new rules, landlords were finding excuses to refuse potential tenants with pets, according to Russell Hunt, founder of Pets Lets, which matches clients with pet-friendly rentals.
He lives with a Basset Beagle cross, called Biscuit, and his three teenagers, who he jokes are more disruptive than the dog.
He said pet CVs should be used and landlords should consider the circumstances more carefully, such as older dogs being calmer and sleeping more, rather than simply ruling out tenants with large or multiple pets.
Cost to landlords
Representatives for landlords say they understand the importance of companionship that pets offer to tenants, but they can still face costly damage.
"Many landlords have legitimate concerns about the risk that some irresponsible pet owners pose to rental properties, or that some owners may try to keep pets in properties that are not appropriate for animals," said Chris Norris, chief policy officer at the National Residential Landlords Association.
He said that landlords faced issues including:
- No power to compel tenants to take out insurance 
- No legal right to request an additional deposit 
- A burden of costs should a pet cause damage to a property 
Lesley Horton, the UK's chief property ombudsman said that landlords should not be levying pet surcharges as this fell outside permitted fees for issues such as late payments or lost key replacements.
However, a landlord could make deductions from the tenancy deposit at the end of the tenancy for proven pet-related damage.
