title: Losing my leg has elevated my life, says world champion surfer
summary: Llywelyn Williams says anything is possible with any kind of disability.
full_text:
Losing my leg has elevated my life, says world champion surfer
- Published
Four-time world champion adaptive surfer Llywelyn Williams says losing his leg as a teenager elevated his life.
Surfing played a pivotal role in his recovery and in the years since losing a leg after being hit by a car in 2011.
It had been a passion of the then 16-year-old prior to the accident - and it was not going to stop him despite being severely injured while out skateboarding.
In fact, he recalled coming around from a coma in hospital amid a dream that a surfboard came between him and a bright light "like you see in the movies".
"It wasn't my time," said Williams, from Abersoch, Gwynedd.
A friend asked him what he wanted to do while he lay in his hospital bed; he wanted to get back in the water - and go surfing in Australia.
"The rehab was to drive myself to get back into the ocean," said Williams, known as Sponge by friends.
"As soon as I got back in the ocean, I felt like I was born again.
"When the board and you connect perfect on the wave, it just feels like you're flying."
His mother, Eirian Parry, described the "beautiful moment" his friends carried him into the sea as he continued his recovery following the amputation.
But she still recalled with visible emotion the time she and Williams' father faced up to a "nightmare" - when doctors asked them to sign a consent form to amputate their son's right leg.
David Williams told BBC documentary Our Lives: Beyond the Waves it was the hardest decision of his life "but it was the only way to save" his son's life.
"To think he was nearly dead on the side of the road when the accident happened... to being the world champion," he said.
"Once he got his first wave back, there was no stopping him."
His father can also remember tough times early into his son's recovery, one in which he told him he had to be strong while at a low point, and then took himself off and cried in the room next to his son.
"The way my parents have brought me up is you've just got to get on with it so, yeah, I had one leg and that was it," said Williams.
He works as a digger driver in the family construction business when not surfing.
"I've learned how to do everything with one leg, except to be able to use a wheelbarrow," said Williams with a wry smile.
"When I turned 18 I wheelchaired my way into the kitchen and said we're heading off to Australia.
"We did a year out there travelling around the coast surfing, living in a camper van.
"To be able to go back there now every year for a competition is just brilliant."
In March, he won the 2026 Bright Sky Australian Pro Adaptive Surfing Championship as the kneeling champion and proudly held the Welsh flag aloft on the beach at Byron Bay, New South Wales.
And he was third in the North Shore Prosthetics Hawaiian Surfing Championships in May.
He self funds participation in surfing competitions and has been thankful for his supporters close to home.
Williams has also been lobbying with others for his sport to be included in a future Paralympics Games.
"Surfing has been a huge part of my recovery and the adaptive surfing community has helped me so much," he said.
"Disability for me has elevated my life - anything is possible if you have any kind of disability."
Our Lives: Beyond the Waves
After losing his leg as a teenager, surfer Llywelyn Williams became a four-times para surfing world champion. Now he’s on top of the adaptive surfing world, the challenge is to stay there.

title: 'South Asian programmes helped us settle into our new lives'
summary: Early South Asian programming included music and practical tips to settle into British life.
full_text:
'South Asian programmes helped us settle into our new lives'
- Published
For the first generation of South Asian migrants to the UK, dedicated radio and television broadcasts by the BBC were a lifeline.
As well as lighter content such as music, the early output included practical advice to help new arrivals settle into their lives in areas such as West Yorkshire, where many South Asian families were attracted by jobs in the textile industry.
Sixty years on, three generations have shared their memories of South Asian programming and spoken about how it shaped them.
When Nirmala Rani arrived in the Leeds suburb of Hyde Park in 1979, life felt quiet and unfamiliar. She was a Punjabi speaker from India and knew few people in England.
Aged 17, Nirmala had come to Leeds to join her husband, whose family had already settled there. Like many South Asian families then, she followed relatives who had moved first to build a new life.
"When a letter came from home, we'd read it 10 times."
With no telephone and no relatives nearby, each letter was a lifeline.
She was adjusting to a new country, new culture, and a loneliness that came from being far from the sounds and language she understood.
The BBC had already begun making programmes for South Asian audiences. One of the first, 'Apna Hi Ghar Samajhiye' (Make Yourself at Home), offered language lessons, music and advice.
By the late 1960s, a magazine programme for South Asian viewers, 'Nai Zindagi Naya Jeevan', had become a weekend fixture.
"We'd wait the whole week to hear one Hindi song," Nirmala says. "Music was food for our souls."
Sunday mornings became something to look forward to. Families gathered around the television with homemade food.
"We'd make chole puri or aloo tikki. It felt nice, everybody sat enjoying together.
"It got rid of the loneliness."
Those same programmes meant just as much to Krishna Devi, who arrived in 1967 and lived in Harehills, another inner-city neighbourhood in Leeds.
Krishna was also just 17 when she came from India, joining her husband and his family.
"It wasn't easy," Krishna says. "We didn't understand English and they didn't understand Punjabi."
One programme helped new arrivals learn the basics: 'Look, Listen and Speak', a BBC English learning series widely used at that time.
"They used to teach us word by word. They taught us how to cross the road. Look left, right."
Even simple tasks could feel unfamiliar.
"When I went to the shops, I didn't know how much things cost. I'd put the money out on my hand and let the shopkeeper take however much it was."
Like Nirmala, the programme she looked forward to most was Nai Zindagi Naya Jeevan.
"There was one Hindi song in that half hour. We waited for it."
Asked why those songs mattered so much, her answer is simple.
"Because it was our language. That half hour made us forget everything else."
Her Sundays followed a familiar pattern: chai, parathas and three generations gathered around a television.
Experiences like Krishna's were shared in living rooms across the country, but inside the BBC, broadcaster and Asian Network pioneer Anita Bhalla was pushing for something more than comfort.
She wanted representation, and a voice.
"When I started, we didn't exist," she says. "There was nobody like me, except in the specialist programmes."
Those early shows mattered because they were the only place migrant families could see or hear anything familiar.
"There was nothing else where people could connect with home, with language, culture, anything."
She later helped shape the early Asian Network in the late 1980s.
"We were no longer new arrivals. We were integrated communities. So, what was our voice? That's what we were trying to find."
She pushed for South Asians not just on screen, but behind it.
"Where were the people behind the scenes? That's where the real power was."
Reflecting on young South Asians entering the industry today, she says: "I hope their ambitions aren't capped. They should be everywhere."
For Yasmin Shabir, who grew up in the Leeds suburb of Armley in the 1990s, programmes like 'Network East' and 'Goodness Gracious Me' helped a new generation of British Asians see themselves on screen.
Raised in a Pakistani household, she remembers these programmes as a weekly link to the culture her parents had grown up with.
"Those programmes were our only way of actually finding out what was going on in Bollywood and the entertainment world.
"Seeing Salman Khan on the BBC was surreal. We were like, 'Wow, how did they get him?' "
But it was 'Goodness Gracious Me' that resonated most.
"The competitive aunties comparing their children, 'my son's doing this...well, my son's doing that'
"We could relate to the characters. It felt like real life.
"They'd say a word in Hindi and I'd think, 'I know that word.'
"It felt like it was made for us. They brought a bit of flavour to life."
By the early 2000s, British Asian culture was breaking into the mainstream.
In the middle of that shift was Bobby Friction, who now presents on BBC Asian Network.
"The revolutions of the 1990s paved the way for the riches of the early noughties," he remembers.
" 'Goodness Gracious Me', for us, was monumental - that specific British Desi humour was on national TV."
Seeing members of the cast who were from the same parts of London as he was felt, he says, "like the revolution wasn't just in my head, it was happening across the country".
"In 2002, Radio 1 decided to do a South Asian music show, and Nihal Arthanayake and I were chosen to present it.
"My ambition since the age of 15 was to be on Radio 1 playing South Asian music."
That same year, Asian Network went national, and Desi DNA launched soon after.
"Suddenly you're in this new era which has already started when the other era hasn't even finished yet.
"At that time, if you were young and South Asian just coming of age, it was very, very different compared to even 10 years before."
For millennials like Tasmiyah Manan from Oakwood in north Leeds, South Asian broadcasting didn't just entertain; it shaped how she understood herself.
She remembers watching Network East Late, Desi DNA and tuning into Asian Network as teenager, long before streaming and TikTok reshaped how music travelled.
"It was the main station playing the music I grew up listening to. I connected to it, the songs, the language, the artists."
Seeing presenter Noreen Khan on air inspired her.
"She's been a staple in my life. Seeing her in the media inspired me to want to go into the media."
She loved the fusion artists like Jay Sean blending R&B, Punjabi, Hindi and English into something that felt exactly like her life.
"I was born in England, I'm British Pakistani, I live my life with fusion. Those artists sounded like us."
Comedy mattered too. Shows like 'The Kumars at No. 42' reflected her world.
"The paratha smoke filling the kitchen, the brutally honest elders, that was us.
"When I see someone like Anita Rani in the media, it makes me feel seen.
"It means we've finally made it to the mainstream."
"If they can do it, I can. It's representation. It's connection. It's my identity."
When Arzu Dutta was growing up in Castleford in the 2000s, representation still felt limited.
Now a BBC Look North reporter and presenter on Radio Leeds, she can see how far things have changed.
She watched Indian entertainment channels at home, but it was the BBC that quietly shaped her British identity, especially the moments she shared with her dad before school.
"My dad would make chai, and we'd sit and watch the news, and watch Naga Munchetty presenting.
"It forms your subconscious of who you are and how you view yourself and the heights you can reach."
Today, she says British Asian identity feels more defined.
"We are at a place where the hyphen between British and Asian is really important.
"As long as South Asian people exist, South Asian broadcasting will matter because you can relate to it.
"I don't walk around thinking, 'I'm Indian.' I just am."

title: 'Antisemitism felt relentless' - Jewish students on life at UK universities
summary: Some students said they are having to hide their Jewish identity, fearing physical and verbal abuse.
full_text:
'Antisemitism felt relentless' - Jewish students on life at UK universities
- Published
Some Jewish students have said they feel antisemitism has become "normalised" at UK universities and they routinely hide signs of their identity for fear of abuse.
Students at more than 10 universities in England and Wales told the BBC they had faced hostility, and warned of a "culture of antisemitism" on campuses.
A report into the issue by the Union of Jewish students in March 2026 called for new enforceable standards for how universities investigate and punish hate crime.
Universities UK, which represents more than 140 higher education institutions, said universities were working to improve support, reporting and campus safety for Jewish students.
Cardiff University student Oliver, 21, said being Jewish had always been a central part of his identity.
He described his first week at the university in 2023 as "terrifying", because it had coincided with the 7 October attacks when Hamas militants attacked Israel, killing about 1,200 people and taking hundreds hostage.
Israel responded to the attack by launching a military campaign in Gaza, in which it is estimated more than 70,000 Palestinians have died.
Like many campuses across the UK, Cardiff University has seen pro-Palestine protests in recent years and Oliver said he believed some behaviour he witnessed crossed the line from criticism of Israel into antisemitism.
Holding Jewish people responsible for the actions of the Israeli government is a form of antisemitism, according to the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance.
"That first year was absolutely terrifying," he said.
"You go home and think, 'do I carry on? Do I try to go to the next day?'"
Oliver said he stopped speaking Hebrew outside his home, and hid his Star of David pendant when on campus.
Over the following three years, Oliver said the antisemitic abuse he experienced at university became "relentless".
"I've been in clubs [or] just wandering around the uni and you hear these conversations and you see pamphlets being handed around where it's literally saying that your belief and your history is fake," he said.
"I've been at house parties where, when someone's found out I'm Jewish they started calling me Netanyahu behind my back.
"Like you found out my religion and you've decided I'm a bad person."
Oliver said when he had reported antisemitic incidents that had happened to him and others, he had felt they had been often "swept under the rug" by the university.
Although he said some positive action had been taken, he feels more needs to be done.
Cardiff University said it was sorry that "any student felt unsafe" on campus and that it adopts a "zero-tolerance approach to harassment and discrimination of all kinds".
It said there was no place for antisemitism or hatred at the university and they have "robust procedures" in place for investigating allegations of antisemitism. Where it is found, the university said appropriate action would be taken.
It said it had reached out to the university's Jewish Society and reminded students to report incidents to them.
'Hiding their identity'
Oliver is not alone in feeling this way.
There are about 9,000 Jewish students in the UK and reported antisemitic incidents on UK campuses rose by more than 400%, from 53 in the 2022-23 academic year, to 272 in 2023-24, according to the Community Security Trust, which monitors antisemitism in the UK.
Universities UK acknowledged antisemitism is a growing challenge.
Its chief executive, Vivienne Stern, said her organisation was committed to tackling campus antisemitism and was actively working with Jewish students to bring about change.
"I think that Jewish students should be able to wear signs that they are Jewish," she said.
"They should be able to wear their Star of David necklace or their kippah, and they should be able to celebrate Jewish life."
Daniel, the incoming Jewish Society vice-president at Manchester University, said Jewish students in the city had started "hiding their identity" after the 7 October attacks and later the Heaton Park attack in October 2025, when two Jewish people were killed after a car was driven into pedestrians outside a synagogue.
He said antisemitic slogans and swastikas had been daubed on walls and a swastika drawn on a fridge at a house party after partygoers had discovered the host was Jewish.
Daniel said he was aware a Jewish student wearing a kippah had also been warned by staff not to enter an academic building during protests for fear of their safety.
"To be Jewish at university is to have an identity that is inherently politicised by everyone around you," he said.
"That becomes very exhausting because it's a very difficult place to navigate."
A University of Manchester spokesperson said previous incidents of offensive graffiti on campus were removed promptly, with involvement from police.
They said the unversity took antisemitism "extremely seriously" and investigated it, and that the university has worked closely with civic and faith leaders to promote dialogue and understanding between communities.
They added: "We are working with Jewish students, staff and community representatives to strengthen our response to antisemitism.
"There is however more to do, and we are working with the Antisemitism Policy Trust and other universities to share learning, identify effective practice and strengthen our collective response to antisemitism."
The president of Swansea University's Jewish Society said she had to alert local counter-terrorism officers when organising routine activities for the society.
"I don't think anyone running, say, the Manga [Japanese comic books] Society has to consider whether there's a hate crime risk from having a stall," said Aviva.
"I'm a 20-year-old just going about university life. Getting calls from the police to tell me there isn't a terrorism risk isn't a normal experience."
Swansea University said it supports students through dedicated wellbeing, academic and faith services, and is maintaining a zero-tolerance approach to harassment and discrimination.
A recent survey, external of 1,000 students commissioned by the Union of Jewish Students, conducted by JL Partners between January and February 2026, said Jewish students were being "isolated by their peers" because of the Israel-Palestine conflict.
The poll suggested "apathy" towards antisemitism, with one in four (25%) students saying they did not care "very much" or "at all" if students are able to be open about their Jewish identity.
Lloyd said he felt vulnerable for the first time after he had moved to Bangor University last year and witnessed students chanting "you're a Jew, Jew, Jew" at another student.
Lloyd said it was handled "really well" when he raised it with the society responsible.
But he said incidents like this could leave Jewish students feeling unsure about how and when to challenge antisemitic behaviour.
"I'm lucky. I'm a big guy, and I don't feel particularly scared for my physical safety," he said.
"[But] it's enough to make me very hesitant, most of the time, to say that I'm Jewish."
Bangor University said it had a zero-tolerance approach to harassment and discrimination, and any formal complaints would be thoroughly investigated.
Oliver has now graduated from university and said that, in his final year, he started wearing his Star of David again.
"I deserve to be here, I've earned my place, and I'm going to get the degree I've earned."

title: Norris and McLaren almost perfect as Ferrari flounder in Hungary
summary: Lando Norris' first grand prix win of 2026 was a long time coming as the mistakes piled up for Ferrari in Hungary, writes Andrew Benson.
full_text:
Norris and McLaren almost perfect as Ferrari flounder
- Published
Lando Norris ended the first half of the Formula 1 season with a victory in the Hungarian Grand Prix that he described as "one of my best performances".
It was a drive that had been a long time coming, after a difficult start to the season for the reigning world champion and his McLaren team.
But when McLaren finally gave him a car of the performance level he had become used to in the past season and a half, he more than made the most of it.
While Ferrari, the pre-race favourites, floundered and made, in the words of their team boss Frederic Vasseur "too many mistakes", Norris and McLaren were almost perfect.
Even in the context of Kimi Antonelli's stellar start to the season for Mercedes, this was one of the most impressive and convincing victories of the season.
Norris' one mistake was on the first lap. He converted his pole position into a lead at the first corner, only to misjudge the grip available at Turn Two, slide wide, and gift his position to team-mate Oscar Piastri.
It looked to have been a potentially fatal error to his victory hopes on a track where overtaking is all but impossible between evenly matched cars on similar strategies, but Norris stayed calm.
Seeing he could easily keep pace with Piastri despite being in the dirty air, he said he always believed the win was on.
"It wasn't my finest Turn Two," Norris said, "but after that, seeing what my pace was like and I was just better in every sense, in terms of degradation and pace, I was convinced I could still win the race."
Trapped, Norris begged for a different strategy to give himself a chance of victory, and eventually circumstances presented it to him.
Around half-distance. McLaren pitted Piastri to cover off Lewis Hamilton's Ferrari, which had just stopped for fresh tyres. That gave Norris clean air and he set a blistering pace.
Piastri might still have held the lead, but for a collision with Carlos Sainz as he lapped his Williams. The Australian was angry after Norris came out ahead from his stop a few laps later - but at the Spaniard, not McLaren.
"The fact I could keep up with Oscar on this kind of track, where it's impossible to follow and impossible to overtake, I was within 0.8 seconds or something for, I don't know, almost 40 laps, the fact I could do this is what gave me confidence that I'd win the race no matter what, whether he boxed early or late or whatever," Norris said.
"The pace advantage I had was huge today. But I don't know why. The cars are identical, and I've just been feeling very strong lately.
"I've worked on many areas from last year. I feel much more confident lately with how to extract performance, and I've worked a lot with my engineers to understand this car because it's certainly not an easy car to understand and figure out how to drive on the limit consistently.
"So, why? Just hard work. Hard work from my engineers and from myself to improve me as a driver and improve my driving. That is the answer."
- Norris wins his first grand prix of year in Hungary - Published7 hours ago
 
- Complete weekend for Norris but poor result for Sainz - driver ratings - Published6 hours ago
 
Norris 'more in control of his emotions'
Norris believes he is driving better this season than he did in the first half of his championship year in 2025.
Last year, he was struggling for feeling from the McLaren.
Like all his rivals, he does not like this new generation of cars as much as the last - especially their engines and the need for so much energy management, and the way they have compromised the driving experience.
But he has gelled with them, while Piastri - so strong in the first half of last season - is struggling.
Team principal Andrea Stella says this is a continuation of the trajectory Norris has been on since a lot of self-assessment led to his strong second half of last year, and eventually the title.
"Lando is much more confident. He's much more aware of his tools that he has in his driving, how to deploy these tools. And I think he's also, let me say, more in control of his emotions," Stella said.
"Because today, when he was behind Oscar, he said a couple of times that he had pace in hand, but he didn't get overly frustrated. And the fact that he wasn't overly frustrated, I think, then allowed him to use the pace at the right time and lead him to the victory. We've seen a great trajectory of development for Lando."
This performance came after a major upgrade to the McLaren car, and there is another to come at the next race, the Dutch Grand Prix after F1's four-week summer break.
Norris' win moves him up to 98 points behind Antonelli, but he cautioned against expectations of a charge up to the top of the championship of the kind Max Verstappen and Red Bull mounted against him and McLaren last year.
"I'm just happy with today," Norris said. "It doesn't mean if I'm quick here, we're going to be quick everywhere.
"One thing I've learned for sure is just to have no expectations of the future and just to work in the present. I think that's the way we've been doing everything as a team.
"That's why we're back on top today: just working hard on ourselves as individuals and also as a team.
"Of course, I'm optimistic for the future and I think we can win more races, but we have good competition and there are still plenty of races I'm not confident in because the car is not to the standard that it needs to be in certain areas."
Piastri angry with Sainz over collision
During the race, it appeared as if Piastri's anger over the radio might have been partly directed at the off-set strategy that led to Norris passing him for the lead.
In fact, he was instead furious with Sainz.
"The timing of my stop was fine," he said. "We wanted to cover off Hamilton, which was perfectly normal. Without getting crashed into, I would have been ahead of Lando still.
"In the moment, I was incredibly annoyed. In fact, annoyed is not the word I would use, but there was a multitude that I would, with Carlos. And, yeah, then obviously, when Lando came out ahead, I knew I had no pace to go and attack him.
"I knew my chances of winning the race were done from there."
Discussing the collision with Sainz, Piastri added: "I don't really care if he didn't see me. The fact that he didn't and no-one told him, or there was a lack of complete awareness, is unacceptable.
"He's quite critical of others, and others have given him some stick before for being frustrating on track."
He was not at all mollified by a problem with the GPS system that shows teams where all the cars are on track.
Sainz said he had "no idea I was trying to get lapped", he "didn't expect" Piastri to be there, and it was "impossible to avoid it".
For Piastri, it was academic in the end, a gearbox failure sending him into retirement and denying McLaren a one-two.
'Too many mistakes' from Ferrari
As for Ferrari, they appeared to have the fastest car in Hungary, but underperformed in qualifying. Then Hamilton, after qualifying second, was dropped to fifth on the grid with a penalty for impeding Piastri.
Norris will have been worried about Charles Leclerc starting alongside him on the front row. But instead of challenging Norris, Leclerc lost out to Piastri, Verstappen and Hamilton.
The seven-time champion got ahead of Verstappen in the first pit stops - only to be overtaken again the next time around, the Dutchman making a brilliant move at Turn One that caught Hamilton napping.
A penalty for pit-lane speeding cost Hamilton a further five seconds, and left him behind Leclerc at the end, the Ferraris finishing fourth and fifth.
Hamilton, who remains second in the championship, 50 points behind Antonelli, said "you can't make these kind of mistakes if you want to challenge for a title".

title: Trump’s border czar probes possible vetting failures after ICE shooting
summary: ICE officer under review for alleged mental health struggles, violent behavior amid deadly shooting case in Maine.
full_text:
Trump’s border czar probes possible vetting failures after ICE shooting
ICE officer under review for alleged mental health struggles, violent behavior amid deadly shooting case in Maine.
United States President Donald Trump’s border czar says the vetting of an immigration officer involved in the deadly shooting of a Colombian native in Maine is under internal review after the officer’s relatives revealed to The Associated Press that he had a history of serious mental health struggles and violent behaviour.
Tom Homan said on Sunday that if the allegations against the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer are true, “I don’t think he should ever have cleared vetting.”
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items- list 1 of 3Sons of immigrant killed by ICE in Texas share grief, demand accountability
- list 2 of 3Protests continue in Houston over ICE killing of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo
- list 3 of 3US court affirms release of pro-Palestine scholar as legal battle continues
“There’s several things under review,” Homan said on CNN about the officer, Army veteran David Brouillette. “The training is under review. I know this specific case, as far as the vetting, is under review by the internal affairs section.”
Questions about the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) rush to hire, train and deploy thousands of new ICE officers to carry out Trump’s immigration crackdown have come into stark focus after back-to-back deadly shootings of immigrants in Maine and Houston.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin ordered a pause in vehicle stops after the Maine shooting, but Trump almost immediately reversed course and insisted the stops resume as a necessary tool in his campaign to round up and deport immigrants without current legal status.
DHS did not immediately respond on Sunday to a request for comment about the internal review.
ICE mandates body cameras during vehicle stops
Homan said that “changes have been made” and that acting ICE director David Venturella has issued a new directive that body cameras must be in use if officers make a vehicle stop.
“Right now, on all vehicle stops, there’s at least one body camera on site to record the entire event,” he said.
He said Venturella “sent an instruction out that he wants at least one body camera on those vehicle stops, so we have everything on video”.
It is unclear if the steps the department is taking will be enough to quell the concerns coming from certain Congress lawmakers over DHS training and tactics as it tries to reach Trump’s mass deportation goals.
Lawmakers push for answers
Lawmakers from both parties have raised concerns.
Democrats pressed ICE officials during a closed-door briefing for the House of Representatives Homeland Security Committee last week, leaving some with more questions than answers.
Lawmakers were told during the briefing that there have been 56 complaints of excessive force against ICE officers – 32 were cleared, and one was referred for disciplinary action.
No discipline had yet been handed out, the lawmakers said they were told. The rest of the incidents are still under investigation.
Meanwhile, Republican Senator Susan Collins of Maine, chair of the powerful Senate Appropriations Committee, has pushed for the use of body cameras and ensured funding for the effort. She had said it was “extremely unfortunate” that the officer involved in the shooting in her home state was not using a camera.

full_text:
Advertisement
How Trump’s Iran ‘own goal’ is hitting long-term US strategy to contain Chinese influence
An Indian-backed port long seen as a counterweight to Beijing is now caught in the crossfire of the US war against Iran
3-MIN READ3-MIN
The United States has spent decades trying to blunt China’s strategic rise. Yet in the Middle East, sanctions and the war against Iran are now dismantling one of the few assets built to constrain Beijing’s influence in the region.
The Iranian port of Chabahar has received strong backing from India, which hoped it would gain both a trade corridor into Afghanistan and Central Asia that bypassed Pakistan and a strategic counterweight to the Chinese-operated Pakistani port of Gwadar.
Both Washington and New Delhi have long feared that Gwadar – the key element of the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) – could give the Chinese navy a logistics hub and intelligence window close to the Strait of Hormuz.
Successive US administrations recognised Chabahar’s value in helping to counter that risk and quietly granted sanctions waivers that allowed the Gulf of Oman port to continue operating even as Washington turned up the heat on Iran.
The core Indian commitment to the port terminal stood at US$120 million – a modest sum compared with the estimated US$62 billion poured into the CPEC, a flagship project for Beijing’s Belt and Road Initiative.
But the calculation has shifted under US President Donald Trump, who has adopted a more conciliatory tone towards China. Meanwhile, he has shown markedly less enthusiasm for the Quad – a security partnership between the US, India, Australia and Japan – even to the extent of causing a summit to be cancelled last year when he refused to travel to India for the event.

title: AusAlert test: what time will national emergency warning siren sound on phones in Australia today? Here’s what to know
summary:
National emergency test alert will be sent to all compatible mobile devices on 27 July, with domestic violence advocates advising how to turn off safe phones

  • Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Virtually every phone in the country will blare an emergency siren at 2pm AEST on Monday 27 July as part of the first Australia-wide test of a new national warning system called AusAlert.

Most phones, and some smartwatches and tablets, will receive a pop-up notification and an alert sound that cannot be silenced – even if your device is on “do not disturb” or silent mode.

Continue reading...
full_text:
Virtually every phone in the country will blare an emergency siren at 2pm AEST on Monday 27 July as part of the first Australia-wide test of a new national warning system called AusAlert.
Most phones, and some smartwatches and tablets, will receive a pop-up notification and an alert sound that cannot be silenced – even if your device is on “do not disturb” or silent mode.
What is AusAlert? AusAlert is Australia’s new national warning system, which will send emergency messages to mobile devices during local and widespread disasters.
Authorities currently use SMS texts to alert people about safety information. The new system will instead send a mass broadcast via mobile phone towers, with an alert popping up on devices, similar to a phone notification.
It will launch nationally in October, months after the national alert test.
What will happen during the national test? “On Monday 27 July 2026, a test alert will be sent to all mobile devices in Australia. This includes most phones, and some smart watches and tablets,” the National Emergency Management Agency (Nema) advises.
Users will hear a siren and see a pop-up notification on their phone, which will look different depending on the device, but with text including “TEST MESSAGE” and “NO ACTION IS REQUIRED”.
Video of the AusAlert test “What people should expect to hear is a siren that will last for about 10 seconds,” said Pat Hetherington, the interim coordinator general at Nema.
He said it would be “loud enough to get people’s attention” but quieter than a fire alarm.
“It will be noticeable, but it won’t won’t be too over the top.”
What time is the AusAlert test around Australia? There have been local tests, but Monday will be the first nationwide test, occurring at 2pm AEST, which is:
 
  2pm for New South Wales, Victoria, the ACT, Queensland and Tasmania.
 
 
  1.30pm in the Northern Territory and South Australia.
 
 
  12pm in Western Australia.
 
 Why is the AusAlert emergency warning system test needed? Hetherington said AusAlert came from a recommendation of the royal commission into the 2019-20 black summer bushfires, which called for a nationally consistent warning system.
“The existing system is based on standard SMS capability, and throughout a series of emergencies and disasters, that system has had real latency in terms of people receiving the messages,” he said.
“You [could] get network congestion, text messages may not come through in a timely way … or come through at all, dependent upon who your provider is.”
Kristy McBain, the federal emergency management minister whose electorate of Eden-Monaro was hit by the black summer bushfires, said some people in her area didn’t receive emergency text alerts during that disaster because their phone provider was unavailable.
The new system allows nationwide alerts as well as localised “geofenced” alerts such as for floods or even warnings to boil water in emergency situations.
The emergency services minister, Kristy McBain, says the AusAlert is ‘far superior’ to current warning systems.  Photograph: James Ross/AAPMcBain said AusAlert was a “far superior” system and would reach “more people in a more timely manner” than current warning systems used by state governments. Existing systems will still be used in future, with McBain describing AusAlert as “another tool in the toolkit”.
Will every phone ring or make a sound during the alert test at 2pm AEST? Essentially, yes. Hetherington said phones made after 2019 should receive the alert, but some older phones may not.
The alert will come through on all compatible devices even if you are on a call, or if the phone is on silent. Nema has advice that about 80% of Apple iPhones will ring, and some 16m Android devices.
“The only way to not receive a critical alert is to turn your mobile device off or switch it to ‘airplane mode’,” Nema advised.
The agency said the alert will go to:
 
  iPhone models 11 and up running iOS 26.4 or later.
 
 
  Apple Watch models SE2, SE3, Series 6 and up running watchOS 26.4 or later.
 
 
  Android devices running Android 12 or later.
 
 Older Androids, or those not using iOS or Android “might still receive AusAlerts”, Nema said, but Apple iPads will not.
Hetherington and Nema’s deputy coordinator general, Katarina Carroll, said the agency had engaged with “thousands” of groups including schools, businesses and even funeral associations to warn of the alert test.
They said it was important to run the test during an “ordinary” time of day so people knew what to expect in future.
But noting some people may find it inconvenient to have a loud siren ring alert, such as during an important meeting or a funeral, Hetherington and Carroll said “if you have your phone off an hour before and an hour after [2pm AEST], we’re confident you won’t receive that message”.
Other countries around the world have had problems in testing or using such systems, with alerts delayed or not arriving at all. Nema said it had “learned a lot” from tests around the world and it was well prepared for Monday.
What about ‘safe phones’ for those experiencing domestic and family violence? Domestic and family violence advocates have raised concerns about the risk of the alert exposing “safe phones”, or devices kept hidden for safety reasons by those experiencing violence.
Nema said the agency had engaged with family violence experts about the test, including assisting advocates to disseminate safety information, and posting a safety guide on its website .
Hetherington said phones switched off or on airplane mode would not receive the alert, and said: “The message for safe phones and hidden phones is very much [to switch off for] a 24-hour period.”
Carroll added: “The advice is if there’s anything that’s happening [during the test], have it off for an hour or so. But certainly for domestic and family violence, there’s that broader advice for that extension of time [24 hours].”
Groups such as the Women’s Safety Commissioner, DV Connect and the Council of Single Mothers and their Children have issued safety advisories to this effect.
What do I have to do when I receive the AusAlert? Nothing at all. The test requires no action.
However, Hetherington encouraged Australians to answer a survey or give feedback after the test to help Nema assess the success of the trial and any changes that may be needed.
“People should read the message. But it is a test that doesn’t require people to do anything,” he said.
“We’re obviously interested in hearing if people haven’t received the message.”
When will AusAlert be used for real? Nema suggests the warnings could be used for legitimate hazards such as bushfires, floods, cyclones and earthquakes; serious public safety issues or terrorism; biosecurity incidents; and major public health incidents.
States and territories will be able to send alerts.
“I would expect some states to use it quite a lot, particularly where you want information to get out almost in real time,” Hetherington said.

title: Jacinta Allan expected to face leadership challenge after Victorian Labor factions meet
summary:
Minister says premier ‘not going anywhere’ and describes leaking of Sunday-night meeting as attempt to build momentum for spill

The Victorian Labor premier, Jacinta Allan, is expected to face a leadership challenge when state parliament resumes this week, though supporters insist she is “not going anywhere”.

Just four months out from a state election, factional conveners from Labor’s left and right met on Sunday night to discuss whether Allan still had the support of a majority of the caucus. It is understood the group agreed she did not.

Continue reading...
full_text:
The Victorian Labor premier, Jacinta Allan, is expected to face a leadership challenge when state parliament resumes this week, though supporters insist she is “not going anywhere”.
Just four months out from a state election, factional conveners from Labor’s left and right met on Sunday night to discuss whether Allan still had the support of a majority of the caucus. It is understood the group agreed she did not.
But the pathway to a challenge remains unclear, as Allan’s most likely opponent – the deputy premier, Ben Carroll – has indicated to colleagues he would only run for the leadership if the position were vacant.
One option being floated by the factions on Sunday was for a group of ministers to approach Allan on Monday before a planned cabinet meeting to inform her she had lost the support of her colleagues.
It was their hope that she would stand down before a vote during Tuesday’s caucus meeting, the first day of parliament after the winter break.
But if Allan contested a leadership ballot, the entire Victorian Labor membership would also get a vote in a weeks-long process, thanks to rule changes introduced after the instability of the Rudd-Gillard-Rudd era. The rules have been untested.
One minister close to Allan maintained she was “not going anywhere” and described the leaking of the meeting as an attempt to build momentum for a spill. Another said not all parliamentarians within the left faction were consulted before the meeting and that there was “no uniform position” within the grouping.
“There is no vacancy, no challenger and no consolidated position within the left,” the minister said. “It’s just one big smoke machine.”
The attorney general, Sonya Kilkenny, a key supporter of the premier, said leadership speculation was “idle gossip” earlier on Sunday.
“She has my full support, and this idle gossip doesn’t help Victorians,” Kilkenny said. “It is only hurting Victorians at a time when Victorians need us all to be focused on them, and that is exactly what Jacinta Allan and our Labor government, our team, is doing.”
Allan became premier after the resignation of Daniel Andrews in September 2023.
Momentum had been building for a leadership spill before parliament rose for a winter break in June due to poor polling and Allan’s weak personal approval ratings, rising support for One Nation and concerns about her response to organised crime infiltrating the state’s Big Build, via the construction union.
Allan, who previously served as the minister for transport infrastructure overseeing the Big Build, has rejected growing calls for a royal commission.
But Carroll ruled out a challenge at the time, at an awkward press conference where he looked Allan in the eye and declared he would not challenge her for the leadership.
At the same 15 June press conference, he told reporters: “I’ve got a young daughter at home, and I couldn’t be more proud to make sure she grows up knowing that I supported Jacinta Allan to be a world-class premier and get re-elected in her own right.”
It is understood Carroll, if elected leader, would immediately call for a royal commission, work to resolve the pay dispute between the state government and public school teachers, and attempt to improve the party’s economic credentials and standing with the business community.

title: Former NSW Liberal powerbroker at heart of Icac allegations now living in UK and not expected to appear
summary:
Christian Ellis, a former registered lobbyist, is named in two Independent Commission Against Corruption allegations

  • Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A key figure at the centre of an anti-corruption inquiry involving the New South Wales Liberal party has moved to the UK and is not expected to give evidence during eight weeks of public hearings.

The Independent Commission Against Corruption will start its Operation Rosny hearings on Monday. The first witness will be a hotelier, Michael O’Hara, followed later in the week by a former Liberal staffer, Dylan Whitelaw, and a consultant, Robert Assaf.

Continue reading...
full_text:
A key figure at the centre of an anti-corruption inquiry involving the New South Wales Liberal party has moved to the UK and is not expected to give evidence during eight weeks of public hearings.
The Independent Commission Against Corruption will start its Operation Rosny hearings on Monday. The first witness will be a hotelier, Michael O’Hara, followed later in the week by a former Liberal staffer, Dylan Whitelaw, and a consultant, Robert Assaf.
O’Hara and Assaf are among 10 individuals Icac has said it is investigating. Whitelaw is not named in the Icac allegations.
Christian Ellis, a former registered lobbyist and Liberal powerbroker who once received a glowing endorsement from the federal opposition leader, Angus Taylor, is named in two Icac allegations but is not expected to appear.
A 2023 parliamentary inquiry preceded Icac’s current examination of “possible offences under the Electoral Funding Act”. Since that parliamentary inquiry, Ellis has moved to the UK, Guardian Australia can reveal.
Icac is investigating several allegations, firstly that Liberal figures, including Ellis and Assaf, “solicited or accepted” donations, including from prohibited donors, in amounts which were undeclared or exceeded caps, to recruit or renew members to the party – a practice known as “branch stacking”.
The corruption watchdog is examining a second allegation that between 2020 and 2023, the fugitive property developer Jean Nassif and his company, Toplace, made prohibited donations solicited or accepted by Liberals, including Ellis, “in exchange for the pursuit of outcomes sought by Mr Nassif”.
The 2023 parliamentary inquiry was prompted by allegations made in a 2022 speech under parliamentary privilege by the Liberal MP Ray Williams that Nassif had met Ellis and other senior Liberals, who were paid significant funds to arrange for new councillors to be elected to the Hills Shire council.
Ellis did not appear at the 2023 inquiry because he could not be served with summons after multiple attempts.
The inquiry’s final report recommended that Ellis be called before any future inquiry to give evidence.
Ellis, a director and shareholder of the former registered lobbying firm Beckington, whose clients included Toplace, was elected to the NSW Liberal state executive in 2019, following which he stepped down as director in favour of his wife.
In 2022, Taylor wrote an endorsement of Ellis for a position on the NSW party’s state council, saying “our party will do well to have people like Christian elected to positions of state council”. Taylor, now the federal Liberal leader, is not accused of any wrongdoing.
Ellis declined to comment when asked about the Icac allegations and his move overseas.
